Information and complaint of Thos. Naylor, minister in the 
chief church of Newceastle-wpon-Tyne, to the Bishop of Dur- 
ham. There was a public meeting on the Lst of November in 
Barber Surgeons’ Hall, Newcastle, of 500 of the congregation 
of Kaints, headed and led by Gilpin, notoriously known to be 
disaffected to Government, who caused the 149th Psalm in 
meter to be sung, containing the Lnes— 

To bind their stately kings in chains, 
Their lords in iron bands, 
To execute on them the doom 
That written is before, 
This honour all his Saints shall have, 
Praise ye the Lord therefore. 
thus giving notice to all others in the town and country what 
their seditious designs wre, in applying this Psalm to them- 
selves. Gilpin much molested Westmoreland and Cumberland, 
and was so prosecuted by Sir Philip Musgraves legal proceed- 
ings that he made him leave the country, and, fearing he might 
do as much mischief in Newcastle, gave notice thereof, that 
heed might be taken of him, and his evil designs prevented. 
There are 3 others named, Durant, Leaver, and Pringle, 
who join themselves together, and keep great assemblies of 
people in a house at Newcastle. The Mayor has forbidden 
them all to meet any more at so public a place as Surgeons’ 
Hall, but I hear of no further proceedings being taken.— 
16 Nov. 1668. [Lbid. No. 1461.]

Rich. Bower to Williamson. Eight ships have sailed with red 
herrings, lead, and tar for the Straits. The town never had such 
great adventures thither before, 40 sail having gone or going on their 
own account. Six Yarmouth ships have arrived from Rotterdam. 

It is reported that George England has got clear of being sheriff 
for the county, by means of Sir Wm. Doyley, who could do no less, 
Mr. England being a grand instrument to get Sir William burgess 
for Yarmouth. I cannot imagine what excuse can be made, as he has 
an estate worth 30,000/. or 40,000/., and is a healthful, stirring man. 
There are in other corporations, as well as this, gentlemen who have 
in the late troublesome times, by a fair compliance, got great estates, 
whilst the loyal party have been ruined; men of mean extract, and 
as meanly bred, who deride the gentry, and will no ways concern 
themselves with public business that may create them either charge 
or trouble. [Jbid. No. 159.]

Sir Hen. Smith to Williamson, I write from gratitude, not ambi- 
tion, to give an account of my charge. Mr. Clifford, since his entrance 
into the Academy, has done nothing unworthy of a noble father, is 
pure from the vices of the age, of good disposition, and very docile ; 
he loses daily his rustic shyness. His backwardness is the fault of 
his former tutor, who soothed when he should have chastised him, 
so that the sparkle of intellect being now laid to sleep, it will 
require Herculean force to awaken it. I will spare no industry 
therein. [Latin. Ibid. No. 167.]

Rich. Bower to Williamson. I repeat the contents of my letter 

of 9 October as to the proceedings of the Independent party and 
Mr. Bridge. I find that my information was sent to Mr. Bridge 
by a friend at Court, and that James Johnson of Yarmouth has 
received an order to draw up some queries and require our minister, 
Mr. Spendlow, to answer them, with strict charge to be very private 
in it. Spendlow asked me if I had written up anything concerning 
Bridge. I urged him to give me a reason for his asking, and was in- 
formed of the demand from Johnson, who stated the King had read 
the letters concerning Bridge. I told him that there was a puzzle 
in it, and that the order to Johnson must come from some person 
that wished well to Bridge and his party, and therefore advised him 
to decline answering, unless required by authority, or unless 
Johnson would let him see the hand that was set to the order, 
which he refusing, Spendlow refused also, adding that if he gave 
any answer, it would be only confirming what had been stated. 
Johnson replied that then he should not desire it. I believe it was 
Sir Wm. Doyley that wrote to Johnson, as Johnson is his agent ; and 
it is not denied by Bridge’s son-in-law. 
. It is not the first time the people here have been acquainted with 
the contents of my letters, which gives me the report of a turbulent 
person; I have no prejudice against any man for his judgment, 
unless tending to subvert Government, whose commands make in- 
different things lawful or unlawful; I have never been contentious, 
and only state miscarriages because required. I must be sparing 
in things of this nature for the future, but whatever I have written 
for truth, I will make so appear. I desire that Spendlow may be 
required to give his answer to the letter of 9 October. 

There are 20 sail of light colliers passed northward, and a vessel 
has come in from Malaga, bound for Dantzic, upon some London 
merchants’ account. A wreck being espied near the sands, several 
boats went off, and report it to be a Swede of 200 tons, laden with 
clapboard. [14 pages. Ibid. No. 170.] 


Fras. Anderson to Henry Brabant. The fanatics have had a 
public fast, but for what is not known. Gilpin, Durant, Pringle, 
and Leaver were the preachers. It was a business above any 
example I have heard of, and is only in the power of the King and 
his Council. Deputy-lieutenants are much wanted. [Jbid. No. 171.]

to be without one. They are mighty high since you went to

CHARLES II. 79 


Navy Commissioners to the Farmers of Customs. The masters 
of 2 ships, arrived from Scotland with masts for his Majesty, 
complain that interruption has been given in their delivery at 
the yard, upon pretence of customs due. Desire, as such inter- 
ruption will occasion loss by demurrage, that they will suffer 
them to be delivered, assuring them that the delivery shall be of 
no prejudice to them in their receipt of their due, as the same 
shall be made to appear. With note that the messenger 
that carried this letter to the Farmers brought it back, with 
the message that they had let out the customs of Scotch goods; 
that if the lading of the ships is duly entered, and the customs paid, 
their stop shall be removed, but not otherwise. 1 Dec. 1668. 
[S.P. Dom., Car. TI. 249, No. 177.] 


Report by Surveyor Thos. Middleton to the Navy Commissioners, 
of the charge of converting the timber into plank in Aliceholt and 
Whittlewood Forests, and of the carriage. [Lbid. No. 178.] 


Giles Bond to the Navy Commissioners. The Hope galliot has 
returned from the Downs, and is lying at Woolwich to assist in the 
weighing of the wrecks. Desires order for her repair. [Ibid. 
No. 179.] 


M. Wren to Pepys. Sends a letter from Sir Thos. Allin. 
Though dated from Tangiers, it is manifest that it was from Algiers, 
so it is 50 days old; and considering how many more it must be 
before any letter will reach Leghorn, fears he will be past that place 
before orders about his victualling can come thither. Suggests, as 
the surest way, to give Sir Thos. Allin the whole credit he desires at 
Cadiz, with directions, if they come in time, to take in such 
provisions lying at Leghorn as he finds fit, and to make it up 
2 months, by the credit which he shall find ready for him at Cadiz. 
[Zbid. No. 180.]

college, he being chosen by Charles, Earl of Carlisle, going Am- 
bassador Extraordinary to Sweden, to attend him in his embassy, as 
his long travel and experience may be of assistance. [S.P. Dom., 
Entry Book 19, p. 90.]

The Hope of Scarborough has arrived with deals from Norway, 
having been at sea a long time, and forced to throw some of her 
goods overboard through the weather. The Mary, from St. Malo, 
reports that at Jersey and Guernsey, they felt the effects of the 
late earthquake at the same time as St. Malo; they complain of 
the bad trade for drapery, through the great importation of wool 
from Ireland. Other vessels are making into the harbour, and more 
are expected. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 249, No. 183.] 


Rich. Watts to Williamson. The Drake has gone in to be paid. 
A pilot from Flushing reports that there is a very brisk trade there 
with English butter, cheese, corn, and other commodities, which are 
cheaper there than here. Also that one of the greatest bankers has 
broken for many thousand pounds, and made his escape, and 
another was making his, but was secured by the Lords; this trick 
of such breaking was never known there before. [Zbid. No. 184.] 


H. Decry to Rob. Francis. I would write oftener, but fear. you 
have not time to read my ill-composed letters. I beg you, in sealing 
the Gazettes, to put the date of the receipt of letters. [Prench. 
Ibid. No. 185.] 


John Pocock to Hickes. Several vessels have sailed for Portugal 
and France, and others have come in; one from Cherburg reports 
the launching there of a small frigate of 200 tons for the King’s 
use ; also that the French there behave themselves very rudely to 
the English, cutting away their cables and ropes by violence, and 
without satisfaction. Iam informed from St. Malo that a great 
frigate, of 120 guns, has been launched, and that she is so well 
liked that 2 more of the same dimensions are ordered to be put 
upon the stocks. She treads 140 feet by the flower beam, and has 
16 port-holes on a floor. They discourse that the French King will 
have a fleet of 120 sail ready by the spring, that they hope to break 
with the Dutch, and that the tonnage is to be taken off trom the 
English in a short time. [Jbid. No. 186.]

Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. Twenty-three Dutch vessels have 
been forced in by contrary winds. The East India ships that came 
from London, and 2 merchantmen bound for the Straits, are in the 
Downs, but not one King’s ship. Deal castle fired the gun last night 
and this morning. [S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 249, No. 188.] 


Sir Wm. Penn to the Navy Commissioners. The examination of 
the victualler’s accounts,—many whereof were never produced but at 
this juncture of time,—is committed to my charge, just when I daily 
expect to have this office, and join with Sir Denis Gauden in 
carrying on the victualling by a new contract. I think you should 
appoint a person to examine and cast up the papers and accounts 
that have not passed your view. I doubt not that all faithfulness 
and diligence has been used, but as most of it depends upon cast- 
ing, and that of such variety and intricacy as the best of men have 
erred in, any error would in part reflect on me. [2 pages. Ibid. 
No. 189.] 


Wm. Bodham to Thos. Hayter. Particulars of 85 bundles of 
Riga and Quinborough hemp received from Messrs. Doggett and 
Upton, and put on board the Hardercen, to be sent to Chatham, 
17 Jan. 1668. The mistake is not his, the negligence of the 
master and his crew is only to be blamed. [Jbid. No. 190.] 


Wm. Sheldon and 3 other officers [of the dockyard], to the 
Navy Commissioners. Only part of Sir John Shaw’s hemp 
answered in goodness to his contract, but it was a small part indeed ; 
we deny that the entire part, or as much as one draught, was delivered 
suitable to contract, and unmixed with what was worse ; all was 
of 2,3 or 4 sorts. Our omitting to certify the quantity of the 
best upon the bill was not to do the merchant an injury, but for 
several considerations, one being that we did not wish to brand the 
merchant by recording that of 58 tons, only a few cwts. were 
answerable to contract. [Zbid. No. 191.] 


Earl of Anglesey to the Navy Commissioners. I have given order 
to Mr. Fenn to attend you with the best satisfaction that can be 
given ; I desire you, if he has not been, to send for him; as things 
stand, I cannot give personally that satisfaction which I desire for 
the King’s service. [Zbid. No. 192.]

a great Dutch prize in custody; but receiving 2 or 3 guns from 
the Apsom man, she bore away, [Jbid. No. 193.]

the tears of this afflicted old man have often grieved my heart.

CHARLES II. 87 


Thos. Blount to John C , at Sir Mark D’Ognaté’s, London. 
I perceive by a letter from a friend and fellow sufferer in England, 
that some overtures have been made to him, by command of his 
Majesty, for the taking of Granger, and that they have some 
intention of proceeding publicly against him by way of proclama- 
tion, if they had but sufficient descriptions of his person for the 
framing of it. If they proceed this way, they will only frighten 
him from ever being taken. I am sure no person in England is able 
to give a proper description of him, nor of his several haunts, but 
myself; I could take him, but only by ingratiating into him. I 
beg you to acquaint Sir Mark D’Ognaté that if I can have my 
liberty, and be allowed to come to England and discourse with the 
King, the Lord-General, or Lord Arlington, I would give them such 
satisfaction as would make them of my opinion; if set upon the 
work, I doubt not of taking him in a very short time. [S.P. Dom., 
Car. If. 250, No. 1.] 


—— Potticary to Account of various descriptions 
of canvas at St.Malo. If I can serve you or your friends with 
any named, command freely. Endorsed, with memorandum and 
notes of account. [Zbid. No. 2.]

John Clarke to Williamson. A Plymouth ship sailed for the

board perished. A ship from the Canaries and Bordeaux arrived 
with wines and prunes. [Jbid. No. 5.] 


John Clarke to Hickes, To the same effect. [Ibid. No. 6.]

Capt. Silas Taylor to the Navy Commissioners. At the sale of 
the hulk, I publicly declared, before the lighting of the candle, that

Reference to the Judge of the Admiralty of the petition of 
Antonio Basso, late commander of the Abraham’s Sacrifice of 
Genoa. The petitioner sailing with the Duke of York’s passport, 
March 18, 1667, his lading belonging only to Italians and Spaniards, 
his ship was yet seized by the King’s ships, brought into Ireland, 
condemned as prize, and the goods sold at a fifth of their value. 
On appeal of the Republic of Genoa, the King consented that the 
case should be re-heard, and the remaining goods secured, and he 
prays that attestations from merchants and factors abroad may be 
admitted, instead of proofs. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 18, f. 343.] 


Petition of Arthur, Earl of Anglesey, to the King, to know in

miscarriages in the management of the revenue as Treasurer-at-War 
in Ireland ; and that, until better satisfaction, he is not to be trusted 
with the Navy treasure. With answer thereon that the Commis- 
sioners are still sitting on the accounts of Ireland, and that the King

Sir Denis Gauden to the Navy Commissioners. I cannot obtain 
letters of credit for Leghorn and Cadiz, without engaging. to pay 
the like value in London, whether there be occasion for it or not; 
as the merchants cannot draw on their factors whilst those credits 
are in being, lest they should frustrate the credits. I hope no further 
will be expected from me than to provide bills of exchange for 
the supply of the fleet with so much as may fully answer in 
lieu of beer, or what else shall not be sent from hence. If 
Clutterbuck shall supply them at Leghorn, beyond what he has of 
his Majesty’s in store, I shall pay for it in such manner as you direct. 

With note, Oct. 10, that Sir Denis Gauden and Mr. Clutterbuck 
acquainted the Board that an agreement had been come to between 
them, so that the King was to depend on Sir Denis Gauden alone 
for this supply. The terms of their agreement were that Sir Wm. 
Penn should be umpire between them of the price Mr. Clutterbuck 
should receive of Sir Denis Gauden; no mention was made of what 
Gauden was to receive of the King, but the presumption on all sides 
was that it is to be done upon the price of the new contract, though 
it be not sealed. [114 pages. Ibid. No. 45.]

John Dodington to Williamson. I pray that if any reference is 
made on Hart’s petition about incontinency, it may be to Lords 
Arlington, Sandwich, Carlisle, and Holles, but not to any Bishops 
or Churchmen, as that will be to put us in a worse condition 
than we were before. Rather than that should happen, we would 
withdraw the petition. I spoke to Lord Arlington and Sir Thos. 
Littleton, and we settled that affair of Sweden, so I am resolved 
on it, and pray your assistance in it. Endorsed, “Dec. 9, Mr. 
Hart’s pardon.” [Jbid. No. 64.]

Rich. Bower to Williamson. A copy of my letter of 9 Oct.

they were doing, saying, “ What! are you persecuting Paul, and 
will you do this now the King and Council are setting about a 
sufferance?” Upon which Spendlow asked if it were so; he 
replied he had heard so.

the Covenant ; it was never tendered until this order came, and 
now the bailiffs have sent for them to do so, which they obstinately 
deny. Capt. Thos. Ravens, another of the Common Council, who 
kept the greatest conventicles in the town at his own house, is put 
in a great fright. The whole town is much nettled at the order ; 
James Johnson and Rich. Huntingdon have taken coach to wait 
upon Lord Townshend, and will use all endeavours, without doubt, 
to take up the business. Here are several strange persuasions 
used to make the people believe a toleration will be granted, as 
that Mr. Manton, Dr. Bates, and Dr. Jaguer had been with his 
Majesty, to give him thanks for his indulgence, which the 
King took very kindly. I conceive these to be stratagems of their 
own invention, to keep their members from falling off, and to gain 
more disciples. 

Three ships have been cast away to the northward, but a vessel 
coming that way picked up 7 or 8 of their men upon a piece of

the Act which forbids his residing within 5 miles of the town. The 
2 sects act as brethren in trying to subvert the Government. 

After the house here was purged of all the Independent faction 
in 1660-61, Sir Thos. Meadows and Arthur Bacon were chosen 
bailiffs; the Independents’ meeting-place was then in the chancel 
of the church, where some thousands of them met; Sir Thos. 
Meadows put them by, and locked up the doors; they were much 
exasperated, and sought all ways to defame him. The Government 
continued in his hands, and those of his principles, until the end of 
1665, in all which time the laws against Nonconformists were by 
them put in execution, insomuch that there was not a private meet- 
ing but what was by stealth, and if discovered, they were prosecuted ; 
so that a great many of Bridge’s members came to church, and the 
rest durst not open their mouths against the Government, or report 
such notorious lies as now fly about. Had those who followed them 
discharged their duty, all would have been in a happy condition by 
this time, but in 1665 and 1666, the Presbyterians, with the assist- 
ance of the other, got the Government into their hands, and have 


kept it. Then the Nonconformists forsook the Church, and the 


turbulent spirits, who left the town in the time of Sir Thos. 
Meadows, have returned ; their meetings are public, their numbers 
increased, and no notice is taken of it. 

They next send Sam. Shipdham, a member of Bridge’s congrega- 
tion, to the Presbyterians interested in the Government, for charity 
towards the relief of the ejected ministers, which gives the In- 
pendents, upon their so free and general contribution, such satisfac- 
tion, that Bridge is immediately sent for to town, when they flock 
together in great numbers, and meet publicly in the face of autho- 
rity ; they say such'things are winked at under the King’s nose. All 
who oppose them suffer in trade or reputation for it. 

Iam informed that not one half of the Aldermen and Common 
Council have received the sacrament, and that since 1666, several 
have been taken into the House suspected not to have renounced 
the Covenant, as the magistrates would not put them upon it on 
their admission. John Woodroff, the head bailiff, moved for 
omission from the bailiff’s oath of the words, “ That you shall keep 
secret the King’s counsel,’ and “you shall govern by law and 
reason ”; also that All Saints’ Day, Twelfth Day, and the Coronation 
Day, be left off from being Scarlet days. He is the grandee of the 
Presbyterian party, and has much influence, being the only one in 
the town that lets out, money, not only of his own, but of others, 
so that he supplies all men’s occasions when they want, upon good 
security. l am threatened to be spoilt in my trade for giving a 
knowledge of these things; no interest can stand if the party com- 
plies not with them, so I must expect to suffer for what is done. 
[2 pages. S.P. Dom., Car. II. 250, No. 96.]

Levant Company to Sir Dan. Harvey. We congratulate your 
arrival at Smyrna. We do not think it well to press free trade for 
English ships to Alexandria, without Avanias ; the trade is of small 
consequence, giving little vent for the sale of native commodities, 
and the place subject to frequent Avanias and disasters, which we 
find, from sad experience, fall by some pretence on us. 

We renew our request that you will attend to the orders about 
suppression of false moneys, a large quantity being imported by the 
ships; all English ships importing those moneys into Turkey are not 
to be allowed to relade there; the money is to be weighed on ar- 
rival at Smyrna, and the ministers of state informed of the King’s 
dislike to the injury done to his subjects by the use of such moneys ; 
they hinder the import of English goods, which are of much import- 
ance to the Turkish empire. We hope the Earl of Winchelsea will 
not be detained, owing to the Grand Seignior’s absence, but receive 
his dismission from the Caimachan. [S.P. Foreign, Levant Com- 
pany 5, pp. 204-6.] 


Levant Company to the Consul at Smyrna. Complain of the 
continued import of false moneys. Repeat the directions of the 
preceding letter thereon. [Jbid. p. 207.] 


Levant Company to the Consul at Aleppo. Similar directions 
for preventing the further import of false moneys. [Ibid. p. 208.] 


Levant Company to Tho. Dethick and Ephraim Skinner. Ap- 
prove their execution of orders in shipping for Wm. Hedges at 
Constantinople the two cases received from Genoa and Venice. 
[Ibed.]

Warrant to Joseph Williamson, Keeper of Papers for matters of

Thos. Blount to John Crosse, at Sir Mark D’Ognaté’s. I saw 
your letter to Father Felix, and perceive that I am more obliged 
to Sir Mark and you than I am able to requite ; I understand that 
his Majesty has a great desire to take Granger. I blush to think 
that I was ever concerned with so unworthy a person; what is 
past cannot be recalled, but I hope to live better for the future. 
No person in England can take Granger but me, and the know- 
ledge of this makes Granger write to me now I am in prison, and 
clear himself of being the occasion of it, and try to ingratiate him- 


self with me again, which he shall never do, unless it be thereby 


to take him. 

If. I got out of prison, I could inform his Majesty not only of 
Granger’s several names and places of abode, but also where all 
his trunks and moneys were kept, which are worth looking after, 
as it was a very considerable sum; I can also give an account 
both of the Irish business and Mr. Fitton’s. If Sir Mark thinks 
fit to acquaint his Majesty with this, it would be a great induce- 
ment towards my enlargement, and a little persuading would make 
Nicholson withdraw the actions, by reason of the great charge 
of prosecuting me. If his Majesty will give me a protection 
for 2 or 3 months, I doubt not but in that time to take Granger, 
or set others to do so, which will be of service to the whole king- 
dom, and prevent any more rogueries; if not taken, he would 
be frightened out of the kingdom. I beg this may be kept private, 
as I have many correspondents in London. Endorsed by [Wil- 
liamson], “ Counterfeiters of writing.” [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 250, 
No. 109.]

Thos. Goose, purser of the Sweepstakes, to the Navy Commis- 
sioners. Begs their perusal of certificates sent, conceiving they 
have received some satisfaction from Capt. Fras. Saunders, late 
commander. Requests not to be turned over to the purser of the 
Pembroke, for provisions lent to his ship for his Majesty’s interest. 
Conceives that no purser is obliged to find the carpenter wood and 
candle for caulking; did it by his commander’s desire, but hopes 
not to be a sufferer. Begs allowance for victuals given to carpenters 
and caulkers. Beseeches them to do him justice; has been faithful, 
and by his care, has saved his Majesty hundreds of pounds in 
23 months and 10 days. With note that the certificates were 
sent to Sir Wm. Penn, 29 Dec. [Zbid. No. 119.]

much dearer rate, and therefore loses by it. Has put a mark as 
ordered upon his goods, at his own charge, on which his Majesty by 
proclamation forbad all others to do the like. Has many of those 
goods on hand, which he desires them to take; will then ask

Leghorn Road. 


they of Tripoli used me civilly; but had I not come, they had 
thoughts of taking some of our rich ships, upon the belief that they 
were slighted, their Consul’s time for return being elapsed ; but that 
is salved upon a promise that he or some other should be sent. The 
Basha desired that Consul Tucker might return, but he cannot live 
there upon his Consulage, and for buying and selling, the King is the 
sole merchant, and none can do anything in merchandize until his 
turn be served, and then it is what he pleases; therefore there 
must be some thoughts that the Turkey Company may allow him 
some salary, for if they break, it will fall heavy upon them, they 
[of Tripoli] lying always with men-of-war in their passage. i 

I sent the Montague to Malta, where her commander, Capt. 
Francis Digby, with many gentlemen with him, kindly entertained 
and answered his Majesty’s letter ;, he came to me at Messina, and I 
sent him to Palermo. I have since been at Naples, where we were all 
kindly entertained by the Viceroy, answering gun for gun upon 
promise, and saluting him with 15 pieces of ordnance, he answering 
with 17; at Messina they would only answer with 4, saying they 
never gave more to their own King’s ships, so I did not salute 
them at all. I hada very tedious passage from Naples, which I 
left on 5 Dec., to Leghorn Road ; I intend touching at ela and 
over to Algiers to see how they have behaved since I left on 29 Sept.

The Fleet has been in a very healthful condition ; I shall make all 
haste homeward. I write this before entering Leghorn; I have 
received no letters from England since I parted. Sir John Finch has 
been aboard, when Lord Arlington’s health was drunk, and his 
business settled about bringing home his marbles. I hope I shall 
have a line from you at Cadiz. [S.P. Dom., Car. TI. 250, No. 125.] 


Rich. Bower to Williamson. A vessel coming from Newcastle with 
coals was driven to sea, and foundered upon the coast of Yetland 
[Zealand ?] but the men were saved by a boat from shore. A flyboat 
has arrived with masts from Scotland on his Majesty’s account, and 
a vessel from Norway with raft; 4 vessels have sailed for the Straits 
and 2 for Bordeaux. A deacon of Mr. Bridge’s church was buried 
this ‘afternoon. When they had brought him to the grave, the 
minister being there, they set down the corpse and fled, only one 
staying, which caused another to return, so that there were only 
those 2 and a friend of mine, to put the corpse into the grave. Pray 
acknowledge receipt of my letter of the 14th, and send a Gazette. 
[Ibid. No. 126.] 


John Clarke to Hickes. Arrival of 2 ships, one from France, 
laden with wine and prunes for Ireland, and the other from Bilbao 
with iron. [Zbid. No. 127.] 


John Clarke to Williamson. To the same effect. [Jbid. No. 128.] 


[Henry] Oldenburg to Williamson. The enclosed begs a speedy 
conveyance to Vienna for one of our [the Royal] Society, employed 
for the benefit of philosophy, who intends for Constantinople and 
the Morea. [Ibid. No. 129.] 


The King to the Vice-Chancellor of Cambridge. We wish the

Thos. Elyot [or Elliot, Master of the Harriers] to Williamson. 
Please to advertise in the newspaper the loss of a young white

the near shoulder. [Jbid. No. 131.] 


Information by John Winter. I went yesterday with Roger 
Vaughan to the house of Thos. Leach, printer, who works journey 
work with Mr. Redman, printer, and informed him that I wanted 
a sheet of paper lately printed by Redman touching the affairs of 
Ireland, having a friend going there whom I was obliged to satisfy, 
though I purchased it at any rate. He showed me a copy, but 
Vaughan said it was a private thing, and somewhat dangerous, and 
that it was not possible to get a copy, as he had offered a crown for 
one himself and been refused, and could only procure the-loan of 
one overnight, to be returned the next morning. [Zbid. No. 132.]

Rich. Watts to [Francis ?]. The great East India Dutch ship that 
came into the Downs ran aground on the Rip-raps, but did not 
suffer much. Fifty English and foreign ships are in the Downs, 
outward bound. I beg your assistance in regaining my employ- 
ment as surveyor in the Customs at Deal, which I lost in February 
last, though with no complaint against me. Sir Rob. Vyner and 
Alderman Backwell are made my friends by the Archbishop of 
Canterbury. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 250, No. 144.] - 


Benj. Francis to Rob. Francis. Family affairs. [Ibid. No. 145.] 


John Pocock to Hickes. We hear by a ship from Rochelle that a 
frigate of 120 guns has been launched at Toulon, and order given 
for building 50 small frigates of 36 guns each. A vessel with wine 
has been driven ashore at White North, 2 leagues north-east of this 
port, and staved to piéces. [Zbid. No. 146.] 


Wm. Bodham, clerk of the ropeyard, to the Navy Commis- 
sioners, Desires an order to sell 2 or 3 tons of decayed shakings 
to the paper makers; it has been picked already for oakum. 


[Ibid. No. 147.] 


John Hatch, boatswain of the Assurance, to the Navy Com- 
missioners. Having passed his accounts, begs payment of his wages, 
amounting to 65l. 9s. 11d., for which he has 3 tickets. [Zbid. 
No. 148.] 


Capt. John Tinker, master attendant, to Pepys. Has bought 
6 dozen oars for present use, and desires payment for them. 
Asks for a further supply, and for other stores. The boatswain of 
the Estrig hulk died this morning; there will not need another, as 
the Slothany hulk will soon be fitted, when there will be no need 
of this; will put a man to take care of her meanwhile. [1} pages. 


Ibid. No. 149.] 


Examination of Jo. Redman, printer, before Lord Arlington. 
Has been abroad for debt since the fire, and his wife took the 
book headed “Queries about Ireland,” to print; 200 copies were 
printed for 1/.5s. 0d. It was brought by Everard, a Papist, lodging 
in Southampton Buildings, Holborn, Redman keeps 4 servants at 
work, and attends his parish church, St. James’s, Clerkenwell. 
Everard had all the copies and the MS. also. [Zbid. No. 150.] 


John Powell to Williamson. A ship has been cast away near 
St. David’s, laden with wines and fruit, but the crew all saved; the 
ship fell into the hands of the rude multitude, who turned the 
wines out to carry the casks away: it is not yet known to what 
place she belonged. [Ibid. No. 151.] 

John Powell to Hickes. To the same effect. [Zbid. No. 152.]

cargoes of Newfoundland fish, and brought home money and some 
iron in return. [Zbid. No. 158.]

Rich. Bower to Williamson. I was mistaken in my statement that 
the Presbyterians gained the government of this town in the 
year 1665, it being in 1666. Edmond Thaxter, one of the party, 
was chosen bailiff by the townsmen in 1665, but was laid aside, 
and Rob. Nicholson and Wm. Bateman took place by mandamus, 
but these will not be owned by the Presbyterian party to have 
been bailiffs, upon which account they have several times been 
affronted in taking their seats in the church. There is a peculiar 
seat in the church for the bailiffs and the aldermen, the bailiffs sitting 
at the upper end, the justices next, and every alderman that 
has been bailiff in order; those that never bore the office, ac- 
cording to the time they have been aldermen, sit next the lower 
end; but if a junior alderman be chosen bailiff, he sits above his 
seniors that never bore that office. Wm Bateman, coming to his 
place yesterday during divine service, James Johnson—formerly an 
alderman, but turned out—being in the aldermen’s seat, set up his 
feet and would not let him pass, upon which Bateman forced away 
his leg, and had like to have passed by; Alderman Thaxter, per- 
ceiving this, caught hold of his gown behind, and pulled him back 
violently, and Mr. Johnson struck him, so I fear it will not be long 
before they are all together by the ears. Further details of the 
quarrel. [Ibid. No. 157.] 


John Pocock to Hickes. Several parcels of wine and casks have 
been driven on shore. The Palm Tree of Weymouth, from the 
Canaries, reports that the London fleet had not arrived there when 
she left 5 weeks since. Other vessels have come in from Lisbon, &c. 


[Ibid. No. 158.]

Dec. 21. Rob. Williams, cook of the Triumph, to the Navy Commis- 
Earl of sioners. Being master cook to the late Earl of Northumberland, 
Norhumer- and an old servant, I waited on him for 6 months, during his sick- 
Petworth. ness, and until his death ; which, with sorrow for the loss of so good 
a master, detracted my thoughts from other concerns, and being 
70 years old, and indisposed, I am incapable of travel. I desire you 
to dispense with my absence and non-performance of duty on 
board, until the spring. With note that his attendance on board 
cannot be dispensed with, but by leave from the Lord High Admiral.

Capt. Ant. Deane, master shipwright, to the Navy Commis- 
sioners. Thinks the Portland will be so perfected that when the 
commander comes, he will have nothing to do but to put in his 
provisions and sail. Has launched the Vonsuch, which is completed, 
except some little joiner’s work; shall despatch the hulk with all 
diligence. Is in great want of elm timber, and cannot be supplied 
until the money is ordered, which was promised by them some time 
since. [Ibid. No. 164.] 


Capt. John Tinker to Pepys. Will make all possible despatch 
of the Portland, and shall launch the new ship this tide, of which 
Capt. Deane will give an account. Is in great want of oars, candles, 
and shovels. [Jbid. No. 165.] 


Petition of Henry, Marquis of Worcester, to the King, for a re- 
grant of the advowson of the parish church of Chalton, co. Hants 
granted by King James to Edward Earl of Worcester, for 1871. 1s. 84d., 
but to which the late King, on some misinformation, presented 
Dr. Gillingham, who made a private agreement with —_—— Price, 
presented by Henry, Marquis of Worcester, so that the right of ad- 
vowson is lost. With reference thereon to Lord Keeper Bridgman, 
and his report, 18 Jan. 1669, in favour of the re-grant, but recom- 
mending that, as the Marquis cannot legally recover the advowson, 
Dr. Edmund Barker, the King’s presentee on this vacancy, should 
receive institution. [Jbid. Nos. 166, 167.] 


Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Citizens of Bath to Lord 
Arlington, to assist their petition [to the King], committed to the 
hands of the Duchess of Monmouth, that the assizes may be annually 
held in their town; they have many opposers, who plead the settle-

Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. A vessel from Bordeaux reports

men, one of the Frenchmen desired the herrings, and struck the 
Englishman and knocked him down. Saint’s vessel lying by, the 
company endeavoured to rescue their friend, insomuch that a 
mutiny arose, and one of the Frenchmen was much cut, whereupon 
the cowards of Bordeaux beat up the drums, pretending strange 
things, and the murder of 40 or 50 French, and the next day 
Saint was imprisoned, with all his men, and several other ship- 
masters stayed. [Zbid. No. 175.]

Navy Commissioners to the Treasury Commissioners. We are 
informed by the Navy Treasurers that the sole fund upon which we 
are to be supported for the expense of the ensuing year, and for de- 
fraying the remainder of the last year’s charge, is an assignment 
upon the Customs for 200,0007. This sum provides neither for the 
great charge necessary for putting the Navy into that repair which, 
—through the ill state of the stores, want of money, and the clamorous 
condition of the workmen in the yards,—they have required ever 
since the close of the late war; nor for the payment of any pre- 
ceding year’s debts; so that if the 200,000/. is strictly reserved for 
the current service, the discharging debts for past services, and fit- 
ting the Navy for service to come, will be wholly unprovided for. 

The credit of the Navy, from failure of payment, and disappoint- 
ment in receipt of money actually assigned, has come to that pass 


120 


1668. 


Dec. 29. 


Dec. 29. 


DOMESTIC STATE PAPERS, 


that we can get no further trust; so that if any part of this sum 
shall be called away for other uses, there will be a total stop to the 
present service. 


Having observed the reproach our office has suffered, by submit- 
ting to see the stores, through want of money, supplied at dearer 
rates, and the advantage arising from of late being able to buy with 
ready money, we have resolved no more to carry on the service at any 
other than the market prices, without having first laid the case 
before his Royal Highness or you. We have been directed by the 
Lord Admiral to revive the method of governing ourselves by esti- 
mates on each particular service ; the want of orderly supplies of 
money has occasioned the disuse of these,and the introduction of many 
irregularities, and an utter incapacity to distinguish the charge of any 
particular work. We desire either a further supply of money, or 
advice how to dispose of the 200,0007., under its insufficiency to 
answer all. 


We renew our request for a warrant that the money arising from 
the sale of lops, tops, and bark of trees, felled in his Majesty’s 
forests for the use of the Navy, may be employed towards defraying 
the charge of felling, converting, and transporting the timber sent to 
the King’s yards, as they are disposed of by the under-officers of 
the woods, to uses less advantageous to his Majesty than if employed 
for the Navy. Endorsed with a note that the lops and tops of trees

“ The preparations and method necessary for the right keeping of 
distinct accounts for receipts and issues of the naval stores in the 
magazines of his Majesty’s respective yards, and thereby giving 
each person entrusted with the said stores his due charge and dis- 
charge.” First, what is necessary to be done in the Comptroller’s 
Office: A distinct ledger to be kept of the bills sent up from the 
respective yards; with note of the letters of the instrument, which 
are to be entered into his book. A book to be kept of goods re- 
turned by boatswains and carpenters, and of the sale of old provi- 
sions. Stores supplied to be entered into the ledger for the yard, 
classified books being kept for each yard. An account to be 
taken of timber and plank from his Majesty’s forests sent in by 
purveyors, to be sent up by the respective clerks of the cheque and 
storekeepers to the Comptroller’s Office. Quarterly accounts to be 
kept and preserted to the Board at the year’s end.

and Bristol. She stopped at Brest, where they are building 3 ships 
of 50 or 60 guns each. Several vessels have sailed for France, 
Ostend, and other places. [Jbid. No. 6.] 


Capt. Ant. Deane to Williamson. I send a list of [French] ships, 
but the new ones are omitted, not being yet Jaunched. I will send 
all the letters I receive from my friend, and also a copy of the 
draft, as soon as made. Pray forward a letter enclosed, to satisfy 
my friend’s wife. I enclose a letter in character (cypher) to my 
friend, to be exact in all the drafts of the ports. [bid. No. 7.] 


Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. They are much troubled at Dover 
by so many French daily coming. The usual court has been held 
at St. James’ Church for the examination and admission of pilots, 
when special notice was given that if any dared to go out of sight 
when any of his Majesty’s ships had to be carried up, they would be 
immediately dismissed. [Jbid. No. 8.] 


James Baskerville to Williamson. The fleet outward bound still 
lies in the Road. Christmas was kept after the late, but here usual 
custom. [Zbid. No. 9.] 


John Powell to Hickes. The Star of Topsham has arrived from 
Faroe, with oils and figs for London. [Zbid. No. 10.] 


Warrant to Sir Edw. Walker, Garter King-at-Arms, to allow to 
Henry Howard, next brother of Thomas, Earl of Arundel, restored 
to the dignity of Duke of Norfolk, the title of lord, and the same 
precedency as though his father, Henry, late Earl of Arundel, had 
been restored to the dukedom. Also to grant him all such ensigns 
and badges of honour as are fit for the second son of a duke, 
[12 pages. Ibid. No. 11.] í

Warrant by Surveyor Thos. Middleton to the officers of the 
yard at Chatham, not to deliver canvas for tarpaulins to carpen- 
ters, except on the master shipwright or his assistant’s certiticate ; 
they are to give warrant to the storekeeper, and he is to deliver it 
to the master sailmaker or his foreman, who are to make the same 
into tarpaulins, according to such directions as they shall receive ; 
and when made, to deliver them to the boatswains of the ships at 
their going to sea, and to charge them by indent for them. En- 
dorsed, “the Ist warrant about tarpaulins.” [Copy. S.P. Dom., 
Car. 11, 251, No. 12.] 


Capt. George Liddell, of the Roebuck, to Thos. Hayter. I desire 
you to order Wm. Griffin, the housekeeper at the Navy Office, to 
send me the tickets left by you in his care, and I will pay the 
charges. [Jbid. No. 13.] 


Same tothe Navy Commissioners. The ship lost on the Goodwin 
9 days since came from Hamburg, had 24 guns mounted, and was 
laden with iron, copper, &c.; the Ramsgate and Deal boats have 
been there, but knows not what they got. One of the Holland East 
Indiamen left an anchor and cable behind, which has been weighed 
by Wm. Trebet, of Deal. The Roebuck is ready to sail, and only 
requires a small supply of rigging. [Jbid. No. 14.] 


John Pitt, purser of the St. George, to Thos. Hayter. When the 
St. George was ordered for sea, Capt. Hubbard sent for me to 
London; after many delays I went down to Portsmouth to attend 
on the Fairfax, not being entered on the St George, but was dis- 
charged from the Fairfax by reason of absence. Remind Pepys of 
his promise to procure an order from the Board for my allowance, 
having been pricked out of victuals and wages, and at great charge 
while waiting in London for the St. Georges going out. [Jbid. 
No. 15.] 


R. Waith to the Navy Commissioners. I have presented my 
book of imprests, and find that since the conclusion of Sir George 
Carteret’s account, Sir Wm. Warren is chargeable with only one 
imprest of 600/. on the Earl of Anglesey’s account, to enable him 
to pay the men of the Great Duke of York. The imprests he 
received from Sir George Carteret are all to clear, and are entered 
in his account ending 30 June 1667. I cannot tell what other im- 
prests he has received by assignments on the Exchequer, wherein 
neither Treasurer has been concerned. I cannot ascertain when Sir 
G. Carteret’s last account will be ready. [Jbid. No. 16.]

John Archer, Wm. Jevers, and Nath. Jones, servants to the Queen 
Mother, for the reversion of an estate worth 400/. a year, dis- 
covered by them, which, on the decease of an aged man, will revert 
to the Crown for want of male issue. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 251, 
No. 88.] 


Jonathan Atkins, Governor, and Wm. Sheldon, deputy-governor 
of Guernsey, to the Prize Commissioners, for a grant of a small 


privateer of St. Malo, of 5 guns, lately taken by the Paradoz, 


and now at Cowes or Portsmouth. She would be of very great 
use to them, and they would set her out to sea and man her from 
the island. [Jbid. No. 89.] 


A. Behn, for an order to Mr. May or Mr. Chiffinch for payment of 


the money due to Mr. Butler, she being threatened with an execu- 


tion. [Ibid. No. 90.] 


Aphara [or Fyhare] Behn, to order 1507. to be paid to Edw. 
Butler, who threatens to use all severity with her if it is not paid 
within a week. Mr. Halsall and Mr. Killigrew know how justly 
itis due. [Ibid. No. 91.] Annexing, 


A. Behn to [Thos.] Killigrew. I must go to prison to-morrow 
if I have not the money to-night; they say I am dallied 
with, and will not allow a few days more. I would break 
through all, get to the King, and never rise till he had paid 
the money, but am too sick and weak. I will send my mother 
to the King with a petition, and not perish in a prison, 
whence he [Butler] swears I shall not stir till I have paid 
the uttermost farthing. If I have not the money to-night 
you must send me something to keep me in prison, for 
I will not starve. [Lbid. No. 911.] 


Fyhare [or Aphara] Behn, not to let her suffer for what was done 
for his Majesty, but to order the payment of 150/. to Edw. Butler, 
who, on Lord Arlington’s declaring that he had neither money nor 
orders about it, threw her into prison. [Jbid. No. 92.] 


John Blanchard, for preservation of his life, and transportation, 
being seduced to share in a highway robbery ; was seized by virtue 
of the late proclamation [23 Dec. 1668], and imprisoned in New- 
gate, [Ibid. No. 93.] 


Mary Boynton, showing that in 1662 she spent most of her 
remaining fortune—much of which was lost by her brother, Col. Mat. 
Boynton, in his Majesty’s service—in purchase of Bevill Skelton’s 
pension of 1201. as page of honour; but that, after receiving half a 
year’s profits, the pensions were stayed; begs that hers may still 
be paid, or her purchase money returned. [Jbid. No. 94.] An- 
NeCHING, 

Certificate by Bevill Skelton, of his sale of the aforesaid pen- 
sion to Mary Boynton.—7 June 1668. [Lbid. No. 941.]

Mayor, Common Council, &., of Canterbury, on behalf of the 
inhabitants, to the House of Commons. Complain that by import 
of foreign worsted stuffs, and export of English wool, their trade— 
which is the combing of the rough wool grown in Romney Marsh, 
and other parts of Kent—is ruined. Request an Act for trans- 
porting bales of the combed wool of Kent by licence, on payment 
of 20s. per cwt., and appointment of persons to superintend the same ; 
also for preventing the export of other wool, and import of foreign 
stuffs. With reasons showing the necessity of some such Act for the 
welfare of the county. [2 sheets. S.P. Dom., Car. II. 251, No. 95.] 


Nat. Cocks, for the reversion of the place of Keeper of the 
Council Chamber, after his father, George Cocks, his grandfather 
having filled the place under the two last Kings. With note by 
Lord Arlington that the petition is granted. [Jbid. No. 96.] 


Manuel de Fonseca, factor for the Florentine and Spanish mer- 
chants interested in the ship Harl of Flanders. In Aug. 1666 the 
ship was seized by order of Prince Rupert, and the lading of wine 
disposed of to the use of the King’s fleet, and it has not yet been 
paid for. In order to prevent the issuing of letters of reprisal, on 
10 May 1667, Council ordered payment of 1,410/. for the wines, 
but after a year, the money not being paid, we begged that it 
might be paid from the 5,000/. a month reserved from the Cus- 
toms, and you approved the petition, We beg payment of the 
money from the said Customs. [/bid. No. 97.] 


Dan. Fabureau de la Fabvolliére “ Ingenieur,” to be put into a 
better capacity for serving, and have an order for payment of 3501. 
due to him, with constant payment of his allowance. His great 
extremities, these 5 years, for want of salary, compel him to be 
importunate. With notes of his transactions from 1664. [Ibid. 
No. 98.] 


R. D. [Col]. Rob. Duckinfield], for leave to go beyond seas with Lord 
———. Was sent prisoner to the Tower, on suspicion of offences 
against his Majesty, and has been in custody there and in the Isle 
of Wight 3 years, although much diseased ; hopes for clemency, in 
spite of the flying calumnies wherewith he has been aspersed. 
[Col. Rob. Duckinfield was sent to the Tower in August 1665 ; see 
Calendar, p. 534. Ibid. No. 99.] 


Lieut.-Col. Thos. Duncan, for a special warrant for his arrears of 
pay as a reformed Lieut.-Colonel, his pay in Hull being but 8d. a 
day. Was in arms for the late King, raised 72 horse at his own 
charge, and lost 8,000}. Delivered to Col. Ant. Gilby, deputy- 
governor of Hull, his Majesty’s letter of May 19, 1665, ordering 
him to be mustered as a reformado lieut-colonel of horse, but only 
received 167., and left the garrison 3 years since for Scotland; is 
74 years old, in great trouble and misery, and begs the reformado’s 
place of Capt. Gradey, lately dead. [Zbid. No. 100.] Annexing, 


Reference to the Duke of Albemarle, of the petitioner’s request 
for a reformado’s place in Hull, 3 Sept., 1664, and his

Sir Wm. Killigrew. Brought the pin business into his Majesty’s

been expended on it as proposed, it would have yielded 10,0001. a

Peter Massonnet to Lord Arlington. Is the saddest object of 
pity of all the King’s servants. Has attended 32 years as 
French sub-tutor and writing master, served him in adversity as 
Clerk of the patents and Foreign Secretary, but at the Restoration, 
had only his sub-tutor’s salary continued, now 8337. in arrear, so 
that he is ready to perish; will resign his patent for the arrears 
and some recompense. [Zbid. No. 104a.] 


Same to the Same, to represent his sad condition to the King, 
to procure him half his arrears or a year’s salary ; his wife has now 
only 201. a year, and 5s. a day as the King’s laundress, all extras 
having been taken away. Is in daily danger of outlawry. [Jbid. 
No. 1048.] 


Dowager Countess of Lincoln. On her marriage with Theophilus, 
late Earl of Lincoln, he settled on her the manors of Threckingham

and Stow, Lincolnshire, which were incumbered with an annuity to

Morpain, to be put in the lottery for indigent officers ; came 
over from Holland with the Queen Mother, and served 11 or 12 years 
without pay; served his Majesty when leaving Paris after the 
accommodation with the Duke of Lorraine, by disengaging 3 little 
boats laden with his baggage, which were arrested. Is deprived of 
his place in the Guards, held 6 or 7 years, for being a Catholic, and 
no compensation allowed. [French. See Calendar, 1667-68, p. 53. 
Ibid. No. 106.] 


The gentlemen excluded from the troops of Life Guards of Horse 
in 1667, and some reformed officers. Beg him to find them bread ; 
spent their youth and blood, and underwent all hardships short 
of death, for his Majesty and his father, and now a fate worse than 
death awaits them, being made incapable of employment. ([Jbid. 
No. 107.] 


Eleven underwritten officers, for relief to bear their charges to 
foreign service, being told there is no-hope for them here ; served 
with satisfaction in Portugal, though not made equal to others who 
were not Catholics; petitioned on their return for subsistence, but 
have waited many days in vain. [Zbid. No. 108.] 


The field officers and captains who lately commanded the English

The officers of the Marquis of Schomberg’s regiment of horse in

Peter Parker and Sam. Symmons to Lord Arlington, for dis-

Veronica, widow of Col. Rich. Platt, to Lord Arlington, for 
relief to keep a poor stranger from perishing; is the distressed 
widow recommended by Lord Aubigny, without whose charity she 
must have perished in prison; her husband spent his whole estate 
in service of the late King. [Zbid. No. 112.]

William, Lord Sandys. Queen Elizabeth granted Burleigh Walk,

Anon. to Lord [Arlington.] The farmers of Excise, on complaint 
of a loss of 30,0007. during the plague, obtained a defalcation of 
21,000/., whereby they really gained 12,0007., and to avoid discovery, 
the accounts of those 19 weeks were conveyed away. Since then, 
they demand allowance of 38,0007. more for the contagion, the late 
fire in London, and the hard frosts. These are as false pretences as 
the former, for after abatements, they only pay 9,000/. rent 
monthly, instead of 11,6667. 13s. 4d. Whilst the brewers are far- 
mers of excise, they will be constantly pretending to be losers, 
and yet fill their own pockets; they have menaced officers for 
bringing informations against them, and since the renovation of 
the farm, they abate each other secretly the officers’ charge. The 
brewers at first pretended they would bear any loss on the farm 
themselves, and would rather pay 10,000/. more to have it in quiet. 
Proofs of their fraudulent conduct in pretending losses. Proposal 
that their books should be called for and inspected, that the chief 
farmers should submit to inquiries, and meanwhile that all defal- 
cations should be suspended. [2 sheets. Ibid. No. 137.]

Wm. Ryley, jun., to [Williamson ?]. Detail of the services 
and sufferings of my late father, Wm. Ryley, sen., who served 
in the Records from 1626 till 1667; he was prosecuted for sup-

Office sealed up, and an entry made in their books that “Ryley 
told the King that he had records to prove the Parliament traitors.” 
As Herald, he proclaimed his Majesty on 8 May 1660, but his rich 
coat having been plundered in the wars, he obtained an order from 
the Earl of Manchester, Speaker of the Hovse of Lords, to take 
down King James’ rich coat of arms from Henry VIL’s chapel, to 
perform the solemnity, which was returned the next day. 

I was myself admitted clerk in the Record Office in 1647, and was 
wounded, fighting for the King at Worcester; in 1660, I aided my 
father in sorting the Scottish records, when we found the original 
of the “Solemn League and Covenant,” and refused 2,0007. offered 
by the Scots to deliver it up. I have since drawn up records, made 
searches, &c., for Government. I beg help from Lord Arlington, 
and some allowance, as was customary, for transcribing records for 
the King and Parliament, my family being ready to perish.

Memorandum for Lord Arlington of reasons why the Scottish 
trade and staple should continue at Campvere; the old contract 
ought not to be broken, it has been settled these 160 years or more: 
the town has benefited little by it during the late wars. The town 
sheltered the Scots, and made them pro formd burghers during the 
wars between England and Holland ; it is the most convenient and 
best situated place in the Low countries, and belongs to the King’s 
nephew, the Prince of Orange. ‘I'he Scottish merchants generally, 
and Sir Wm. Davidson, the present conservator, incline to remain 
there. Campvere is willing to continue them on the old contract 
till a new one can be made, and will grant them all that can reason- 
ably be demanded. [2 pages. Ibid. No. 181.]

Arguments for and against the laying an additional imposition on 
Swedish iron, of which 12,000 tons a year are brought in lately ; it is 
better and tougher than the English, and being sent in melted, does 
not consume our timber; if the duty were laid, the Swedes 
might in revenge heighten the impositions on their other necessary 
commodities, as pitch, &. On the other hand, its import reduces 
the decaying manufacture in England, throws the poor cut of work, 
and would much lower the price of coppice wood. [Jbid. No. 183.]

“ A looking glass for George Fox, the Quaker, and other Quakers,

Hen. Rumbold to Lord Arlington. I understand my place of 
Consul at Malaga is disposed of to Hum. Colston, without reserving 
me even so much as St. Lucar, with which I should have been 
content, as being something satisfactory to my reputation. I 
wonder that anyone durst speak against me asa Papist to your lord- 
ship, and that Colston, who is so by profession, and has married a 
Spanish woman in Malaga, should be nominated in my place. I 
shall not do to Colston as Sir Fras. Bedingfield did to me, in- 
flame the merchants, and cause them to petition the King and 
Council for their right to elect, as all those of eminency that trade 
for Spain declared against Colston, upon hearing that he pretended to 
it, and charged him with what he could not answer, much less clear 
himself, as I did most fully of what they alleged against me. 

I beseech your lordship to consider my case; besides the mer- 
chants’ approbation, I paid down the money for my second commis- 
sion, and it has been without the enjoyment of the place. This 
besides the great sums the Consul’s place formerly cost me, and for 
which I have received no satisfaction of Mr. Westcombe. I have also 
lost my former employment as partner with Mr. Upton, which being 
so considerable, I ought in conscience to have a consideration. I 
wrote to the King as to the necessity of having a minister sent to the 
Spanish Court, and took some pains to get the Duke of Medina 
Celi to make a report to the King of Spain, that the person might 
be admitted into his Court. My loyalty is the only cause of my 
ruin, as your lordship would conclude by an inspection of my 
orders and vouchers, both from my brother and those that then 
acted for his Majesty; few men have performed such great services 
for their King, at their own charge. I served faithfully in my place 
in the Prize Office, and laid out 118l., as appears by the account 
annexed to my petition, given in long since, but payment of which 
has been deferred by Lord Ashley, so as not to make it an example ; 
as for salary, I have not received any, nor know what will be 
allowed. [2 pages. S.P. Dom., Car. II. 254, No. 1.] 


John Maurice to Williamson. A small bark, laden with pitch and 
tar for Bristol, was driven ashore in the middle of the night; the 
goods were all landed, and the vessel was not damaged. [Jbid. No. 2.] 


Charles Whittington to Williamson. Two Swedes have arrived 
from Stockholm with pitch, tar, and iron, also a Londoner from 
Holland with tar. The Perregrin of Hull, laden with lead, barley, 
and cloth for Rotterdam, was cast away near Brewers Haven, and 
only 3 men escaped in the boat. [Jbid. No. 3.]

Capt. Thos. Foulis to the Navy Commissioners. Received the stores 
sent from Deptford, after waiting more than a week. [Jbid. No. 5.] 


Edw. Byland to Pepys. Has almost finished trimming the Hope 
galliot hoy, and shall launch her next week, and then finish the 
yacht. Will omit laying decks at this season of the year, the deals 
brought in being green. [Zbid. No. 6.] 

Sir John Mennes to Pepys. The Commissioners of Accounts at 
Brooke House requiring the pay books of 21 ships named, desires 
he will cause their delivery. [Zbid. No. 7.] 

John Clarke to Hickes. The Ruth has arrived from the Leeward 
Islands, and the William and Elizabeth from Barbadoes, having 
been 7 weeks in her passage ; she reports that Lord Willoughby was 
ready to sail to the Caribbee Islands, and so home for England, 
having constituted several Commissioners to manage the govern- 
ment in his absence. The island is in a thriving condition, and 
much of Bridge Town is rebuilt. [Zbid. No. 8.] 

Same to Williamson. To the same effect. [Zbid. No. 9.] 


Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. The 54 Dutch ships that lay under 
Dungeness outward bound have sailed; I suppose that those that 
went out of the Downs with them have scarce weathered Ports- 
mouth. Great wrecks have been seen near the North Foreland, and 
the Thanet men have brought much goods on shore.. [Zbid. No. 10.] 


I. Dorislaus to Williamson. I have been twice to Whitehall to 
receive your commands, but failed in seeing you. [Ibid No. 11.] 


M. Wren to Pepys. I send you an order for Capt. Foulis of the 
Roe ketch, as I know not where to find him. [Zbid. No. 12.] 

John Moore and Edw. Moorcock to the Navy Commissioners. 
We have procured credit for money for one month’s pay for our 
men; we pray you to imprest some money speedily, or we shall not 
have these able men in our employ; and if we lose our credit, we 
shall hardly procure men in the spring. The anchors taken up will 
more than pay for this winter’s charge. [Jbid. No. 13.] 

Same to Col. Thos. Middleton. We shall have the old provisions 
broken down from the Helverstone taken on shore, and put into the 
stores, as this will prevent loss and embezzlement. [Jbid. No. 14.] 

Rich. Bower to Williamson. A vessel with piece goods from 
London was cast away on the Barnard Sand; a coach and several 
goods, as also a woman and some other of the company, were driven 
on shore at Corthy. Another vessel was forced ashore a mile to the 
northward of Yarmouth, where she still lays far up on the land. 

Nine ships have arrived from Rotterdam, one of which reports 
that one Bromwell of Iron Gate, near Tower Wharf, master of a 
ketch that was freighted from Rotterdam to London with merchant 
goods, also took aboard 570 odd pieces of gold, upon the account of 
Mr. Tucker of Rotterdam ; when at sea, the master conspired with 
his company to share the gold and sink the ketch, which they did, 
within 10 leagues of the North Foreland, and were taken on board a

vessel bound for Rotterdam, with some of the ketch’s goods. One 
of the company, being a Frenchman, designed to go for St. Valery 
in an English vessel, and went on board; the master, finding him to 
falter in his discourse, secured him, and acquainted Mr. Tucker,

Thos. Holden to Hickes. Several ships have put in through the 
tempestuous weather, one of which has broken her foremast and 
sprung her mainmast. Several came in yesterday, but the tempest 
is too strong for particulars ; a Falmouth vessel has been cast on the 
rocks, and is too much bulged to go to sea again. [Jbid. No. 16.] 


Ralph Hope to Williamson. A robbery was committed near 
Curdworth Bridge; 3 persons met one Lascelles and his wife from 
London, who had stayed at Sir Clement Fisher’s at Packington, and 
robbed them of 34 guineas, which the woman had quilted in her 
sleeve. After they had robbed these two, they met with others, one 
being from Coventry, whom they set upon and wounded; but the 
townsman got clear off, though not without a wound through the 
shoulder ; they took from the others what they had, and also their 
horses, and have not since been heard of. One of the thieves is 
believed to be Ashenhurst, mentioned in the proclamation. It is 
strongly presumed, there being many circumstances to back it, that 
the first robbery was but a cheat and confederacy to recover the 
money of the country, and that Lascelles, as he pretends his name 
to be, is no better than he should be, and Sir Clement himself has that 
suspicion of him that he has sent after him. Some of those who com- 
mitted the robbery at Coleshill 6 weeks ago are m Oxford Gaol. 

The school boys during Christmas acted a play called “ The 
Indian Emperor” for 2 nights, before a very great concourse of 
persons, a convenient stage being built in the school for the purpose, 
though there was a cabal that much opposed it. There is a pear 
tree in full blossom in the orchard of Mrs. Smith at Brandon, alias 
Brawne, 3 miles from Coventry, which creates some wonder. I 
suppose you have heard of the woman at Hatton in Derbyshire, who 
has not taken any manner of sustenance since St. Thomas’s Day was 
a twelvemonth; she lies in bed talking much, although worn to a 
mere skeleton; all her refreshment is having her lips anointed 
now and then with a little oil, &. [23 pages. Ibid. No. 17.]

Order in Council—recapitulating a former order of 30 Dec. 1668, 
for the farmers of Customs to give their reasons for not entering 
10 prize ships named as free ships, according to the Act for prize 
ships, but detaining them, whether inward or outward bound, in the 
port of London; the reply of the farmers, dated 2 Jan. 1669, that 
the reason why the said ships were not admitted for entry as free 
ships, being taken as prizes, is that oath was not entered before 
1 Aug., according to the statute for making prize ships free, and 
that there are others in like condition which cannot be admitted 
without order—that the farmers are to be asked whether, in case of 
freeing the said ships, they will demand any defalcations ; and their 
reply of 8 Jan. that they shall not claim defalcation. [Copy. 
23 pages. Ibid. No. 21.] 


Original of the above report, and the order, &c., thereon. 
[12 pages. Ibid. No. 22.]

St. J. Steventon to the Navy Commissioners. I went to South- 
ampton, and find the charge of the hemp according to particulars 
enclosed; the master who brought it has left orders that it is not 
to be delivered without payment of freight and other charges. There 
is no close-decked vessel here; shall I hire one at 40s. to fetch it, 
and pay the freight? [Zbid. No. 26.] 


Capt. John Tinker to Pepys. I am daily troubled by the poor 
men that carried ballast to and from the ships in Col. Middle- 
ton’s time, and as a small sum will satisfy the debt, it is a discredit 
to the service that they should complain as they do; I would as 
soon pay them as hear them lament, they having nothing but from 
hand to mouth. I pray that they may be satisfied. [Jbid. No. 27.] 
Encloses, 


Petition of John Roberts, and 12 other inhabitants of Ports- 
mouth and Gosport, to the Navy Commissioners, for 
payment of the amount set against each of their names, from 
171. to 1l. 8s., for carrying ballast to and from the King’s 
ships, the greater part having been due nearly 3 years. 
[Zbid. No. 271.] 


Capt. Ant. Deane to the Navy Commissioners. We lose half the 
time of 100 men for want of a supply of spikes to fasten the works 
of the hulk ; unless there be order to receive them, or the ketch 
arrive with them, as promised, the men must stand and look at one 
another, as they must have done to-day, if I had not promised to 
pay for 2 cwt., rather than see such disorder in the yard. The men 
make a great moan for want of money; pray move his Royal High- 
ness for their relief, they having neither a penny nor credit to keep 
them alive. [Jbid. No. 28.] 


Capt. Silas Taylor to the Navy Commissioners. Sends an account 
of stores. For a new year’s gift, there arose so violent a storm of 
wind that it stranded and staved 40 vessels great and small, and 
amongst others the muster boat, just taken off the oar (?) to be sent 
for Deptford. The fury of the storm continues yet. [Ibid. No. 29.] 


Edw. Byland to Commissioner Thos. Middleton. There are only 
the Crown and Dover remaining here. Some deals and other goods 
were taken out of the barge belonging to Mr. Andrews ; but having 
sent some watchmen, we found the men out. Particulars of the 
timber stolen when the barge was lying near Tower Wharf. 
[Zbid. Nos. 30, 31.] 


Dan. Furzer to the Navy Commissioners. The 2 anchors sent in 
the Edgar were made by your order for the Navy 2 years since, 
approved, and a set price agreed upon. I hope you will consider my 
necessity, and order the money for them, or I shall be undone.

W. Hannam to the Navy Commissioners. I have hauled the

Petition of John Skelton for a free pardon. Had a dispute with 
Francis Edgecombe 3 years since, which he believed had been 
reconciled the same night; but the next morning Edgecombe took 
the petitioner out of bed, and forced him to answer in the field, 
otherwise he would immediately kill him; thereupon wounds were 
given on either side, and Edgecombe died shortly after of one he 
then received, contrary to the petitioner’s hopes and intentions, by 
reason whereof he has been compelled to live in exile. Served the 
Duke of York and the late Princess Royal, and will employ his 
life to serve his Majesty, if the pardon is granted. 

With reference thereon to the Attorney-General, and his report 
that the facts are as stated in the petition, but that upon the 
impanelling of the jury by the coroner, Mr. Edgecombe’s father sent 
several of his servants and tenants to serve upon the inquest, and 
procured such a verdict as he pleased (which proceeding was un- 
known to the petitioner’s father or his friends); they found a 
verdict of murder, and the petitioner not appearing, he was out- 
lawed, but never tried by any petty jury.—Jan. 21. [S.P. Dom., 
Car. TI. 254, No. 71.] 


Draft of the above petition. [Zbid. No. 72.]

Col. B. Reymes to Sir George Downing. What was done in one 
district was done in all; but I suppose Mr. Fillingham can best 
resolve in the general. The prisoners had several allowances, both 
French and Dutch, and when they were at the lowest, both French 
and Dutch allowed them somewhat over and above the King’s 
allowance, which at first was 5d.a day, then 4d., then 1 lb. of bread 
only, then 2d. a day, every proportion and alteration being made by 
Council, according to the reports they had of the usage of the 
English prisoners, and the agreement between the Crowns; the ex- 
change was made according to their respective qualities. When 
a prisoner was released without an exchange, it was ordered that 
he should pay back the charge he had put the King to, but I do not 
remember that they ever did so, except one or two, which the 
Marshals have, or should account for. [Zbid. No. 84.] 


Col. B. Reymes to Williamson. I received your and Sir George 
Downing’s letters as to the French prisoners, and have replied to 
the former, but will explain more fully when we all meet, and 
examine the books. [Jbid. No. 85.]

Petition of John Balldee and 7 other inhabitants of Meeching, 
alias Newhaven, Sussex, to the King, for an order to Sir John 
Pelham and other justices of the peace, to inquire to whom money 
is owing for supplying materials, and lodging workmen, W&c., for the 
erection of a harbour and pier there. The loss of so many lives 
and vessels yearly moved Wm. Halsted to draw up a certificate to 
the King, which was presented by Lord Digby and the Earl of 
Bristol, and was well liked by his Majesty ; but it lying dormant 
for 3 years, Halsted drew up a petition, and obtained 80 of the 
inhabitants’ hands to it, upon which his Majesty granted letters 
patent for erecting a pier and other conveniences, and Halsted 
assisted with his own funds in carrying it into effect, although he 
is now, with many others who have lost their money, hated and 
envied. A breach happening with the said lord and the Lord Chan- 
cellor, the business was put into other hands, and neither Halsted 
nor several others mentioned, who advanced their money and credit 
as detailed, have received any return, although many applications 
have been made, and they are in danger of utter ruin on account 
thereof. Unless respect is had to the promises and engagements

Thos. Bawtree to Rob. Blackborn. I want an answer to my 
former letter, as Ido not know whether you agree to my proposi- 
tions. I find you are willing to abate 5/. towards the improvement 
of the other lands, but I am not willing to do this, as I cannot 
make my rent of it. Iwill give you 65l.a year for the ground 
mentioned in my lease, and that held by John Gell, on condition 
that you will build me a stable, and repair the roof, when I will 
take it for 5 years. I desire you not to think that I undervalue 
your farm ; the one adjoining is let, and they have abated 111. in 
461. I make no benefit by the use of the rent, as I have received 
201. and paid 20l. 10s. 6d., and the charge of Rob. Cox’s house is 
12. 15s. I shall send my bullocks to London by Candlemas, when 
my man shall call with all the money received up to that time. 
[S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 254, No. 105.] 


Rich. Bower to Williamson. Several persons were indicted at the 
sessions held at Beccles, for not going to their parish church, and 
true bills were found, but they were acquitted by the petty jury, on 
the ground that the day they went to church, the doors were shut, 
which uses to be once a month for their excuse, the patron being a 
Nonconformist. Mr. Brewster of Wrentham, and some of the jus- 
tices, were so incensed that they resolved not to come on the bench 
any more. 

Mr. Bridge appeared at Norwich sessions, when Sir John Hubbard 
told him that a letter had been shown to his Majesty by Lord 
Arlington, who directed it to be sent to Lord Townshend; about 
this he was called before the deputy-lieutenants, and although 
they could have proved what was laid to his charge, yet on his 
confessing to baptizing children, keeping conventicles, and residing 
in Yarmouth contrary to law, they were willing to forbear prose- 
cuting him, if he would promise to leave the county of Norfolk, and 
not come within five miles of Yarmouth. Bridge answered that 
he was not willing, but if it was commanded, he must submit.

Councillor Long told him that Lord Townshend was there as a

his unwillingness, when his lordship rose up in a passion, and

Jan. 19. The King to the Commissioners of Sewers for Hatfield Chace. 
We hear that the participants in the level of the Chace, to whom in 
June last we entrusted the preservation of navigation, and of the 
inheritance of the inhabitants, contrary to the contract made with 
the late King, have neglected the works, whereby some are become 
ruinous and decayed ; and that on pretext of our previous orders, 
the said participants suspend the orders of the commissioners for 
repair of the same, discharge the tenants from payment of moneys 
assessed upon them, and refuse to deliver up the records. To avoid 
further misconstruction, we require you our commissioners to proceed 
in the due execution of your commission, and provide for the pre- 
servation of the said level, and the parts of the counties adjoining 
thereto, anything in our previous letter notwithstanding. [SIZ 
Dom., Entry Book 25, p. 81.] >

Petition of John Ludlow to the King, for a pardon. Stands con- 
victed for stealing to the value of 14s., though he never did it. Is

John Howell. The suggestions of the petitioner are true as to the

St. J. Steventon to the Navy Commissioners. As to the com- 
plaint of the Dutch captain, Sir Lawrence Van Heemskirk, against 
me, for not giving conduct money to all he sends with his note, I 
reply that he, not knowing the end of conduct money, which is to 
encourage seamen, gives his note to all that ask for conduct money 
from London, which I refuse to pay when I see they ‘are servants, 
and know they have not come from London. 

I hope I have discharged my duty by well husbanding the King’s 
money, and not paying where it is not due, which is the cause of 
his complaint. Pray acquaint his Royal Highness, that I may not 
be under censure by an untrue information. I sent all the bills for 
provisions to the Comptroller, and the persons concerned in them 


have been several times to receive them. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 254, 
No. 1381.] 


Capt. John Hubbard to the Navy Commissioners. Some men are 
come from London in the Pearl to the Milford under my command. 
I desire an order to the clerk of the cheque for entering them from 
the time they first came to the Pearl, according to Capt. Berry’s 
certificate, that they may have satisfaction without the making of so 
many tickets for so little time. [/bid. No. 182.]

Jan, 22. Roger Baker, purser of the Dartmouth, to the Navy Commis- 

Plymouth. sioners. At the last victualling at Portsmouth, being bound for 
Tangiers and the Canaries, I received all but the beer, and the 
frigate sailing to the Downs, I was forced to take up goods on credit 
in lieu of it, so I bought 2 pipes of wine. I was commanded by the 
captain on Christmas Day to issue a pint of sack to every man, and 
one pipe being out, to bring the other. On 19 Jan. he sent for me to 
his cabin, to know whether I would own the words I had sent up to 
him the day before, accounting for its disposal, when he gave me 200 
blows with his cane, and took me by the hair of my head, intending 
to dash my brains out, had not God prevented by his providence ; but 
he so mangled my face that I fear I shall lose an eye, and while I 
was under the doctor’s hands, he commanded the boatswain to clap 
me into the bilboes, atop of the forecastle, where I continued 
10 hours, being nailed down with a staple to the davit., 

When I was not able to subsist any longer, it being very frosty 
and tempestuous weather, the master commanded the weather sail 
to be taken from me, saying that if I would confess that I had 
wronged the captain, he would release me; on telling him I could 
not make myself guilty, he replied that I should lie there and rot; 
but the captain not being aboard, rather than I should perish there 
that night, he confined me to my cabin, with a sentinel, until 
the commander came on board. On his coming on board, he sent 
for the boatswain, and beat him about the head and face with his 
fist, the rest of the officers not daring to approach, as he threatened 
to have a council of war, and if it lay in his power, to have them 
hanged. 

I desire that justice may be done, in the first place, to his Majesty, 
the commander having been guilty of 9 instances of frauds detailed, 
and that satisfaction may be given for such great affronts. 

I have several other articles to send you, but my bones being 
almost broken, and having the use of only one eye, I was forced to 
desire a friend to write this letter. I would have sent it earlier, 
but it was so late before I came out of the bilboes, and I am still 
under restraint. [4 pages. Ibid. No. 134] Annexing, 


Certificate by Wm. Day, und 5 other officers of the Dartmouth, 
that Roger Baker having been in the bilboes most part of 
- the day, and the weather being cold, and he being in a weak 
condition, they have resolved for his present preservation— 
life being sweet, and Capt. [Rich.] Trevanion being ashore— 
to confine him to his cabin with a sentry, as accustomed, 
during the commanders pleasure.—19 Jan. 1669. [Ibid. 
No. 1341,]

Petition of George, Earl of Bristol, to the King. Though my 
services to his late and your present Majesty have been equalled by 
few, I left my recompense to the charge of the chief ministers, whom 
I thought my friends, but was disappointed until you were straitened 
by bounty to others. At length I proposed several suits for myself, 
none of which were refused by your Majesty, but none proved of 
benefit, except 10,000/. granted out of Mr. Heveningham’s estate for 
my daughter's portion. I request that—as my estates have not been 
restored, and I can no longer maintain my family with decency—the 
proposals presented by me may be referred to some of the chief 
ministers. | 

With reference thereon to the Lord Keeper, Lord Privy Seal, and 
two Principal Secretaries of State, and their report that the 10,0001. 
which was granted him from the forfeitures on prohibited goods 
imported was for service, but was withdrawn on tke King’s dis- 
pleasure towards him, and the money transferred to the Privy 
Purse; that he expects compensation for 16 or 17 years’ loss of a 
pension of 2,000/. a year granted to his late father from the Court 
of Wards, and for the loss of Lord Brooke’s wardship ; they advise 
the renewal of his grant of 10,000/. from prohibited goods, and 
establishment of his pension of 2,0000., so that after his eminent 
services, he may be comfortable the remainder of his life. With 
marginal notes [by Lord Arlington]. [S.P. Dom., Cur. IT. 254, 
Nos. 141, 142.], Annexing,
