John Ruffhead to the Navy Commissioners. Thanks for your 
care in relation to 50/. imprest for repairing anchors at Chatham ; 
but I much admire your compliance with Mr. Littleton, in stopping 
more than one-third thereof for Mr. Fookes, contrary to your own 
order, which plainly says he was to be paid one-third of 246/. out 
of such moneys as should be ordered me, and the whole to be paid 
at 3 payments. Here you first order me 501. imprest, to carry on the 
service, and then order one-third to be paid to Fookes, in part of 
debt, so that of the 50/. I have received (with as much trouble as it 
is half worth) I have only 33l. 4s. 6d.. and I leave you to judge 
how far it will go in carrying on 2007. worth of work. ‘There 
is as much work performed as I have received money for, so 
I pray either to be allowed to desist, or to receive the remainder. 
I beg payment of 9 bills, total 3657. 2s. 1d., for work done in 1668, 
and then Mr. Littleton can pay 80l. to Mr. Fookes, and take his 
receipt. I also need a warrant to deliver articles of ironwork, and 
to receive ready money for them, to make my heart glad, as you 
have made it sorrowful. [Jbid. No. 159.] Hncloses,

Michael Haley to Rob. Francis. Thanks for your letter. I hope 
the noble lady of whom you speak is safely there, and desire 
respects to her. God has provided her a coach at her door, and I 
question not but it was so ordained in Heaven, to the end that my 
service may not be accepted, though it would be freely done. 

As to my affsirs in Ireland, I was left 200/. a year in lands in 
co. Limerick, by my father and friends who died before the wars, 
and my mother was turned out of all by Cromwell, merely for her 
religion, I being in France, as my friend, Lord Philip Howard, 
the Lord Almoner to the Queen, well knows. I complained to him, 
but he could say nothing, only pity me. I have all my deeds and 
writings, but no possession. I never acted against the King nor 
against Cromwell, only Iam a Roman Catholic, which privilege I 
would not lose for 7 kingdoms. I beg you will inquire into the 
state of those affairs, in regard a new deputy goes soon to that 
kingdom, and certify to me what might be done. [JZbid. No. 183.]

April 15. Statement signed by Ralph Smith, warden, Roger Norton, and 
Sam. Mearne, on behalf the Stationers’ Company. King James, in 
the first year of his reign, by patent granted the company licence to 
imprint all manner of primers, psalters, and Psalms, in metre or 
prose, and prohibited all others to print, sell, or cause to be printed 
or sold any such books, under the pain of forfeiture. Sam. Speed, 
stationer in London, has surreptitiously obtained a licence from 
Sam. Parker, chaplain to the Archbishop of Canterbury, for a book 
entitled “The King’s Primer,” which is now printing, which licence 
Mr. Parker has since revoked. Sam. Speed also obtained another 
licence in like manner for a book entitled “ Psalterium Carolinum ; 
or, the King’s Psalter,” &c., from Thos. Grigg, chaplain to the Bishop 
of London, which said licence Mr. Grigg has also revoked. [Jbid. 
No. 197.] 


April 16. Warrant to search for and seize “The King’s Primer,” and the 
“ Psalterium Carolinuwm, or, the King’s Psalter,” printed by Sam. 
Speed, stationer, of London, under licences which have been revoked, 
and also printed contrary to the patent granted by King James to 
the Stationers’ Company. [Draft. Ibid. No. 198.]

John Clarke to Hickes. The Montague and Tiger, two of Sir 
Thos. Allin’s squadron, have arrived from the Straits; 6 or 8 mer- 
chant ships came under their convoy from Cadiz, but they lost them 
in a storm. A vessel has come in from Ireland with hides and 
tallow, and several others have been seen in the offing, [S.P. 
Dom., Car. II, 258, No. 209.] 


Ralph Hope to Williamson. John Olds, a young mercer here, 
and newly set up for himself, being some time in league with Mary, 
daughter of Capt. Owen, a citizen of good repute, the business pro- 
ceeded so far that they had been thrice asked in church, and 
nothing remained but to celebrate the nuptials; but she desired, 
before she would be married, once again to see London, where she 
had once lived. 

Whether she then renewed some old acquaintance, or entertained 
some new favourite, is not known; ‘but on her return, she expressed 
so much indifference and coldness, that in the morning after their 
meeting, Olds was found drowned in a well, into which he must 
have got with great. difficulty, it being covered at the top, and the 
entrance so narrow that it was thought impossible for a less man to 
have got in. He had lately been at London, where he bought 
goods, mostly on credit, to the value of 1,4007. or 1,5002., which are 
all seized upon by the sheriffs. It is pretended he was non compos 
mentis, but the jury have not yet given their verdict. His brother, 
also a mercer in town, has fallen distracted, and his wench so 
repents it, that it is feared it may endanger her life or wits. It is 
a matter of great grief to our new congregation, of which they were 
both zealous members; but it illustrates that profession is but a 
weak protection against the devil and women, from whose tempta- 
tions I hope Heaven will preserve me and you. [14 pages. SP. 
Dom., Car. II. 259, No. 1.] 


Charles Whittington to Williamson. Some vessels are expected 
from the East with corn, contrary to his Majesty’s proclamation ; 
being searcher of the port of Hull, things of that nature require my 
observation. This proclamation has not, as others have done, em- 
powered searchers to seize or secure the goods, and therefore I desire 
to be informed what has been ordered by his Majesty and Council to 
be done by the Customs’ officers, if any corn be imported, and I will 
proceed accordingly. [Lbid. No. 2.]

Report by Lord Holles, on an order of Council requiring him to 
state what is fit to be done for the relief of Sir Francis Topp and 
Company. I find they complain of great losses sustained in 1664, 
whilst living at St. Malo, by the French seizing thcir goods in time 
of peace, in the very harbours of France, where they had been 
brought in the way of trade, and where—-by several treaties, and the 
law of nations,—they ought to have been free from arrest, the owners 
not having done anything to forfeit their interest. If such a course 
is suffered, it will be the destruction of all commerce between the 
two kingdoms, and it is very dishonourable to his Majesty, that the 
public faith should be broken to his subjects, who trade under his 
protection, by virtue of treaties between the two Crowns. 

Sir F. Topp’s is not a single case, the like having been done 
several times to the English merchants at Rouen, who are not yet 
free of trouble about a capture at sea, made in 1616, by an 
English privateer, of a French ship belonging to one Delaunay, 
valued but at 6,000 livres. While I was Ambassador in France, 
2 English ships coming into harbour at Marseilles, when they had 
landed their goods and paid all duties, were seized upon, and not- 
withstanding all my solicitations, were not discharged, but given 
some months after to the East India Company there, they pre- 
tending some of their ships to have been formerly taken by the 
English. 

I hear the same usage is threatened, if not begun, against the 
English at St. Jean de Luz, for reparation of the widow De Lazin, 
for some goods of her late husband’s, taken from him here by Par- 
liament in 1643; so all this makes me fearful it will become a 
constant custom, if not prevented. I think all care should be taken 
for prevention of it; and for this case of Sir Francis Topp and 
Company, in the first place, a fair application should be made to the 
French King, as well by his Ambassador here, as by his Majesty’s 
Ambassador at Paris, for the just satisfaction of the petitioners, 
which it may be hoped will prove effectual; should it not, it will 
then be time for his Majesty to consider what is further to be done, 
for the vindication of his own honour and the protection of his 
subjects. [Printed. SP. Dom., Car. TI. 259, No. 3.]

Commissioner J. Tippetts to the Navy Commissioners. I am 
sorry that you have grounds to fear making good your contract, 
and that the credit of the Board may be yet exposed, and the stores 
remain unfurnished with timber. The 302 trees are sold to Cozens

at 40s. a load; I think he would accept it, as he has promised that 
none shall be butted till 14 days are over. 

The 3 victuallers have arrived, and are much troubled at their 
stoppage. I want 20 able calkers; Lawrence Williams, a calker, 
may procure and come down with them; those sent from Deptford 
are very inefficient. The country affords no fir timber, and deals 
will soon be wanting. The Dragon has but 64 men entered,

conduct money to fetch their clothes. The pursers promise to send 
up their books. [14 pages. Ibid. No. 10.]

Petition of Henry, Lord Arlington, and John, Lord Berkeley, 
Farmers of the Profits of the General Letter Office, &c., to 
the Duke of York. We have taken to farm the profits of the 
Letter Office, at a considerable increase of rent, under confi- 
dence of enjoying the same, with all the emoluments and 
benefits, in as ample a manner as any former Postmaster- 
General, by virtue of the Act of Parliament, and according 
to his Majesty s proclamation. The collection of letters and 
packets,and the horsing of men for hire, by persons not author- 
ised from the Postmaster-General, are strictly prohibited ; yet 
nevertheless several carriers, stage coaches, and others named, 
take upon themselves to collect letters, to an incredible 
number, and in some stages, double to what the post brings, 
by which means the just profits and dues are very much 
impaired, By these encroachments the rights of the office 
are invaded, and the farm, which vs a considerable part 
of your Royal Highness’ revenwe, will be much lessened in 
value. In 1646, the like proceedings almost proved fatal to 
the letter office, so we beg timely remedies. [14 pages, 
corrected by Williamson. Ibid. No. 151]

[Proposed] Order in Council that—as on 13 March 1668, on peti- 
tion of the City of London, the King dispensed for a year with such 
parts of the Act of Navigation as restrained the import of timber 
and deals, that they might be more plentiful for rebuilding the 
city, whereby they were reduced to a moderate price—his Majesty, 
being unwilling that so much of the stock of his kingdom should 
be spent in freight to foreigners, and yet wishing to encourage the 
speedy rebuilding of the city, lest the carriage of these bulky 
goods should fall into the hands of foreigners, has, on address of 
the Council of Trade, and by advice of the Privy Council, given 
liberty to his subjects to buy 60 vessels fit for this trade, which 


CHARLES II. 291 


1669. 

April 23. shall be naturalized, on the oath of their owners that no foreigner 
shall have any interest therein. They are to be registered as free 
for the Norway and Baltic Sea trade, 40 for the port of London, 
10 for the Western ports, from Dover to Bristol, and 10 to the 
Northern ports, from Harwich to Newcastle. The Farmers 
of Customs are to keep exact registers, so that no more ships than 
those permitted may be made free. With a proviso cancelled, 
signed by the Farmers of Customs, that this order is not to take 
off any aliens’ customs imposed on those ships, and reserved to be 
paid as formerly, by the order of 18 March 1668. [23 pages. 
S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 259, No. 50.] Annexing, 


Report of the Farmers of Customs that the naturalizing of 
60 foreign ships, to be made free for the trade of Norway 
and the Baltic Sea, is contrary to 2 Acts; that for en- 
couragement of navigation, and that for preventing fraud 
in the Customs. Should his Mujesty suspend these 2 laws 
in this particular, the aliens’ duty on those ships need not 
be remitted, as this withdraws money from the revenue, and 
gives it to private traders, and also discourages men fiom 
brinying goods in English shipping, as they can do it 
cheaper in foreign. The dispensation granted last year 
for bringing in building materials continued the payment 
of all duties. 

Most of this trade has been carried on by foreign ships, and 
the materials needed by the city will be brought in, whether 
these ships are made free or not. If the ships are made 
free, it is hoped that they will be limited as to the time in 
which, and the places where, the goods wre to be delivered ; 
that a list of the purchasers will be sent in to be approved 
by his Majesty, and that if the ships are not provided, the 
dispensation will cease—23 April 1669. [Lbid. No. 501.] 


Report of the Council of Trade—on a reference of the 
petition of Thos. Farrington, merchant of London, for 
leave to bring in free from seizure a parcel of timber 
and deals which he provided at Hamburg, for rebuilding 
the city—that the permission will be good, provided the 
timber is imported in English ships, for these reasons: the 
enlargement of trade is the common interest of a trading 
nation, and it would be an advantage if more ports than 
one or two were found for bringing in these commodities, 

The trade in timber and wood from Hamburg would be a great 
advantage, because that from other places is chiefly man- 
aged by the natives in their own shipping, so that although 
the trade in timber has exceedingly increased here, the em- 
ployment of English shipping therein has decreased, but 
would greatly increase, if the Hamburg trade was managed 
by English shipping. 

Hamburg timber would be bought by exchange for our woollen 
goods, whereas Norway timber is bought with ready money 
for the most part.

April 23.

April 24. 


Levant, the commanders requesting my convoy. s 

On the 8th, there being a small vessel of Tangier bound for 
Tituan, to redeem some soldiers that were slaves, the Governor 
requested me to convoy her there, which I did, and then bore for 
Malaga Road, where I arrived on the 11th. If any of his Majesty's 
subjects had been there laden, bound for the westward, I intended 
to convoy them as far as I could; but not finding any, I returned 
for Tangier. 

I sailed on the 13th, and met with a new three-decked French 
man-of-war of 75 or 80 guns, and being covetous of news, I ran 
alongside and hailed him, but could have no other answer but out of 
the mouths of several men speaking English, “Dog, strike your 
topsail.” As I could never understand that language in any of 
his Majesty’s ships, finding the Milford not able to dispute that 
punctilio with him, though very inclinable to it, I passed by, 
telling him in his own words that I scorned to strike a topsail 
for any French dog in the sea; which so disturbed him, that he 
immediately bore up after me, fired, and gave chase for 1} hours, 
when he tacked about. Four other ships coming up, one of which 
was French, on the 15th I anchored in Tangier Road, and gave 
the Governor notice of what had passed. À 

I met Capt. Beary, from Sally, at Tangier, and the Francis 
having arrived from the same place, we consulted with the 
Governor as to the best way of disposing of ourselves, for main- 
taining his Majesty’s honour and annoying his enemies, until 
further orders from his Royal Highness advised us to sail for 
Cadiz to inquire for orders, and if there were none, to keep 
together, and lie off Sally and the Southward Cape. In order to 
do this, we sailed from Tangier on the 19th, and arrived the 20th 
at Cadiz, where I received your letter, directed to Sir Thos. Allin, 
or any of the King’s commanders. Sir Thos. Allin being gone 
home, I opened it, and found his Royal Highness’s commands for 
2 ships to sail for Leghorn, to bring down what merchant ships 
they find ready; and there being no others but Capt. Beary’s and 


mine, we have resolved to proceed there accordingly. [24 pages. 
Ibid. No. 51.] 


Extract of the above. [Jbid. No. 52.]

Edward Byland to Col. Thos. Middleton. I send the length of

proposition concerning fifth-rates for their boats is undeniable, as 
a horse cannot run so fast with a heavy load as a light one; and 
when a frigate is burthened with heavy boats, it is prejudicial to 
her bearing and sailing, and makes her old, and complain before 
her time. I desire that the stores demanded may be hastened 
down, and that you will consider of a spindle for our great crane.

John Brooke and 4 other officers to the Navy Commissioners. We 
have thought fit, from time to time, to commit accounts weekly 
demanded, and all letters, books, and papers relating to the service, 
to Hum. Bray, not daring to trust our uncertain and irregular post

Bray, going out of Rochester early this morning, was stopped by 
Travers, a shop-keeper and the post-officer here, and the accounts, 
&c., including several chest-books lent us by the Brooke House 
Commissioners, taken from him, with menaces of violence if he 
made any resistance, so that his journey was prevented, and his 
tide lost.

Rich. Bower to Williamson. Repetition of part of the letter of 
the 19th. It has. been reported that his Majesty has given orders 
for an inspection to be made as to private meetings, to see whether 
people meet in great numbers, or with more confidence than formerly ; 
and if so, to quicken the justices to more diligence in prosecuting 
the teachers, and the principal of the faction. I know not whether 
this has wrought upon the captain, but he has taken his place as 
alderman, and yet goes to the meeting, where they now sing psalms, 
and may be heard at a great distance. 

His Majesty’s Coronation Day has hitherto been kept with great 
solemnity ; but last Friday it was all laid aside, and no notice 
taken of it, Woodroff, the bailiff, having moved the assembly to 
that purpose at their last meeting. The Earl of Aylesbury and 
Lord Belasyse arrived, and viewed the town, and went away for 
Norwich, but no notice was taken of them, though they were 
known. The Edgar has sailed for the Straits, and the Forester 
and several others are riding at anchor in the Roads. [S.P. 
Dom., Car. TI. 259, No. 75.] 


John Pocock to Hickes. A fleet of 30 sail of Straits men was 
seen yesterday, towards the Isle of Wight, one cf which, the 
Agreement, stopped to put some passengers ashore from Jamaica, 
whence she came in 11 weeks. She reports that the island is in 
a thriving condition, and that the French captain, who was taken 
before the blowing up of the Ozford, was condemned to die; 
but it was supposed the Governor would only keep him in prison 
until he had orders from England. Also that a fleet of privateers 
was plying to the windward, but their design was not known.

April 27. Earl of Winchelsea to the King. In my voyage from Malta here, 

oe 7. JT touched at Catania in Sicily, and was invited by the bishop to 

Nepia lodge in his palace, which I did, the better to inform you of that 
extraordinary tire which comes from Mount Zibell [Etna], 15 miles 
distant, which may be termed a fiery inundation, being 15 miles 
long and 7 broad, advancing into the sea from 600 yards to a mile 
in breadth. It was wonderful to see in the sea this matter like 
ragged rocks, burning in 4 fathoms water, 2 fathoms higher than 
the sea, some parts liquid and throwing about vast stones red hot, 
some part hissing into the sea with a horrible noise and smoke, 
and making a firm foundation in the sea itself. 

I stayed from 9 a.m. Saturday to 7 a.m. next morning, during 
which time this mountain of fire, stones, and cinders had advanced 
20 yards into the sea in several parts, forming a passage like a river 
with steep banks, in which flows liquid fire, with large red hot . 
stones swimming on the fire. 

The stones are 3 fathom, high all over the country, and there are 
secret conduits sending fire and heat into all parts, melting stones 
and cinders, and turning rocks and houses to ashes. The com- 
ponents of these fire stones are sulphur, nitre, quicksilver, sal 
ammonia, lead, and other metals. In some places it has made 
valleys hills, and hills valleys. At night I went upon two towers, 
and could see, at 10 miles distance, that the fire rose from the moun- 
tain as high and big as one of the biggest steeples, and descended 
terribly red, with stones of a paler red, as bigas a table. The country 
is covered with great flames, and smokes like a furnace of melted iron. 

A cavalier of Malta, who attended me, told me the river was as 
liquid as a torrent when it issued from the mountain, and was 5 or 
6 fathoms deep and as broad. Nothing can divert it; in 40 days it 
has destroyed the habitations of 27,000 persons, and made 2 hills, 
one 1,000 paces high and 4 miles in compass, as you may see by the 
draft I send you. 

Of 20,000 persons who were in Catania, only 3,000 remain; all 
their goods are carried away, the brass cannon removed out of the 
castle, great bells taken down, the city walled up, and preparations 
made to abandon it. The fire met a lake of 4 miles’ compass, filled 
it up, and made a mountain of it. I send a relation given me by a

Rich. Watts to Williamson. There have 30 sail come in from 
various parts, one of which reports that an East India ship bound 
for England was met by some Turkish pirates of Algiers, who 
plundered her of 20,000/. in commodities, and all her provisions, 
and then let her go. A Virginia ship reports that 2 which were in 
company with her have foundered. Several would have made land 
5 or 6 weeks since, but were kept back by contrary winds; 40 sail 
more are in the Channel, homeward bound. [S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 
259, No. 154.] 


Capt. Ant. Deane to the Navy Commissioners. I will send a 
draft of the dimensions of a fifth-rate ship, as soon as I can get 
time to draw it. I want the money for felling and converting the 
trees imprested to Mr, Eastwood, the purveyor, who will have the 
charge of doing it, being accustomed to that work. I shall order 
the trees fit for use as often as the service requires it. I hope you 
have the [Treasury] Commissioners’ order for felling, the season 
being far spent for the bark. [Jbid. No. 155.] 


John Huntington, master of the Adam and Eve ketch, to the

[Proposed] bond of George Taylor, of St. Paul’s, Covent Garden, 
and his security, to the Navy Commissioners. Taylor—having 
accused James Adamson and Clement Palmer of making and selling 
false tickets, whereby his Majesty is defrauded—in order that they 
and other persons may be brought to condign punishment, offered to 
the Navy Commissioners, if they would imprest him money, within

convicting them. With note that, Taylor objecting to a penalty of 
201. being inserted, in case of non-performance of the conditions, as 
being double the money placed in his hands, the whole was broken 
off. (Draft. 14 pages. Ibid. No. 157.]

I hope you will supply money for the timber purchased; I have

the continual absence of pursers from their ships; they come on 
shore as soon as they hear there is a muster master in the Downs, 
and take horse for London, so that their stewards may have the 
excuse that they have carried away the keys, and cannot come at 
the books, except the mess book, wherein there are neither entries 
nor discharges. I request that orders may be given for the pursers 
being on board, and furnishing the books required, so as to enable 
me to make a proper muster. I have sent three muster books for 
ships named by the Canterbury coach, and beg an acknowledgment 
of their arrival. [14 pages. Ibid. No. 176.]

Commissioner J. Tippetts to the Navy Commissioners. Particulars 
of the payment and repair of ships, and turning over of their men. 
I am sorry for your difficulty in obtaining money, not so much for 
myself, although I have gone too far by near 1,000/.; but I am 
troubled to think of the condition of the Navy, that a ship three- 
quarter built should lie another year unfinished, and that we can- 
not proceed with the repair of others, for want of materials. We 
must discharge the workmen also, and if without money, their 
cry will be great; my ears are daily filled with their complaints. 
I entreat that they may speedily receive their two months past, 
and the quarter promised them. 

I will let Capt. Deane have 40 men from here for the forest, 
as notwithstanding they are required in the yard, yet the want of 
materials being considered, they may be better spared than that 
number added to the service. 

I cannot give an account of my engagements, but the value is 
about 3,000/., fitting out the ships included; this sum will make 
but a mean supply of timber and plank, works in hand considered ; 
so that were the 500/. in Mr. Ridge’s hands sure, it would make but 
2,1002., which is 900/. short of what is agreed for; if money cannot 
be had, I must relinquish the bargain with Mr. Cozens for the 
302 trees, which will be to his damage, they being in part already 
squared; but he would rather you should leave the bargain, than 
disappoint him of his money. [2 pages. Ibid. No. 193.]

May 7. James Hickes to Williamson. Divers letters of late directed to 

London. Mr. Holder, at the African House, have come to the Letter Office, two 
of which he opened and read, and then gave them back, refusing to 
pay the postage, as there was treason in them, for aught he knew, 
and from whom and whence they came he knew not. I gave them 
to Mr. Ellis, who delivered them tomy Lord. More have since come 
from the same hand, which Ellis showed me, all speaking of per- 
sons coming to the city, with fire balls and grenadoes, to fire White- 
hall, the stables, and his house in Broad Street. In one to-day, 
divers persons are specified as coming to the Strand to-night, and 
to other places to-morrow. I know not whether the letters come 
from some mad or distempered person, but a serious consideration 
and inquisition ought to be had, for the preservation of his 
Majesty’s person, the whole Court, and the remaining part of the 
distressed city. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 259, No. 206.]

Brooke House, Clerk of the Pells, to bring in without delay an account of all 
Holborn. moneys received and paid at the Exchequer, upon the Acts of 
Parliament for raising moneys by the Poll, Additional supply, &c., 
according to a former order of the Committee, dated 5 March 1669,

It grieves me to hear the sad complaints of the workmen for 
want of money ; the discontinuance of their monthly pay will ruin 
them, as it has put them out of credit, and none will trust them. 
I refer you to my last as to a supply of stores; you very well 
know that want of seasonable repairs is as destructive to a navy 
of ships as the wars. 

I have stopped the pay of the boatswairt of the Nightingale, several 
of the seamen accusing him of having sent ropes, oars, and sails on 
shore, belonging to the ship. I sent the Clerk of the Survey on 
board the Princess, and he found 42 coils of Flemish rope in the 
boatswain’s store room, which he alleges were sent by Sir Edw. 
Sprage as an adventure, but not sold | off. [13 pages. S.P. Dom., 
Car. II. 260, No. 13.] 


Hugh Salesbury, Clerk of the Survey, to Pepys. I went on board

Daniel Fleming to Williamson. Iam glad to hear of. your late 
purchase at Winderwath, since it will oblige you to have more 
kindness for this county [Westmoreland], and I hope it will make 
you a suitable return. I know of none that envies you this or 
your other purchase in Cumberland, and for my part I am very 
joyful of it. 

The Presbyterians are designing some mischief, for besides the 
boldness of the highwaymen in divers places, there are many false 
reports; such as that the Scots are up in arms; that the Bishops’ 
and Deans and Chapters’ lands will be sold, or annexed to the 
Crown, in place of the Excise or Hearth Money, and the Bishops 
be maintained by salaries out of the Exchequer. I believe mischicf 
is intended, as a field officer in the late war amongst them was told 
by one faction in Yorkshire that, if he would stand for a Parlia- 
ment man, he should not only have his charges of the election, but 
be defrayed during his stay at the Parliament, out of a common 
purse; and if he doubted, he should have good security. But he 
declining, they endeavoured to engage him and his interest 
against the election of any courtier, or episcopal person, which 
shows the activity of the party to undo us; if that fails, then 
probably they'll follow some martial method. “1 hope God will 
be so favourable as not to permit the King and Kingdom to be

On some dispute as to the pensions granted 26 Oct., 1660, to John, 
Earl of Bath, made groom of the stole, and first gentleman of the 
bedchamber, in place of the late Duke of Somerset, it was proved 
that the Earl’s predecessors had enjoyed 5,0007. a year above the 
diet and board wages; viz., 2,000/. from the customs, 2,0007. from the 
privy purse in lieu of plate from the jewel house, and 1,0007. from 


the cvstoms in lieu of liveries from the great wardrobe ; therefore 


on 10 May 1661, the said Earl was appointed to be paid the said

then he has had a patent for the 2,000/. on the customs, and now

arrears. We order for payment of the said 3,000/. in addition to the

a debt due by the late King to my father. I cannot but lament 
that, after so many years spent by iny father in the service of King 
James and the late King, and the consumption therein of so great 
an estate, his Majesty cannot reward so loyal and deserving a ser- 
vant as he ought and would. But the thorn presses deeper now, 
as I am destroyed by a patent granted by his Majesty to Colonel 
Vernon which, if it does not absolutely determine my command in 
Needwood, so lessens it that in esteem I shall be worse than nothing ; 
his patent is for 3 lives, instead of during pleasure, which is con- 
trary to your lordship’s statement to me. 

Pray solicit a similar grant in my patent, which will restore my 
honour, and be a comfort to my family and posterity, as otherwise 
I shall be looked upon as one high in his Majesty’s displeasure. 
I conceive that Col. Vernon’s services merit great reward, but 
nevertheless that I ought to have been consulted before any grant

Surveyor Thos. Middleton to the Navy Commissioners, I think 
the Fountain the most proper ship for the voyage to the West 
Indies, if his Royal Highness does not appoint the Sweepstakes. We 
shall find sufficient Spanish tables for present supply aboard other 
ships, but the reason of the demand is that as Capt. Kempthorne 
had two for the accommodation of the Ambassadors, and some other 
ships wanting them, and no joiners to make any, we thought it best 
to have some in store. Spanish tables are much cheaper to the 
King than those formerly used, and I do not find any waste has 
been made; but if they were made of deal boards, they would be as 
useful and of half the price. The copper demanded is for the 
chimney of the St. David, and for funnels for the houses of office, 
which were formerly made of lead, but it is believed copper will be 
cheaper. 

I have not been negligent in my duty so far as I have understood 
it, and I may say without presumption that I understand as much

1669. : ; 
of tle King’s naval affairs as anyone that shall teach me; but if 
new work is cut out daily, there is no man in England shall ever

I had given order for a supply of lime, copper, &c., and a promise 
to pay when delivered, before your order arrived. Mr. Pett’s timber 
is very ordinary, and not fit for the new ship; I sent Mr. Lawrence 
to view it, and he says Sir Roger [Twysden] has 500 loads stand- 
ing, the like of which is not to be found in any other part of the 
country, and is convenient for transporting. Mr. Tippetts has dis- 
coursed about it with Sir Roger, who will fell, bark, and take the 
lops, and sell it for 40s. per ton by the girth, so that you can have 
a load of 6 feet for 40s. The charge of bringing it into the yard 
will be 10s. a load, but you may judge it a good bargain at 3/.; 
and it will be much cheaper, as there must be knees and compass 
timber in it. Particulars of other timber offered and agreed for. 
The wharves and dock need repair, they going very much to decay.

Petition of Edw. Phillips to the King, for a free pardon. Was 
convicted of felony at the York assizes, but upon report his 
Majesty was pleased to stay the execution of the sentence of death 
during pleasure. With reference thereon to Baron Chris. Turner, 
and his report that the petitioner was convicted of taking a horse, 
bridle, saddle, and 35l. in money, from one Hotham; that it 
appeared that the petitioner had notice the night before that 
Hotham was going to take a journey with the money, and de- 
signed to rob him, and accordingly waylaid him, and finding him 
on the road, unhorsed him and cut the strings of his portmanteau ; 
but Hotham seized and kept him down until some company came, 
and took him to prison. That during the scuffle, the petitioner at 
one time had Hotham’s horse’s bridle in his hand, when Hotham 
had not hold of his horse, and consequently, by construction of law, 
possessed both the horse, bridle, saddle, and money, and was found 
guilty accordingly. This verdict he considers was very just, but 
somewhat severe, and he conceives the petitioner may be a fit object 
for pardon.—25 May 1669. [S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 260, No. 92.] 


Entry of the above reference. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 33, p. 28 |

Phin, Pett and Edw. Homewood to Surveyor Thos. Middleton. 
There are 12 copper furnaces returned from the ships lying in the

Edw. Byland to the Navy Commissioners. I was at Dartford 
yesterday, to treat with the merchant for a spindle for the crane, 
but I never treated with so lofty a fellow in my life ;-what induces 
him to it is that he has bought up all the timber hereabouts, 
and says if he knew where one load was to be bought, he would 
have it, and so make people pay his own price. I proffered him 
3l. 15s. Od. a load, but he stood at 5l., and fell to 4l. 15s. Od., the 
greatest rate, I presume, that was ever given since Noah’s Ark was 
built. I desire you will empower my servant to set the broad 
arrow upon the timber, giving the market price, which is 31. a 
load, to the merchant. I would have given 4l. rather than have 
come away dissatisfied. Pray be mindful of my poor brother, 
the smith, who will be utterly ruined unless he is commiserated. 


[Zbid. No. 117.]

Capt. Rich. Beach to Lord Brouncker. I have your and Sir 
John Mennes’ order for discharge of Robert Dowter and Thos. 
Walter—the one a pretended mate and the other his boatswain— 
and beg you will take notice that there was no protection, and 
therefore I have committed no error. I should not have wanted 
men had not merchantmen advanced their wages ; I had 130 volun- 
teers entered at Deptford, but since then they have deserted, and 
others are not to be had without pressing, as all other ships have 
done, and must do before they go, except one who has some of my 
men. If we must clear every man that their Honours are im- 
portuned for, we must expect to carry but few able men to sea. 
I have cleared the boatswain, but kept the other till further orders. 
Pray hasten down the provisions, that we may be gone. [Jbid. 
No. 121.]

H. R. [Wm. Haggett to Sir P. Musgrave]. Iam glad to hear of 
your good journey from London, and safe arrival at home. The 
gentlewoman showed me at least 20 books [by] the authors of 
“The Judgment with those called 5th Monarchy men”; I borrowed 
one, which is in several pieces, by Mr. Moore. She informed me 
that what books I desired were at my service; her husband is 
expected home in a fortnight, so I will send you an account of 
what I gain from him. ; 

All friends are generally discontented. I meta Quaker returning 
from a meeting at Heighington [Durham], and took notice of him 
as he was very well mounted; he said that it was time to look 
about them, or they would be all run down; and that they had had 
a meeting of 55. Rob. Markendaile, at Barnard Castle, told Mat. 
Sowerby and me that they are much troubled at Newcastle by the 
Act being put into execution, but that they will suffer with 
patience for a time, and wait the Lord’s call, and then doubt not 
but all will be in readiness to work out their deliverance. I was 
with Chr. Eyons and others of that clan, who say that trading is 
much down in London, and that the greatest traders are so much 
discouraged at the late Act against meetings, that they draw in 
their moneys apace, to the undoing of most young tradesmen ; also 
that a great quantity of cloth was shipped for beyond sea, and all 
taken out again. They think, if there be a rising, it will begin 
in the South, but the North will produce powerful backers. 

I desire to hear from you, as without assistance I shall spoil 
myself with charges in the business. They think there will be 
much mischief; I shall write every week if Ican. The meetings are 
kept up at Newcastle; Gilpin is the boldest of any of the speakers, 
and Pringle the next. The Mayor slights the informers when they 
give notice of the meetings. A lieutenant, one of them, broke 
his own neck, which was not a little made -use of. A constable 
apprehended one of the speakers, but was compelled to let him 
go, or the people would have beat out his brains; he informed 
the mayor that if he gave him 1007., he would never meddle with 
any of them again, as he should have lost his life if the speaker 
had not risked his own to save it. 

I have been informed of several ways they have of avoiding the 
Act, one of which is to choose a convenient house where others 
are pretty rank on either side and opposite, and so hear the 
preacher from the window; at other times they preach in the 
street. I hear from 2 Quakers that the Turks have taken many 
English ships, with 1,700 young men, and 700 married ; I believe 
from such stories that the Quakers would rather be ruled by Turk 
or Pagan, than that the present authority should continue where it 
is. [2 pages. S.P. Dom., Car. II. 260, No. 186. See p. 418, infra.]

May 25. Jonas Shish to the Navy Commissioners. I want a supply of 
Deptford. sheathing board for the Sweepstakes, ordered on a voyage to the 
West Indies. [Zbid. No. 141.] 


May 25. Capt. Rich. Beach to the Navy Commissioners. I find there 
The Hampshire. have been complaints against me and my officers, about the im- 
pressing of men, and that some of our officers have taken 2 salmon 
as a bribe for clearing some men. I have examined it upon oath, 
and find that it was the master’s voluntary gift, and that my men 
had not pressed a man, but were coming away when the salmon 
was forced upon them; it was neither kind nor just to believe such 
a fanatic fellow, before examination, or the truth found out. I 
have not committed any action that I am afraid or ashamed of, nor 
do I believe my officers acted anything contrary to his Royal 
Highness’s warrant, or my orders. None have been pressed that 
had a protection, and I should have had no occasion to press at all, 
had not the merchantmen advanced their wages; whatever preten- 
sions are made by others, they will have as much occasion to press 
before they get to sea as I had. [Zbid. No. 142.] 


May 25. Rice Freeman, purser of the Hampshire, to the Navy Commis- 
sioners. I cannot stow the 6 months’ bread ordered, by 7 or 8 ewt. ;

[Sir Edm. Windham, Knight Marshal, to Lord Arlington.] Jane 
Lutterell, widow, of Marshwood, co. Somerset, being possessed of a 
treasure in gold and silver value 15,0007., Maynard her coachman, 
and Ann Cory who attended her, with assistance of others, after her 
death, got the keys of the chest, and secretly conveyed away the money. 
Maynard and Cory, with 2 others named, were indicted, and a bill was 
found against them, but their trial was suspended till next assizes, in 
order to a further discovery. The 2 latter are at large, and residing 
at a common inn, where their confederates make daily application 
to them, and the justices of peace will not act unless commanded 
by the Lord Chief Justice. Request that the prisoners may be 
arrested and secured, and that Justice Kelynge may be desired to 
engage some justices of the peace for that and other purposes. 
[S.P. Dom., Car IT. 260, No. 164.] 


The King to Lord Chief Justice Vaughan and Justice Archer. 
Statement of the above case of Jane Lutterel]l. As the justices of 
the county omit vigorous prosecution, and some of the accused are 
at liberty, and countenanced by persons of interest, we require you 
to order the justices of the county to make a thorough examination 
of the parties accused, and to use all lawful means for a full dis- 
covery of the fact, and of all the accomplices, that justice may be 
done therein. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 31, f. 24.]

Levant Company to Sir Dan. Harvey, Ambassador [in Turkey]. 
Pray procure the Grand Seignior’s usual command, investing Sir 
Clement Harby as Consul in the Morea, and send it with your lord- 
ship's commission by express to Petras, so as to meet Sir Clement

[Lord Arlington] to the Mayor of Exeter. All the use I could 
make of your letter, about. Mr. Glide’s impertinent and indiscreet 
appearance in the Council Chamber of the city, with a pretended 
message from his Majesty, was to acquaint his Majesty with it, who 
commanded me to bid the mayor, in his name, to prevent, with care 
and discretion, all unlawful assemblies of that kind, which by their 
excess in number, or manner of behaviour, may endanger the public 
peace, and give affront to the established worship or government of 
the Church ; and to proceed according to law against the preacher 
and the principal offenders therein. As for Mr. Glide, you may 
make such account of him as his deportment and value in the city 
have put upon him. [Draft, holograph. 1} pages. S.P. Dom., 
Car. II, 261, No. 1.] i

Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. The wind changing, nearly all the 
ships have left ; there is a report that Taffaletta intends to besiege 
Algiers by land, and us by sea; the Dutch joining us, and Taffaletta 
taking it, we are to be free for ever. Two Virginia ships have 
come in. [S.P. Dom., Car. TI. 261, No. 2.] 


Dr. Thos. Lamplugh to Rob. Francis. I desire your assistance 
in hastening a grant of a prebend of Worcester, which the King 
has conferred upon me. [Jbid. No. 3. See p. 358, imfra.] 


Earl of Winchilsea to [Lord Arlington]. Particulars of a journey 
from Malta. At Florence the Grand Duke showed me a new map 
of the progress of the fire of Catania, which is now entered into 
the city, and is progressing into the sea. I expect to have a per- 
fect draft of that fire, which I design for his Majesty. Virgil, in his 
Georgics, names this fiery mountain [Etna] as breaking out on the 
death of Julius Ceesar. 

From Florence I went to Pisa and Leghorn, and thence to Venice, 
where | met a galley from this State sent for me. The Republic 
would have received me publicly, but I went by invitation to the © 
house of Signor Giovanni Agostino Durazzo, to whom I had shown 
civilities when he was Ambassador at Constantinople ; all our nation 
here much express their obligations to this family. This morning

Thos. Page to Williamson. The enclosed are recommended to

Sir Geoffery Shakerley to Williamson, Hearing that one 
Garside, —amongst divers others that had long fled from authority 
by shifting from county to county, and changing his apparel—-was 
keeping a conventicle at Bosly Chapel, 5 miles from Chester, I took 
a friend, and one of my own men, and went to the place, where I found 
him in the act of his pretended devotions, with about 200 persons, 
from whom I received much opposition, but more abuse by their 
foul language. I secured Garside, who confessed he had never been 
in orders, and sent him to prison, for refusing to give security to 
answer the law for this unlawful assembly. I hope to see the laws 
executed upon some more of the ringleaders. Their insolence is 
grown to that height that some of the chief of the female disciples 
said openly that the King tolerated their meeting, and that they 
therefore wondered I disturbed them; it will much lessen his 
Majesty’s authority in his subordinate magistrates, if some severe 
course be not speedily taken to restrain those confident expressions 
and practices. [Zbid. No. 22.] 


St. J. Steventon to the Navy Commissioners. I want direc- 
tions as to checking and keeping the time of 40 shipwrights, sent 
into the Forest by the master-shipwright, it being a new thing 
to send men out of the yard to hew a ship’s frame. [Jbid. No. 23.] 


Account of necessaries required for going down to sound ,the 
Galloper Sands; viz., 3 vessels and 2 good skiffs, 6 buoys, 2 able 
pilots, sounding leads and lines, and fitting instructions. [Jbid. 
No. 24.] 


Capt. Martin Carslake to Thos. Hayter. Particulars of the 
length and breadth of the Golden Hand. I have not taken in 
any of the stores, but hope to do so by next week, if we have the 


help of the ordinary. I need a carpenter, and a gunner, mine being 
ill. [Zbid. No. 25.] 


Capt. Ant. Deane to the Navy Commissioners. I have been to 
Shoreham, Arundel, and Pulborough, to see what plank may be had 
for the new ship; and also to the New Forest, where I found all 
the men at their labour, of which you will have an exceeding good 
account. I marked out several suitable trees, and can see nothing 
to hinder the work, except their month’s pay, which they much 
urge, to procure provisions and credit, the country people being shy. 
I have seen all the shipwrights, and can only discover 18, although 
8 ships are building; they are forced to get house carpenters and 
labourers, and what other help they can; men from London are 
wanted. The King’s monthly pay of 2s. 1d. a day will not invite, 
while the builders are giving 3s. and 8s. 6d. to good workmen, there 
being a scarcity of men in these parts. I propose that the few 
men in the Forest may work overtime, as it comes to little or 
nothing, and much is to be done in avery short time. I want 
leave to come to London to attend his Royal Highness. [23 pages. 
Ibid. No. 26.]

Petition of Broome Whorwood to the King. Before your restor- 
ation, my wife sued me for alimony, got a Chancery decree in 
the suit, and obtained several orders of sequestration of all 
my estate, for not observing the decree. Thereupon I appealed 
to your Majesty, who. heard the whole matter, and made 
order that I should settle 3001, a year upon trustees for her 
maintenance during her life, and also pay her 1,0001. in 
satisfaction of all arrears and costs: thereupon I sealed the 
writings, and paid her 5001, as also another 5001. by her 
direction to the sequestrators, who, as they pretended, 
had a much greater sum due to them by her. 

The sequestrators being clamorous for the remainder of 
their money, amounting to above 1,0001., there was a second 
appeal to your Majesty, who declared that what money had 
been paid, by reason of the sequestration, by my wife should 
be wholly borne by her, but that what was due to any officer 
or persons in the country should be paid by me; in obedi- 
ence to which, I have paid above 5001. more to the said 
sequestrators, and have their discharge for the whole, being 
above 1,0001. ; but I am nevertheless again prosecuted to 
repay to my wife the 5001. which was paid to the sequestru- 
tors, although your Majesty declared in your order that what 
was paid should stand, and commanded me to pay the

you to permit Stephen Akerman, late a soldier in the Dutch war, 
and now a grocer in your town, to exercise his trade, dispensing 
with the statute requiring the serving an apprenticeship, for breach 
of which he is indicted. Many persons in the town follow trades 
without apprenticeship, and he, for his services, deserves equal 
encouragement. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 25, f. 106.]

Petition of Sam. Free, English merchant at Hamburg, to the 
King, for leave to bring in boards and timber of German growth 
which he bought, considering that the Act of Navigation rendered 
their import in English ships lawful; but some persons intend to 
take advantage of a passage in a later Act against frauds in Cus- 
toms, and to order them to be seized on if he sends them. Pleads 
that without such import of materials, at the present price of 
building, London never can be rebuilt. With note thereon, 
23 June, to consult former similar orders; reference by Council, 
30 July, to the Farmers of Customs; and their report, 3 Aug., that 
such import is not contrary to the Act of Navigation, and that 
since that Act, a special privilege was granted for import of Ham- 
burg goods, whether in English or Hamburg vessels. [S.P. Dom., 
Car. II. 261, Nos. 504, B, C.]

Levant Company to Paul Ricaut, Smyrna. Complaint having 
been made to us by the administrators of the late Consul Cave, that 
you detain his estate, and the books and papers, we have denied 
that it is done by our order, we having only directed detention of 
such as would answer our demands on him which, with 2,000 dollars 
deposited by the owners of the Greyhownd, and interest thereon, we 
judged to be about 6,000 or 7,000 dollars. Supposing that the 
principal has been made good to our and the owners’ account, of 
which you are to take care, we have agreed with the administrators 
that only 2,504 dollars of the Consul’s estate shall remain in our 
hands, which is to be made good to our treasurer, with such interest 
as vou shall find has been received by Cave. As to the rest of his 
estate, together with his books and papers, we refer you to such 
directions as you shall receive from the administrators, to whom 
you are to give such assistance as may prevent any further cause 
for complaint. [Levant Papers, Vol. 5, p. 209.] 


Petition of the merchants trading to the Canary Islands to the King 
and Council, showing that since the reinforcing the Act for prizing 
wines, their trade is much injured, and the export of English goods 
and the receipt of customs reduced to one-third, whilst during its 
discontinuance, trade revived, more shipping was employed, goods 
exported value 140,000/., and bullion, &., imported, and customs of 
60,0007. a year paid; they request aid by a free commerce, to 
prevent the utter ruin of the traders. [6 signatures. S.P. Dom., 
Car. IT. 261, No. 72.]

Dr. Ralph Cudworth to Williamson, I desire you will stop any 
dispensation for Mr. Bambrig to hold a living of the college’s 
presentation with his fellowship, beyond the time allowed by the 
statute. He has had all favour imaginable, but is insatiable, and 
cannot continue longer holding these two together without great 
grievance to the college. Very deserving persons will wait upon you 
shortly, not for a dispensation, but for his Majesty’s recommendation, 
lest unworthy persons should obtain mandates elsewhere, to obstruct 
their preferment and the college’s liberty of choice. Mr. Bam- 
brig’s place, lawfully void, will be filled by virtue of a letter 
lately received from your office, and I hope nothing will issue to 
invalidate that act. [S.P. Dom., Car. 1I. 261, No. '73.]

his head. The Duke of York stated the rule to be that English 
ships are everywhere to be saluted first, but not to strike again, 
only answer with guns; but if a single English ship meets a fleet 
out of our seas, he is to salute first, but neither are to strike.

Rules as to precedence in saluting; that the sea salutes the land,

Report of the Earl of Sandwich and 7 others, that no foreign 
man-of-war should pass above the forts at Gravesend and Sheerness, 
in the Thames and Medway, without orders from the Lord Admiral, 
nor in other harbours, without leave from the Governor. That all 
foreign ships bearing flags are to salute first, and be answered gun 
for gun; other ships to have 2 guns less; that the point of flag 
striking is too important for them to decide on, and must be left to 
the King; and that all merchant ships must strike to the forts. 
[Ibid. No. 86.] 


Queries on which Sir John Griffith desires the Duke of York’s 
orders in writing, with replies thereto. No foreign man-of-war is 
to be allowed to pass above the forts at Gravesend or Sheerness, or 
any other harbour, without leave from the Lord Admiral or Governor 
of the fort; all are to strike the flag as long as they are in sight of 
the fort, and in case of refusal, they are to be compelled; all mer- 
chant ships whatsoever are to strike to the forts. The salutes of 
foreign flagships are to be answered gun for gun; of other foreign 
ships with 2 guns less. [Jbid. Nos. 87, 874, 87B, 87c.]

Petition of the Aldermen and Stewards of the Bakers’ Company 
for the City of Chester to the King, to augment the liberties of their 
corporation, so that they may extend to any place within 2 miles of 
the city, and thereby remedy ali abuses and inconveniences suffered 
by the trade. Were incorporated in the time of Henry VIL, and 
had their rules and orders confirmed by Arthur, then Prince of Wales 
and Earl of Chester, and several succeeding kings, whereby they 
were bound to find sufficient bread for all the people that came 
to Chester, and were to keep and deliver the assize of bread once 
a week; no persons not belonging to the craft were to sell any 
bread within the city, but twice a week in the market place. 
Notwithstanding this, several country bakers have crept into a 
place within the city, to which the petitioners’ liberties do not 
extend, and make and sell great quantities of bread not of assize, 
whereby they abuse the people, and disparage the corporation. 
With reference thereon to Solicitor-General Heneage Finch, and 
his report that it will be for the good of the City of Chester to con- 
firm the said charter and extend its liberties as desired. [S.P. Dom. 
Car. IT. 261, No. 107.]

chain already made is 100 fathoms, and the weight 140 tons; the 
money received is 2007. If it is to be completed for the old place, 
it must be 150 fathoms more, the whole weight whereof will be 
35 tons, and it will cost 1,5007. I desire 400/. in hand to buy 
stock, 500/. more in 10 weeks, and the residue on the finishing of 
the work, which will be in 18 weeks. 

The master of attendance promises to move the hulk into 
another place, which will be more convenient, and there 150 
fathoms shall serve better than 250 where she was to lie; and the 
weight of this will be 22 tons, which will cost 9007. If this be 
ordered, I shall require 400/. in hand, and the remainder when 
finished, which will be in 10 weeks. I would rather do the former, 
the money being much more, but am so much a subject that I

Wm. Penn [Quaker] to Lord Arlington. As thou art supreme 
Secretary of State, the person to whom I surrendered, by whose 
order I was committed, and who took my examination about a note 
suspected. to have fallen from me at Goring House, and as thy 
candid promises of assistance are strong encouragements, I make no 
apology for troubling thee with the enclosed, thinking that the 
honour which will redound to thee, by assisting the helpless, will 
far exceed any advantage that can succeed to me. Endorsed [by 
Williamson] “Young Penn, from the Tower, July 1669.” [Jbid. 
No. 130.] Annexing, 


W. Penn to Lord Arlington. Were I as criminal as my ad- 
versaries have represented me, it might become me to bear 
my sufferings without resentment of injustice done, and to 
esteem a vindication of my cause as an aggravation of 
my guilt; but it is notorious that common fame (a most 
incompetent accuser) has maliciously belied me, and that I 
stand not guilty of what my adversaries would fasten on 
me, namely, the denial of the eternal Deity of Christ and 
the Holy Spirit. 

If the observation be of any notice that Cornelius Tacitus makes 
upon the case of Petronius Turpilianus—who, though he 
deserved the punishment inflicted, yet because it was done 
without due examination and conviction, suffered wrong- 
fully—then for a greater reason must my confinement be 
injurious, who have been shut up under a strict and close 
imprisonment for 6 months, without the least formal cause or 
reason why exhibited against me. The Quakers, of whom I 
am one, are not remiss in pursuit of just, sober, and indus- 
trious courses. I hope I shall not longer continue a 
prisoner, merely to persuade the world I am not innocent of 
what I am not guilty. I desire that thou wilt give me a 
hearing, or that I may be allowed access to the King, to 
answer all interrogatories ; and also be allowed the liberty 
of the Tower, which it is customary for prisoners to enjoy, 
after the first or second month of their restraint. With a 
long vindication of his innocence. [6 pages. Ibid. No. 1801.]

Information of David Ogilvy, late major, now in the Guards, to 
Lord Arlington. Calling on 6 June at the house of Thos. Bird- 
whistle, a cutler,in Church Side Alley, nigh to Fetter Lane, a friend 
of mine offered to buy some swords; but they not agreeing to the 
price, Birdwhistle said he was indifferent as to parting with them, 
as he had sold more within a few months than he had done for 
several years past; and upon being asked to whom, he replied that 
it was not for tradesmen such as he was to be inquisitive, but 
that they were taken from him faster than he could make them. 
Endorsed “ Arms bought up by Scotchmen.” [Zbid. No. 133.] 


John Pocock to Hickes. Several ships stopped by contrary 
winds have put to sea for Newfoundland. The Paradise of Lon- 
don has arrived from Virginia. [Jbid. No. 134.] 


Sir Geoffrey Shakerly to Williamson. Since I took the Conven- 
ticlist at Bosley Chapel, I have taken another at Congleton, where 
were 100 people assembled, and their chief speaker, one Boden, a 
pitiful, broken butter merchant, has been committed to prison, for 
refusing to give security to answer his unlawful practices. The 
way we take to punish these people, and prevent their meetings, is 
by committing or binding them over to the next sessions, and pro- 
ceeding against them by indictment for keeping riotous and unlaw- 
ful assemblies. There is one Ambrose Price, a notorious and 
dangerous fellow, upon this account, who made his essay both at 
Bosley and at Congleton, where he resides; and as the mayor and 
his brethren are very remiss in his apprehension, I shall be forced 
to issue a warrant, as deputy-lieutenant, to some officer of the 
militia. [Zbid. No, 135.] 


E. Wall to Williamson. What the men I spoke to you of do is 
not in opposition to authority, they being men of a peaceable 
temper, and willing to serve and take the oaths of Common 
Councilmen, though they are not satisfied as to subscribing. The 
Common Council here, knowing them to be peaceable, only 
begins with them, and if they were brought in, would fall on others 
whom they conceive would not willingly join with them, rather 
to raise money by fines, than from any desire they have of their 
company. I could show several reasons to this purpose, but will 
not be tedious; only they are told that some put upon the like in 
other places have been excused by a letter from the King or Lord 
Arlington, and if it could be obtained by your means, it would very 
much engage you to your friends here, and continue peace amongst 
us ; there are enough willing to take the employment, and therefore 
there can be no necessity for those. [Jbid. No. 136.] 


Jo. Fitzherbert to Williamson. Particulars of the arrival of ships 
from Virginia, Barbadoes, &c. Percy, a Nonconformist from Lon- 
don, having by his zealous craft cheated a rich widow and married 
her, has set up a congregation in the town, and had upwards of 
600 people at Mr. Hollway’s last Sunday. [Jbid. No. 137.]

“ Advices received,” being notes from letters calendared above, 
and from the following :— 


Amsterdam, 47 June.—The Prince of Tuscany has arrived, on 
his way to Italy, upon the sickness of his lady. 

Warsaw, 8 June—The Castelain of Poland has proposed that 
the future King shall conform to their habit; learn their 
tongue, if not of the country ; not marry without consent of 
the States; admit the Salic law, as in France ; not resign his 
crown. To which the Chancellor added, that no foreign 
Ambassador should continue long in Poland. 

Stockholm, 11 June.—The Tartar Envoy is gone, but Seliendael 
went not with him, only an officer to treat for the ransom of 
Swedish prisoners. The Earl of Carlisle is yet incognito. He 
went to-day to the place called the Black Sea, to salute their 
Majesties. 

Copenhagen, 15 June.—The Countess of Carlisle has passed the 
sound with 9 vessels. Baron de Guldenlew is still in Norway, 
the ship that was to transport him being damaged. 

Hague, 47 June.—The Rheingrave is expected daily. The Queen 
of Bohemia’s creditors petition the States to order Boreel, their 
Ambassador, to solicit the debt in England. The Spanish 
Ambassador has acquainted the States with all that passed at 
Lisle between the Commissioners. Utrecht has consented to 
the reinforcement of our company, and a general view of the 
army this year. Capt. Evers complains of ill-usage in the river 
of Lisbon, on pretence that a Portugal ship had been as ill dealt 
with in Holland. The States order complaint to be made to 
the Portugal Ambassador, and information to be taken whether 
any Portuguese have suffered here. [13 pages. SP. Dom., 
Car. IT. 261, No. 143.] 


Jo. Carlile to Williamson. I can sometimes send news, but have 
been hitherto prevented through illness. I suppose Mr. Lodge is 
careful to do that as to Deal. Lords Chesterfield and Clifford have 
arrived, and informed me that the Queen Mother has again re- 
covered. [Ibid. No. 144.] 


Ma. Anderton to Williamson. Darcy Lassells, the notorious 
highwayman, has been executed. A ship laden with deals, hemp, 
&e., bound for Dublin, is reported to have foundered off Holyhead, 
and of 11 men, only 3 escaped. The fanatics are very bold, and 
have frequent conventicles, and there vent dangerous doctrines, 
tending to sedition, if not rebellion. Sir Geoffery Shakerly, the 
Governor, broke up one of their meetings yesterday, and carried 
the speaker to the castle; so I doubt not but in a short time, we 
shall suppress these unlawful assemblies, and thus prevent the 
ill effects of them. [Jbid. No. 145.]

Honour, of which I am high steward, and being informed by you 
that there is an order from his Majesty not to allow any such thing,

Petition of Edward, Bishop of Carlisle, to the King. During the 
rebellion, the greater part of Rose Castle, the only residence of 
this bishopric, was burnt or taken down. The late bishop, now 
Archbishop of York, had as much money for fines of leases and 
casualties as might have repaired or rebuilt the castle, but he only 
fitted up a few rooms that remained, and built some outhouses, 
leaving the rest, as well as the reparation of the chancels of several 
churches, a burden to his successors. Has appealed to his Grace to 
rebuild the house, but as he declines to do it, the only remedy is 
to sue him by ecclesiastical law; as his Grace is the supreme 
judge in the court of York, begs his Majesty, as supreme ordinary 
in all causes ecclesiastical, to appoint a commission to examine into 
and decide upon the case. With reference thereon to the Lord 
Keeper of the Great Seal, the Lord Chief Justices and Chief Baron, 
and their report, 7 July 1669, in favour of the grant of a com- 
mission as requested. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 261, No. 173.]

&c., at Oxford, and obstructed the enemy’s pamphlets, but lost 9000. 
by burning of his house, &c., at Reading, was taken prisoner at

John Bower to Hickes. A ship of this town picked up a boat 
with 4 or 5 men belonging to the Forester, the convoy to the Iceland 
fleet, and set them on shore at Whitby. They reported that a 
Danish pirate had surprised and plundered many ships, and 
taken possession of a pink belonging to Hamburg, in which the 
captain of the pirate embarked, she being a better sailer; but 
the Forester, having notice of it, took the pink and sent her to 
England. The captain, who was put in charge with these men by 
the Forester, to bring her home, forced the men into a boat, to go 
on board a Holland dogger to buy fresh fish; and as soon as they 
were put off, directed his course towards Hamburg, leaving them at 
sea in a boat 5 miles from land. With note by Hickes that the 
writer has not corresponded of late. [Jbid. No. 182.] 


John Clarke to Hickes. Four or five London ships have put in 
outward bound, 2 French vessels with salt, and 3 or 4 from 
the Isle of Wight with timber. [Jbid. No. 183.]

Report of Lord Arlington and Secretary Trevor to the King, 
on the reference made to them of the petition of the Earl of 
Bristol, as to his right to the 10,0007. granted to him from the for- 
feiture of prohibited goods imported, &e. We find that the amount 
was granted to the Earl in consideration of several sums due, as 
certified by Lord Ashley and Sir Wm. Morice, and that the Lord 
Privy Seal obliged the Earl to give his acquittance for the 10,0000. 
before a Master in Chancery, before he would pass the grant, which 
he did; nevertheless the grant was suspended, upon a particular dis- 
pleasure of his Majesty towards the Earl, and the profits of the pro- 
hibited goods were applied to the privy purse, though with a promise 
by the Earl of Falmouth, in his Majesty’s name, that the Earl of 
Bristol should not be frustrated of his grant thereby. That the 
Earl purchased of Charles I., for a valuable consideration, a pension 
of 2,0001. a year for 21 years, by a rent-charge on the revenue of 
the Court of Wards, of which 16 or 17 years remained unexpired 
at the Restoration, for which he expects satisfaction, as well for 
the grant of the wardship of Lord Brooke, given to him by 
Charles I. for services rendered. We conceive, in consideration of 
the eminent quality, sufferings, and services of the Earl, that 
according to justice, it is incumbent on his Majesty to restore him 
the means of raising the 10,000/..so due, out of the profits of pro- 
hibited goods, or any other fund to his Majesty’s better liking ; and 
to further recompense him by re-establishing the pension of 2 0007. 
for such time as his Majesty shall think fit, he being in possession 
of no other mark of favour, and holding no office under the 
Crown. [23 pages. Ibid. No. 189.]

Sir John Skelton and Jas. Blackborne to the Navy Commissioners.

Capt. Rob. Clark to the Navy Commissioners. The [late] Trea- 
surer of the Navy said my money was not stopped in 1667, but 
suspended until the Earl of Anglesey should bring money into the 
office. I take the suspension to be as bad as stopping, when I can- 
not have it paid; I have nothing to say to the Earl, whether he 
ever brings money or no; the money was ordered by his Majesty in 
Council, for payment of the ships that came home with Sir Thos. 
Allin, and all the other commanders and officers have been paid, 
and mine only suspended. I only desire my own, and beg you will 
order payment. If you want money, there is enough left here of men 
run away, and 10 times as much as mine is. [S.P. Dom., Car. TI. 
262, No. 1.]

The King to the Duke of York. Having sent forth a fleet into 
the Mediterranean, under Sir Thos. Allin, you are to issue to Sir 
Thomas the following instructions, to be kept secret, that no 
Algiers ship may suspect his intentions and avoid him. 

He is to make himself master of any such, even by force if need- 
ful, but to use no further violence, and carry them to Algiers. There 
he is to signify to the Government that he is sent to demand repara- 
tion for injuries done by their men-of-war to English subjects, con- 
trary to the Articles of Peace, and absolutely to insist on the release 
of the Spaniards taken in the John of London, and now captives at 
Algiers, and to break with Algiers, in case they are not delivered. 
He is also to demand restitution of their goods or the value thereof 
but not to break about those; also restitution of goods taken out 
of any English ship about which he has authentic information,

particularly the Phenix, William and Benjamin, and the Morn- 
ing Star, belonging to the East India Company, or of the value of 
the goods in them; and in case of refusal, to break with them. 

He is to demand, but not to insist on, the punishment of the 
commanders cf men-of-war or others who have infringed the peace. 
In case he be satisfied, he is to proceed to treaty, demand ratifica- 
tion of former treaties, especially as regards probibition of search 
in ships which have the Lord Admiral’s pass, promising that no 
ships shall have such passes which carry more foreigners than 
English. If they insist on English ships not carrying Turks or 
Mussulman slaves, he is to endeavour to prohibit search of persons 
on English ships on any pretence, or examining them by torture 
to extort confession. In case of a peace, he is to restore entire all 
ships, goods, and persons taken from them, and make fitting pre- 
sents, either the satisfaction he shall receive from merchants’ goods, 
or of gunpowder; but if not, he is to attack and destroy their ships, 
within and without the Mole, and in exchange for the prisoners he 
takes, to obtain as many English slaves at Algiers as he can, and sell 
the rest to the best advantage for the King’s use, as also all ships 
and goods taken from them, unless the ships might be made useful. 

We having agreed with the King of France, to prevent disputes, 
that there shall be no salutes nor going to leeward of the wind 
between their respective men-of-war in the Mediterranean, Sir 
Thomas Allin is to give notice thereof to his commanders of ships. 

In case of a rupture with Algiers, he is to send frigates to Tunis 
and Tripoli, to inform the Governors thereof. but also to promise 
faithful observance of the peace with them, and to request the same 
on their part. If on his arrival at Algiers, he finds a favourable 
wind to do execution to the Algiers ships in the port, he is to per- 
form it at once, before delivery of our letters; and if he takes any 
renegadoes from the Turks, he is to reserve those that are English for 
further orders, and dispose of those of other nations to the hands of 
their respective princes, reclaiming from them all English renegadoes 
that shall fall into their hands. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 31, ff. 28-80. ] 


Phineas Pett and 3 others to the Navy Commissioners. We caused 
copies of your instructions to be affixed to the gate, that the porter 
and others might be the better governed ; according to the strict- 
ness thereof, he purposes to lay in small beer for our workmen. 
Judging that would be very prejudicial to the bodies of those 
coming to it hot and dry, we have persuaded him to continue his 
middling beer, and hope you will not be offended. We never heard 
that he sold wine or strong waters, or misbehaved himself; but to 
prevent any abuse, an open place for the men to drink in is set 
apart, with charge that none be harboured within doors, [S.P. 
Dom., Car. IT, 262, No. 9.]

Petition of Hannah, wife of Sam. Herring, merchant, to the King. 
Sir Edm. Allen, Bart., who died in 1655, and his lady in 1657, left 
their only child, Arabella, lands value 2,0002. a year, and personal 
estate 10,0002., also leaving the petitioner, her near kinswoman, and 
Julian Thompson to take charge of her; but a Col. Thompson, under 
the Usurper, got possession of her through her maid, and gave her 
to Wm. Thompson, who took her abroad, and tried to marry her to 
his boy, though not worth 200/. a year. She is kept in restraint, 
to force her to this unequal marriage, and is in great disquiet. 
Entreats that she may be secured and cared for by persons of quality, 
fearing that if ordinary proceedings were taken to recover posses- 
sion of her, Thompson would again take her out of the kingdom. _ 

With reference thereon to the Lord Chief Justices of the King’s 
Bench and Common Pleas, and their report, that a writ of Ne 
exeat regnum should be directed to the sheriff of the county 
where Thompson resides, to take security for his not going abroad, 
and then the case can proceed by common law. [S.P. Dom., 
Car. IT. 262, Nos. 15, 16.] 


Entry of the above reference. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 33, p. 42.] 


Rich. Bower to Williamson. A merchant from Rotterdam reports 
that he saw St. John and Desborow, with 5 or 6 more, daily about 
Major Burton’s house there, and that Malbourne, a teacher, told 
him they expected a call over. A vessel has arrived from Dieppe, 
and 6 from Norway with raft; 150 sail have passed for Sunderland 
and Newcastle. I got our bailiffs to send for a woman living 
against Manley’s; it appeared she was one of Mr. Bridge’s followers 
and swore backwards and forwards, but at length owned his dis- 
course of the bishops and of his Majesty. Major Burton’s son-in-law, 
James Puckle of Yarmouth, has been in Holland and returned, and 
no notice was taken of it until the merchant, who came from Rot- 
terdam, told me he saw and spoke to him there. [S.P. Dom., 
Car. TI. 262, No. 17.] 


Rich. Watts to Williamson. Capt. John Day has arrived from 
Virginia, and reports that 6 weeks hence several ships may be ex- 
pected from there. Another has come in from Dantzie with a 
damaged mast. [Jbid. No. 18.] 


The King to the Vice-Chancellor and Senate of Cambridge. 
Hum. Babington, M.A., fellow of Trinity College, has long ago per- 
formed all the exercises for his doctor’s degree, but he was ejected 
from his fellowship about the time he should have taken his B.D. 
degree, for non-compliance with the usurped powers, and he has 
since been prevented taking it by sickness. We require you, this 
notwithstanding, to admit him to his degree of D.D., with the 
seniority that he would have had if he had not been so ejected. 
[S.P. Dom., Entry Book 27, f. 149.]

Hugh Salesbury to Williamson. The fleet is riding at Spithead, 
waiting sailing orders; Sir Thos. Allin has joined it. [SP. Dom., 
Car. TI. 262, No. '74.] 


St. J. Steventon to the Navy Commissioners. The boatswain of 
the Princess says he knows not the time of the entry and discharge 
of the sailmaker, but is sure he was with them at sea, between the 
times of his certificate, and was checked his time while in harbour. 
He is coming to London on business, and will wait on you. [Zbid. 
No. 75.] 


Sir John Harman to Mathew Wren. Pray move the Duke for an 
allowance to my son-in-law, Jos. Hynde, who has served as clerk of 
the cheque at Deptford since his Majesty’s restoration. He peti- 
tioned the Board for an allowance as is at Chatham, being 2s. 1d. a 
day, of which he has hitherto received but half; the Board granted 
it, but would have the Duke first moved in it. A muster master’s 
place is vacant at Gravesend; Commissioner Pepys can satisfy you 
of his great ability in the performance of such an employ, if you 
would move the Duke for a warrant. [Zbid. No. 76.] 


Sir Denis Gauden to the Navy Commissioners. Pray assign me 
a day for finishing the accounts depending, or I fear they will not 
be ended for a long time. [Zbid. No. 77.] 


Phineas Pett to [the Navy Commissioners]. I send an account of 
the number of workmen, 57 in all, wanted for carrying on the 
works of the wharves, docks, cranes, and storehouses, according to 
an order lately received from you, and 20 shipwrights for the new 
ship. [Zbid. No. 78.] 


Same to the Same. I send a demand of things required for the 
repair of the docks, wharves, cranes, and storehouses. The Marma- 
duke wreck may be of use for carrying on of those works, and I 
desire she may be brought up to the new dock, to be broken up 
for that purpose. 1 send a list of calkers pressed by Mr. Boultwell, 
the master calker, that some course may be taken for their coming 
down, they having not yet appeared. Wm. Denton, a calker living 
in Jacob Street, St. Saviour’s dock, knows where to find them. Mr. 
Lewsley has 6,000 broom at the water side, which you may have 
at a reasonable price; it will be useful in the burning of planks for 
the new ship, &c., there being none in store. I entered 40 shipwrights 
on the new ship, and want 20 more on other works. Let me have 
warrants for entering more men. [14 pages.. Ibid. No. 79.] 


Commissioner J. Tippetts to the Navy Commissioners. I have 
not paid the seamen their stopped money, but intend to pay those 
that appear to-morrow. Capt. Ketcher with the hoy arrived from 
Deptford. I expected a quantity of spruce deals, which are very 
much wanted. I am going to send up a demand for materials 
required to carry on the works. [Jbid. No. 80.] 


Sir George Downing to Sir Denis Gauden and Sam. Pepys. Their 
lordships having read Mr. Pepys’ letter, about provisions delivered 
to several garrisons by Sir Denis Gauden, desire to speak with you 
both on Wednesday at 9am. [Jbid. No. 81.]

Sir Geoffery Shakerley to Williamson. Pray deliver the enclosed 
to Lord Arlington, and get me a speedy answer. When I appre-

been taken; by this you will see the influence those people have on 
their proselytes, who want but their bidding to fight. How am I 
to proceed against the preachers, by indictment or otherwise ? 
Sir Roger Bradshaigh is here. [Zbid. No. 91.]

Sir Edw. Spragg to the Navy Commissioners. I found the

Petition of Thos. Bennett to the King, for letters to the Court at 
the Old Bailey, to be discharged. Was tried in December 1668, for 
the murder of Thos. Janes, and acquitted, but was bound over to 
appear again in December. Having to go to Ireland with the 
Lord Lieutenant, cannot return in December without breach of 
duty. With reference thereon to Lord Chief Justice Kelynge, and 
his report, 7 July. The petitioner was indicted as stated, and the 
evidence being pregnant against him, he was bound to good 
behaviour for a year, which will not expire until December next ; I 
cannot therefore discharge him but by your Majesty's” command. 
[Ibid. No. 100.] 


Entry of the above reference. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 33, p. 44.]

between us. [S.P. Dom., Car. LI. 262, No. 101.]

July 5. Capt. Rob. Clark to the Navy Commissioners. I am sorry you so 
The Mary. far exceed reason with your severe checks, which I never deserved. 
It is like Hollafax [Halifax] law to hang a man first and condemn 

him afterwards. You task me for what I never did, nor any be- 

longing to me, nor has my boat acted so unhandsomely as you 

question him for. I can give an account of whatever I have done 

and should abhor the violating of his Royal Highness’s instructions. 

I have as much love amongst the seamen as any that can task 

me, and never wanted men, but have lived in repute amongst them ; 

it is not the fault of commanders that there is not more love but 

because the men have received abuse from the Ticket Office, in waiting 

so long for their money, and their tickets being bought at a low 


CHARLES II. 397 


1669. 

price. Had I been in the river, I should have had as many men as 
those you so highly: extol; if you had dealt civilly with me, and 
first heard both parties, you had done well; but I desire not to 
receive such lines as you have sent. I know not what you are 
ashamed at, but I am not ashamed with what you task me. I find 
that only one man was pressed out of the vessel mentioned by the 
Bristol’s boat, and if we must not press when in want, I know not 
what to say to it, as men are not so free to enter themselves with- 
out pressing. I want 60 men, and do not find any appearing of 
those you sent to the ships. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 262, No. 108.]
