Opinion of the Judges on the statutes in force against con- 
venticles, in pursuance of an order from the Lords of the Privy 
Council of 30 June 1669. (1) All assemblies that disturb the peace 
are punishable by common law ; (2) the statutes of 13 Eliz. and 14 
Car. II. against those who come to conventicles, and refuse to come to 
church, are in force; (3) the full execution of the laws of 1 and 
23 Eliz., 3 Jas., and 17 Car, II. would conduce very much to the 
suppressing of all conventicles. [Zbid. No. 115.]

Report of the Treasury Commissioners, on the petition of Charles, 
Earl of Ancram, for so much of the remainder of the tin, cast away 
some years since near Ostend, as he may recover from the sea, at 
his own charge. We beg to certify that we had a large treaty with 
Alderman Backwell, by which bis Majesty was to have one moiety 
of all that should be recovered, clear of charge; but Mr. Curtis, 
a merchant of Zealand, proffered 1,000/. over and above the 
one moiety, in case 120,000 lbs. weight should be fished up, and 
offered to maintain all persons we might employ on board his fish- 
ing boat, to receive his Majesty's part; we therefore wrote to 
Sir Wm. Temple to make a final agreement with Curtis; 1,199 blocks 
of the tin have still to be recovered, and having hopes that a con- 
siderable part will be recovered, if his Majesty has any thoughts of 
bounty to the petitioner, he might give him 1,0007., or such other 
portion of the moneys as shall arise out of the profits of his Majesty’s 
part of the said tin. [Jbid. No. 139.]

R. Manley to Rob. Francis. I have translated the letter as near 
as I could, but I do not understand all the words, and have no 
dictionary by me. This is the only language on this side of Portugal 
that could have puzzled me; a piece of the Talmud would have 
been as easy to me, so you had better not send any more papers 
from those parts, unless you will have me spend a fortnight in 
mastering the language. [Jbid. No. 140a.]

Phineas Pett to the Navy Commissioners. I am sorry you should 
find fault with the calking of the Golden Hand; I have made 
inquiry, and attribute the defects to the extreme heat of the 
weather, and her lying here so long after coming off the ground. I 
cannot send a pinnace to Sir Thos. Allin, the ships being gone, and 
the boat requiring repair. I want the provisions formerly demanded, 
and a sail or two to keep the sun from the men; also orders for 
stopping the leaks of the Royal Sovereign, as she makes 3 feet of 
water in 12 hours. [JZbid. No. 147.] 


Martin Carslake to the Navy Commissioners. I arrived here 
with Sir Edw. Spragg, who assisted me with men; but I yet want 
6 or 7 of the number allowed, and when I have them, I shall be but 
weakly manned. I found much trouble by a leak in the stem for 
want of calking; it was stopped, and now we find a defect in her 
rudder, which may prove bad. I shall endeavour to mend it, or 
have a new one when I come to Portsmouth. My master found 
fault with it at Chatham. [Jbid. No. 148.]

July 10. The King to the Duke of York. Having appointed a fleet of 
ships to sail into the Mediterranean, under Sir Thos. Allin, we wish 
you to make the following addition to his instructions of 26 June 
last, viz.: that in case he finds it to be true that some Tripoli men- 
of-war have seized on the English ship Victory, on pretence of 
strangers’ goods on board, and made prize of her, he is to carry out 
the same instructions as given for Algiers, in reference to Tripoli, 
and to Tunis, if they have broken the peace, but not till he knows 
whether he shall have peace or war with them. [S.P. Dom., 
Entry Book 31, f. 30.] 


July 10. Sir Thos. Allin to Williamson. Thanks for letters and news- 
The Resolution, hooks. The Deptford ketch and Sir John Harman, with the Jersey 
Spithead. and 2 others, have arrived at Spithead; we now only wait the 
arrival of Sir Edw. Spragg, when we shall sail with all expedition. 
I hope, at the return of the Bristol and Dartmouth lying off the 
island, to impress seamen; we shall then be well manned. [S.P. 

Dom., Car. IT. 262, No. 153.] 


July 10. Sir Geoffrey Shakerley to Williamson. I have taken Travers, a 

Chester. captain in the late wars against his Majesty, and a very great 
preacher and ringleader of the Anabaptists; on his own con- 
fession, and the testimony of 2 witnesses, Sir Philip Egerton and I 
have committed him upon the statute, and I send a copy of the 
commitment. I desire your judgment upon it, and the opinion of 
the judges as to the course to be adopted for suppressing the con- 
venticles. [Jbid. No. 154.] Enclosing, 


Warrant by Sir Phil. Egerton and Sir Geoffrey Shakerley, to

July 11. Fras. Bellot to Williamson. Capt. Jennifer, with the Truelove, 

Pendennis. has come in, bound for Jamaica, and is taking in goods. The new 
experiment on her proves very well by lengthening her keel, and the 
lacker on her, as the captain calls it, may be of great advantage in 
saving her cargo of pitch and tar, as well as preserving the vessel 
from the worms. Some small vessels outward bound are waiting a 
fair wind. [Ibid. No. 158.]

July 11. Commissioner J. Tippetts to the Navy Commissioners. I went 
Portsmouth. to the Isle of Wight, and bought the provisions mentioned in the 
contract sent, Mr. Newland having disposed of the rest at better 
rates by 5l. per cent. than you give for these. I know your diffi- 
culty in obtaining money, and therefore proposed nothing but what 
is profitable; yet I recommend you to purchase Mr. Newland’s 
masts, being large and good. ; x 
Our money is almost done; 1,0007. more will put us in a good 
condition as to provisions, plank excepted; but Mr. Coles’ was de- 
livered yesterday, and divers persons will be able to supply more 
at the end of the summer. I made inquiries after Wendover, and 
find he is in the Blessing of Gosport, and had but one man pressed 
from him by the Bristol’s boat; this man has since been turned 
over into the Mary, so that he is mistaken in his petition, in all 
but his own name; he should be made sensible of it. I am of 
opinion that the hulks ought to be moored out of the strength of 
the tide, so that they may be able to help ships in and out of dock. 
I send an estimate for a rigging house, which will be advantageous ; 
also particulars of the arrival and departure of ships. Am I to 
supply Sir John Harman and Capt. Poole with sails and junk, 
which they need? [23 pages. S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 262, No. 161.] 


July 11. Capt. Wm. Poole to the Navy Commissioners. I urgently need 

The Jersey, sails, and also junk, as what I had was bad. I do not urge the 

Spithead. want of them to lavish the King’s stores, or give my boatswain an 
occasion to play the knave. I will endeavour to prevent that; 
having had some account of his former deportment, I caused all 
his sea stores to be brought upon deck, and found all to concur 
with his indent; therefore I have no occasion to complain, but 
shall look after the expense of his stores. I pray that my sails 
“may be surveyed and supplied. [Zbid. No. 162.]_ .

ppithead Hiit be expected but what we carry with us, and this is a laboursome

July 12. Capt. Edw. Moorcock and John Moore to the Navy Commissioners. 

Chatham. We removed the wreck 140 fathoms towards the shore, out of 
the way of ships passing, and hope with another tide or two she 
will be dry on shore. We have cast 100 tons of mud out of her 
gun deck, and her hold is as full as it can be, which made her lift 
so exceeding weighty that both her sides were toru from the bottom, 
and the rest of her is equally shattered. The number of men we 
are forced to employ expend the beer so fast this hot weather, that 
our proportion will not hold to expend half the victuals, and we 
cannot put them to an allowance of beer at this time of year. 
Pray order down 10 or 12 tuns, to supply that expended extra. 
[Zbid. No. 164.]

Sir Jonathin Atkins to Williamson. Thanks for favours. The 
world is very quiet, but our bustling neighbours, the French, are 
still moving towards one point or another ; there are 12 frigates at 
Brest, and 5 from Toulon ready to sail, and they have lately built 
12 strong galleys. They are intent on maritime preparations, and 
are supplying the stores and arsenals with ordnance, &c. Six flats 
have reached Breda, laden with ordnance, masts, and cordage from 
Sweden and the Baltic, and 8 more are ordered. 

Duke Mazarin is removed from his charge of Governor of 
Brittany, and is made Governor of Alsace. I hear from St. Malo 
that there was an affront put upon our English frigate, the Milford, 
but the French King so resented it that the offending captain was 
ordered to be hanged. [2 pages. Ibid. No. 168.] 


Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. Sir Edw. Spragg has sailed 
westward; a great fly-boat accompanied him. [Lbid. No. 169.] 


Ma. Anderton to Williamson. I send letters enclosed to my care 
by Mr. Ardrey, employed in the Customs. Since Sir Geoffry 
Shakerley took up some of the persons at the assemblies and con- 
venticles, they have been very submissive and quiet ; if his Majesty 
had as active and vigilant justices in all parts of his dominions, 
there would be less fear of tumults and rebellion. [Jbid. No. 170.] 

Leonard Bower to Williamson. There have 100 sail of laden

liver the enclosed. to my father. [Jbid. No. 171.]

July 13, [Lord Arlington to the Lord Lieutenant of Devonshire.] His 

Whitehall. Majesty having received frequent informations from several parts of 
the increase of unlawful meetings, under pretence of religious wor- 
ship, contrary to law and in affront to the Government, particularly 
within the town of Plymouth, I am commanded by the King to 
desire you to break and disperse them as soon as formed, and to pro- 
ceed against the ringleaders according to law, as much danger is to 
be apprehended from suffering such, within any of the garrisons or 
places of strength. If you find occasion to call for assistance, the 
justices of peace and the magistrates and officers of Plymouth are 
to give it, and you are to furnish an account from time to time, to 
his Majesty or the Lords of the Treasury. [24 pages. Draft. Ibid. 
No. 175.]

Geo. Pley to Hickes. The sea ebbed and flowed 7 times each on 
the 10th instant, between 6 and 9 am., which was the more 
admired, in regard that it was in such a calm season, and fair 
weather, and at the time of neap and low tides. The like has 
never been known but once before, and that was about 3 years 
since. [Zbid. No. 184.] 


Petition of John Adrian and 8 other English merchants to the 
King, for a letter to the English Ambassador at the Hague, to 
interpose on their behalf. During the war with Holland, they were 
necessitated, for carrying on their trade, to use the names of several 
subjects of the King of Spain in the Spanish Netherlands ; 
having shipped goods at Ostend for England in Flemish vessels, 
some of them were taken by a Dutch man-of-war, and carried to 
Amsterdam, the petitioners not daring to claim them. The goods, 
appearing to be shipped in Flemish names, were arrested for some 
pretended losses of the Hollanders, and petitioners were constrained 
to give security to answer the arrest ; the States have since ordered 
the raising of money upon such security, for satisfaction of the 
pretended losses. [Jbid. No. 185.] 


John Powell to Williamson. Our harbour affords no news of any 
kind. [Jbid. No. 186.]

Report by Lord Keeper Bridgeman, Lord Arlington,and See. Trevor, 
on the petition of the Earl of Bristol, referred to them 22 Jan. 1669. 
That the grant to him of the King’s moiety of the forfeiture on pro- 
hibited goods was in lieu of 10,0007. due to him, and of which he 
signed an acquittance. That his Majesty suspended the grant on some 
particular displeasure, but afterwards declared that the petitioner 
should not be frustrated thereof. That John, Earl of Bristol, father to 
the present Earl, purchased a pension of 2,000}. a year, for 31 years, 
from the late King, by way of rent-charge on the revenue of the 
Court of Wards, of which 16 or 17 years remained unpaid ; but the 
3 years unexpired since the Restoration have been paid, and on 
the Act for taking away the said Court, he was promised recom- 
pense. That he has lost also the wardship of Lord Brooke, given him 
by the late King, which would have done much to repair his estate, 
ruined by his loyalty. Advise that the 10,000/. from prohibited 
goods should be restored, and the pension of 2,000}. established 


‘ to him, to make the remainder of his life comfortable, he having 


no office, nor other mark of favour. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 33, 
pp. 48-50. ]

Sidney Godolphin to Lord [Arlington]. I hear, by a gentleman 
sent by Lord Ormond to see Lord Cavendish, that the King intends 
to begin his journey for the New Forest on 5 Aug., at which I am 
troubled, fearing I shall not be able to come to London soon enough 
to fit myself with horses to follow him. It is my highest hope to 
do him some service, and if ever I was useful to him, it was in such 
journeys. You will know best whether it will be fit to make any 
excuse to the King for me, and if it will, pray doit. Ishould be glad 
to know whether you go with the King, and if you go to Euston, or 
any other progress, where one might follow you with less prepara- 
tions. Madame comes next Monday to St. Cloud, to stay till she is 
confined, and the King of France intends making her a great feast 
by the way, at Versailles. [Zbid. No. 3.]

Rob. Wynn to Rob. Francis. I arrived here with Mr. Warren 
on Saturday night; we found Lord Howard withdrawn for his 
diversion 20 miles out of town, where he will continue until 
Sir Thos. Allin’s fleet comes about, which is expected in 8 days; 
this is very unlucky for me, as every man lies at his own expense, 
but I am continued in hopes by Mr. Warren that Lord Howard will 
give me a fair reception. Pray procure a recommendation to his 
Lordship for me. Apply to my brother Thomas, in Mark Lane, 
who laid out 3., in linen for me, for a second supply, as the linen 
was all lost by the carelessness of the post, and the money I received 
from friends was expended in coming down. I hope you will be 
kind to honest Thos. Maddocks, as he is endeavouring your speedy 
payment. Endorsed, “Cousin Wynn.” [Zbid. No. 40.]

Ph. Pett to the Navy Commissioners. I am sorry you are not 
satisfied about the 40 shipwrights entered; if they are dis- 
charged, there are none here to be had, unless by a press war- 
rant. I perceive a general discontent among them, from having 
heard that they were to be discharged at the beginning of the 
winter; but I satisfied them that I knew nothing of it, and that the 
report was false. If the new ship is not launched with all speed, 
her main keel will be rotten, which will be a great prejudice to the 
King, and disreputable to the dock. [13 pages. SP. Dom., 
Car. II. 263, No. 50.]

Sir Phil. Musgrave to Williamson. I encouraged some persons, 
by Lord Arlington’s commands, to give intelligence of the Noncon- 
formist meetings, and disbursed some money therein, and such 
letters as came over were sent to you; but receiving no advice or 
instruction in return, I have since sent to my correspondents to 
discontinue their intelligence, unless they meet with anything con- 
siderable. The enclosed contains something so scandalous and 
base, if not dangerous, that I could not suffer it to rest in my hands. 
I am rejoiced to find the Nonconformists are discovered to be as I 
ever accounted them, though there may be some mistake as to the 
number or danger of them in Carlisle. I was glad of his Lordship’s 
letter, and while I have employment, which age makes me grow 
daily unfit for, I shall be faithful to the trust reposed in me.

very sad, as since the King went to view the several ports

that the King is much blamed for not putting the laws into 
execution against persons using private meetings, and that 
he sent for Mr. Kiplin, a considerable merchant, and two 
other chiefs of the Anabaptists, and was very familiar with 
them ; but informed them that, as he could not give any 
further protection, he wished them to forbear. Cocks has been 
with Sir Thos. Liddell, to whom he always goes when he

Petition of the inhabitants of Taunton, co. Somerset, to the King, 
for a revival or regrant of their former charters and privileges, with 
such alterations and additions as are desired in papers annexed. 
The late King, in the second year of his reign, created Taunton a 
corporation ; but by the late Act for regulating corporations, several 
members of the society were displaced, and no others being sworn 
in their stead, the powers and privileges granted by the patent have 
ceased to exist. With order thereon to the Attorney-General, in 
favour of the restoration of the charter, but he is to consider of 
provisions and restrictions to be made in the new charter, that the 
petitioners may remember hereafter better to deserve his Majesty’s 
grace than they have formerly done, and to take care that all 
officers and members of the corporation are persons of loyalty and 
sobriety. [Ibid. No. 55.] Anneaxing, 


Lord Powlett, Sir John Sydenham, and 10 others to the King. 
The town of Taunton is very populous, and equal to any in 
the west of England, being one of great trade, and where the 
assizes are held; yet there is no officer above a constable, 
although it formerly had a mayor and a justice of the peace. 
We think that the town should be incorporated, with such 
powers as his Majesty shall think fit, apprehending that the 
late miscarriage there has proceeded from the want of an 
authority suitable to the government of a place so great for 
trade and commerce, and where so many persons reside or 
resort.—5 July 1669. [Zbid. No. 551.)

Report of the Duke of Buckingham, and 7 others of the Council 
of Trade, to the King, on the petition of Geo. Herriott, cold presser 
of woollen manufacture. You appointed a committee to receive 
the proposals of the petitioner, and to hear what objections could be 
made against him by others engaged in the art of cloth pressing; 
he affirms that—having lived in Holland 18 years, and observed 
how much, after they have bought English woollen cloth, they 
raise its esteem by a certain way of cold pressing unknown in his 
Majesty's dominions—he has become expert in the said art, and,

CHARLES II. 423 


being the sole operator in England, asks a patent for 14 years for 
bringing over the invention. 

The committee having made their report, we find that the way 
of hot pressing woollen manufacture is practised, though contrary to 
the laws, but it is necessary and useful, and not prejudicial to the 
cloth ; yet that if a better way of cold pressing can be found, the 
inconveniences of staining by rain, &c., to which the hot press renders 
the cloth liable, will in a great measure be prevented; and as it 
will be an encouragement to other ingenious inventions, and the 
petitioner does not propose to hinder any other man from using 
any other kind of cold press which has hitherto been made use of, 
we suggest the granting of such a patent as counsel at law shall 
suggest, with proviso that no heat be used therein. 

With reference thereon to the Attorney-General Palmer, and his 
report that the patent may be granted for the term asked, subject 
to the insertion of a proviso for revoking it, if it shall appear pre- 
judicial to the public, or not a new invention—6 Aug. 1669. [S.P. 
Dom., Car. II, 263, No. 62.]

Lord Townshend to James Halsall, Green Mews, Charing Cross. 
I enclose papers respecting John Blancher. As he is such a rogue, 
and is confined for murder, I do not think his evidence worth 
much, as to Major Wildman being the man that gave the stroke, 
but I believe, if forced, he would confess who did it. Blancher had 
sentence of death pronounced against him at Norwich, but the 
execution was stayed through a defect in the law. 

I desire speedy proceedings may be taken against him, if any 
are contemplated, as it is a great charge to keep him ; many people 
come to the grate every day, pretending to have law from him, 
and give him money, although his education was no more than 
that of a journeyman shoemaker. 

Wildman was at Norwich the other day, with others of his 
principles, and was very open and high; I heard it proved at the 
sessions, against one of the chiefest and most popular Quakers, that 
he should say, “ Neighbour, are you whetting your scythe against 
harvest ? You had more need whet your sword.” And being asked 
why, he answered, “Do ye hear nothing of wars begun or to 
be begun?” I know there is small encouragement to appear in any 
concerns of this nature, but as you are Scoutmaster General, it is 
fit you should know all things, and make discovery if permitted so 
to do. If the papers enclosed are of no use, let them be kept 
until I come to town, Endorsed [by Williamson], “The letter 
which gave occasion to the unkindness between Lords Arlington 
and Townshend,” [Jbid. No. 70.] Anneaxing,

Information of Rich. Wright. I went to the gaol of Norwich 


im 1656 upon business, and hearing that Jno. Blancher, a 
cordwainer of Norwich, was in the gaol, I desired to see 
him. On some discourse, he told me that he had the King’s 
waistcoat, gloves, and garters that he wore on the scaffold, 
and that he was there in disguise. That he was very inti- 
mate with Bradshaw, and had many times ridden with 
him in his coach, as also with Oliver St. John, a pretended 
judge of Oliver Cromwells, and Judge Ask, or Ascue, who 
had his lodgings in Holborn; and that out of the room 
where Blancher and Ask met, there was a room with a pri- 
vate door, descending a pair of stairs, by and through which 
Blancher had his common regress.—Christ Church Close, 
Norwich, 15 July 1669. [Ibid. No. 7011.]

demeanours of John Blancher, a condemned prisoner in

. In 1646 he was convicted for a common barrator, and fined 


1001. and one year’s imprisonment; the bailifs going to 
arrest him, he killed Robert Cooke, and then fled, but was 
retaken and tried, when the jury gave a special verdict. 

The next sessions he was indicted for the murder of Wm. 
Henry, and a true bill fownd, but he broke from gaol before 
the trial, and was not taken for several years after, and not 
until after the evidence for the King was dead ; but he was 
outlawed for felony. During the time of his escape, he went 
by the name of Browne, and was very great with Lords 
Bradshaw and Ask, who murdered the King, has been 
often seen riding in the same coach with them, and was 
also servant to Bradshaw at the time of the King’s trial. 


. He had the waistcoat, stockings, garters, and roses that 


the King wore the day he was murdered, and has been seen 
to wear them in gaol. 


. In 1660, Christopher Jay and John Man, justices of the

his own relation, was wpon the scaffold the day the King 
was murdered, and that he produced 4 staples in the Globe 
Tavern at Howndsditch, which he said were to have been 
knocked into the rails, for cords to manacle the King’s hands 
and feet, so as to draw him down, if he had not yielded to 
lay down his head to the block quietly. Also information 
of Ann Kensall that she was in the house of Edw. Tensh 
the elder when he came from the murder, and saw him 
produce the staples that were to have been used to force his 
Majesty down to the block, in case he had not submitted ; 
and that wpon asking Tensh what his Majesty said, he 
made answer that he thought the King took no notice of 
them; he further said that Colonel Cobbit’s heart failing

upon himself to deliver him up instead, and that she also

Capt. Ant. Deane to the Navy Commissioners. The Golden

Ralph Hope to [Williamson]. The assizes were held at Warwick 
and Coventry last week, when several Nonconformists, amongst 
whom was Dr. Wild, were indicted for keeping conventicles. The 
proclamation proclaimed on Friday has little effect upon the refrac- 
tory conventiclers ; though they forbore to go in their usual public 
manner to Leather Hall, yet they held several large meetings in 
other places in town, and seemed to deride the proclamation. Some 
petty robberies have been committed, and Rich. Bourke—pretending 
to be of the Guards, and in Sir Philip Howard’s house, and going 
for Ireland, where he has a family——was seized and committed to 
prison, upon suspicion of being a highwayman, and concerned in a 
plot to rob Capt. [Rob.] Manley, Lieut.-Governor of Jersey, with his 
lady and a gentleman, who were ina coach on their way from 
London, and for being connected with 2 other highwaymen, named 
[John] Castles and [Humble] Ashenhurst. Particulars of the 
attempt, &c. [2 pages. Ibid. No. 97.]

England ; I have them in the ship. I spent one week of the provisions 
for my own use, but was not able to spend more, by reason of the 
want of weight when boiled, one piece of 4 pounds when raw not 
weighing one pound when boiled; and although I gave them 
double allowance, it caused great grumbling, and almost a mutiny.

Major Henry Nicoll to the Navy Commissioners. I understand 
you have taken out a writ, and employed bailiffs to arrest me; but 
you had no need to proceed that way, for upon notice I would have 
answered the action, and I have an estate sufficient to make 
satisfaction. My chief business being to clear myself from all your 
demands, I shall not stir until I have put a period to all engage- 
ments with the Navy Office. 

I presume the Surveyor-General and Sir John Mennes, who 
were at Chatham during my transaction of weighing the ships, 
will give evidence of my industry and faithfulness, and I know his 
Majesty will not punish me because unsuccessful, when no means 
were omitted ; also I have a petition before him, that he may be truly 
informed thereon. I received but 3007. from the Navy Office, and 
would have been contented to pay 1,0007. not to have come near it, 
as through some accidents, his Majesty’s intention of doing me a 
kindness has turned so much to my prejudice. I want the name

Sam. Thorney to the King. In pursuance of your Majesty’s 
commands to me of the dedication of my work, the Mariners’ 
Magazine, I have at much cost and peril endeavoured to discover 
the great concavity in the earth, 4 miles from King Road, 
Gloucestershire, where the great ships ride, and I find that what 
has been reported about it is fabulous. 

I descended with a mine-man into the cavity 7 fathoms, and 
found the opening, and we went down by ropes 25 fathoms, and 
came to a river, or stagnant lake, 20 fathoms broad and 8 deep ; 
then we found another concavity, and the miner descended and 
called out that he had found what he looked for, a rich mine, but 
his joy was soon changed to amazement, and he returned terrified, 
declaring that he had seen an evil spirit, and he will go thither no 
more. 

“The flooring is of white stone, enamelled with lead ore, and the 
pendent rocks seemed to be glazed with saltpeter, which distilled 
upon them from above, which time had petrified.” After some 
hours’ stay, we ascended without much hurt, but I had an unusual 
and violent headache 4 days after my return, which I impute to my 
being in that vault. [24 pages. Ibid. No. i22.]

Aug. 2. Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. The Guestling and Brotherhood 
Deal. for the Cinque Ports held a meeting at New Rumney in Kent; 
it is as it were the Ports’ parliament, as they have an upper 
and lower house, a speaker, and other formalities the same as at 
Westminster. Several mayors were clapped into prison and fined, 
as also some jurats and others, and amongst the rest, the Mayor and 
3 jurats of Sandwich, for not executing a former order. Some 
good laws were passed ; no writs from any court in England, except 
the Exchequer, are to be of force in the Cinque Ports. [Jbzd. 

No. 157.] 


Aug. 2. Ralph Hope to Williamson. [Rich.] Bourke, who was imprisoned 

Coventry. on the accusation of Capt. Manly of being a highwayman, has been 
discharged, Manly having recanted, and several letters having been 
received from London certifying as to Bourke’s character. The 
meetings have increased since the proclamation, and one held at 
Leather Hall was as full as has ever been known, one Eccleshall 
being the speaker. There has been such a swarm of flies, that 
the streets have been covered, and the sky darkened, which is 
looked at by the superstitious as ominous. Yesterday being Lammas 
Day, the Chamberlain and others, with a company of 600 or 700 
horse, rode the bounds of the common grounds, according to ancient 
custom, which are then thrown open till Candlemas, and afterwards 
they gave a feast to all who were present. [Zbid. No. 158.] 


Aug. 2, Leonard Bower to Williamson. A west country boat laden with

were saved; 200 light colliers have passed north. A ship has 
arrived from Rotterdam. Pray deliver the enclosed to my father. 
[Lbid. No. 159.] 

Aug. 2. Capt. R. Manley to his cousin Rob. Francis. I have got well into 

Wrexham. the country, though not without an encounter, and narrowly escaped 
being robbed by the highwaymen [Johr] Cassells and [Humble] Ashen- 
hurst, having eluded them by securing the trepanner in Coventry. 
“ Our governor's letter to Lord Arlington has followed me here, so 
I return it.” My brother Manley is here with me, and I am almost 
drowned with drinking your health ; I shall make more haste than 
I designed, to save my life, “for I am vanquished with kindness.” 
Do not omit writing, as you promised, to me and Dr. Fiott. [Zbid. 
No. 160.]

Sir Thos. Ingram to Lord [Arlington]. I.have examined the 
person, and laid all the baits I could for a confession, but find 
nothing material. As however he has been an enemy to the

has taken the oaths of allegiance and supremacy, I suggest that he 
may have his liberty. Endorsed, “ Examination of a suspected 
person about gunpowder.” [Jbid. No. 6.]

Capt. Ant. Deane to the Navy Commissioners. Proceedings

The King to Sir Thos. Ingram, Chancellor of the Duchy of 
Lancaster. We have issued a commission under the Duchy seal to 
Walter, Lord Aston, High Steward of the Honour of Tutbury, and 
lieutenant of Needwood Forest, and others, to examine into trespasses 
committed there, in order to prevent abuses in the game and woods, 
and inquire how the same may be improved. You are to order the 
said Commissioners to go down immediately, inquire into conceal- 
ments and encroachments in any of our lands there, the granting of 
offices since the Restoration, their yearly value, all abuses and 
wrongs done by such grants, and what improvements have been 
made in the revenue; the said Commissioners are to have as much 
power as though the words in their commission were particular 
and express. [Zbid.]

The King to the Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. You are 
to signify to Lord Aston, lieutenant of Needwood Forest, that no trees 
are to be henceforth felled in that forest on any pretence, there 
having been great waste of wood by claims of fee trees. [S.P. Dom., 
Car. IT. 264, No. 13.] 


Rich. Watts [to Williamson]. A ship from Gallipoli reports that 
the Grand Seignior has died of wounds received from a fall from 
his horse while hunting. A fish 5 feet long has been caught; 
by some it was supposed to be a dog-fish, but others considered it 
a shark, having two sets of teeth in the lower jaw; 27 Hamburghers, 
outward bound, have been forced in by contrary winds. [Jbid. 
No. 14.] 


Sir Edw. Sprage to Williamson. I arrived at Cadiz on the 
2nd, and Sir Thos. Allin came in with his squadron yesterday, but 
they only stay to take in water, and are then off to Algiers, accord- 
ing to instructions. The Admiral of Genoa has also come in, and 
delivered up voluntarily all the Englishmen he had on board; he 
reports that the seige of Candia is raised. A French man-of-war 
also reported that M. Beaufort, going ashore there, was wounded 
in the arm by a bomb shot into the town. The Sally men-of-war 
are growing very strong; Capt. Holmes forced a small pink of 
theirs ashore and captured her, but the men escaped. They have 
200 English slaves dispersed in the country, and if care is not 
taken to destroy these rogues, they will grow very powerful; we 
must do this when we have shown ourselves at Algiers. What has 
been done in my Irish business? I hope Lord Arlington will give 
a helping hand to it. Pray forward the letters enclosed. [2 pages. 
Ibid. No. 15.] 


Sir Geo. Downing to Williamson. I send an advertisement for 
the Gazette, stating that the Treasury Commissioners will be ready, 
on 11 Oct., to receive propositions from persons, for farming or 
collecting the duty arising from hearths and stoves, in England and 
Wales, and Berwick-upon-Tweed, either in one farm or collection, or 
by several counties and places. [Jbid. No. 16.] 


Fras. Bellott to Williamson. Several ships have come in out- 
ward bound, and are waiting a fair wind. One has the Lord 
Lieutenant’s goods, and is bound for Dublin. [Zbid. No. 17.]

apprentices are bound to do. I shall serve him 4 years, when

post-master of Heidelberg and Mr. Trypon, as neither Mr. Harrell 
nor the indentures made any mention of it. Nebel desires the 
money may be paid by your lordship to Harrell in London.

Thos. Lloyd to Williamson. Sir Rob. Southwell is arrived in

Jo. Carlile to Williamson. Sir Rob. Southwell, Mr. Lloyd, and

John Clarke to Hickes. A vessel arrived from Portugal reports 
that the woods in Newfoundland have been set on fire, but whether 
from accident or design is not known; it is feared when the rain 
falls, and the coals and ashes are washed down to the sea, that it 


will much prejudice the fishery. [Ibid. No. 23.] 


Rich. Watts to [Williamson.] In the Ostend vessel wrecked on 
the Goodwin in February, there was a Governor who was to 
be carried to Madrid, to answer some high erimes of treason, in 
betraying, or intending to betray, a town to the French in Flanders ; 
this, it seems, was a false accusation, as he arrived here yester- 
day, bound for Ostend, to his former, or a greater command; he 
has gone to Dover to embark in the packet boat. It was observed 
that he came alone, and was landed with a small bundle of linen, 
out of a vessel bound for London, so that some imagine he has 
made his escape and intends for France. Upwards of 40 Ham- 
burghers, some Dutch, and 2 Dutch men-of-war, are in the Downs. 
[Zbid. No. 24.] 


The King to Edward, Bishop of Norwich. We hear by George

for 21 years, which he desires to change into lives. We request 
you, on account of his loyalty to our late father and to ourselves, 
to allow him a lease of the priory for 3 lives, but this grant not 
to be drawn into a precedent. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 27, f. 151.]

Note that the Act for regulating the press has defects which may 
be supplied by orders given to the Statitioners’ company, who 
oppose the proceedings of the surveyor of the press; if they still 
obstruct, they should be reported to King and Council. [S.P. Dom. 
Car. IIL., No. 254.] 


The King to the Stationers’ Company of London. Many trea- 
sonable, seditious, and unlicensed books, pamphlets, &c., having 
been printed, on 22 Aug. 1663, we appointed Roger L’Estrange 
sole surveyor of the press; but this appointment has proved 
ineffectual, through the opposition of several members of your 
company. You are henceforth to take due cognizance of his com- 
mission, and employ your utmost power and credit with your 
members, no further to obstruct him, but to assist him in all 
searches and discoveries when needful. 

Also within 8 days after notice given by the said surveyor of the 
press, you are to call a court of assistants, to advise with him, and 
agree on such ways and means for its better government as he shall 
propose, being instructed by us for that purpose, and he is required 
to return to Council or a Secretary of State an account of proceedings 
therein. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 31, f. 27.]

Aug, 11. Sir Thos. Allin to the Navy-Commissioners. We came to an 
Resolution, anchor, and having watered with some difficulty, and dispatched 
Cadiz. the business of the money we were to receive on shore, we are 
weighing for Tangiers, and from thence forward on our voyage. 
The backwardness of the Welcome fireship and the Golden Hand, 
in not joining us, may create great perplexities and disturbance 
to the service we are about, besides the want of the Centurion and 
Dartmouth, which I have orders to convoy. I leave orders for 
them, in this and all other places as I go along, follow the fleet 

as speedily as possible. [Zbid. No, 31.]

Lincoln, 11 Aug.—The grand inquest, having found the good 
effects of the proclamation against conventicles, have drawn up 
a paper of thanks to his Majesty, which was read and sub- 
scribed in a County Court, and have desired Justice [Sir Thos. ] 
Tyrell to present it. Of the great conventicle held at Gedney, 
three-fourths came out of the Isle of Ely and Norfolk, and 
many from Nottingham. [Zbid. No. 43.] 


John Brookes to the Navy Commissioners. I surveyed 85 casks 
of beef and pork aboard the Leopard, and am informed that there are 
36 more as bad as the others. I desire an order for their removal, 
and for heading up the cask standing on deck, as it stinks so that 
no man is able to abide between decks. [Ibid. No. 44.] L'ncloses, 

Certificate by John Brookes and two others, that the beef and 
pork on board the Leopard, brought from Lisbon, are too 
stinking and rotten to be fit for any service.—11 Aug. 1669. 
[Zbid. No. 441.] 


Sir George Downing to Williamson. I send an advertisement to 
be’inserted in the Gazette, that although the Treasury Commis- 
sioners intend to receive propositions upon 11 Oct., for collecting or 
farming the duty arising by fire-hearths and stoves, they will not 
interrupt the late farmers in the collection of arrears due to 
25 March last. I desire you to add the time from which the duty 
is to be let, viz., from 29 Sept. next. Noted to be delivered to 
Mr. Hartlib. [Zbid. No. 45.]

George Pley to Hickes. A vessel from Barbadoes with sugar 
reports that, when in the height of 24 degrees, she was met and 
plundered by 3 Spanish men-of-war from Havana, of moneys, 
clothes, and other goods, and that they used the company very 
badly. They told them that some of our ships from Jamaica had 
also been stopped, and 6,000 pieces of eight in money, besides other 
goods, taken from them. There is a ship in those seas commanded 
by a Chevalier of Malta, who takes all nations he can light upon. 
[S.P. Dom., Car. TI. 264, No. 49.] 


John Powell to Hickes. There is no news of any kind to send.

Dr. Isaac Basire to Rob. Francis. Friendship is the life of 
human society, but constancy is the life of friendship, and corre- 
spondence the nurse of constancy ; I have wanted that favour ever 
since I took my leave of you 2 months ago. Iam informed by my 
son that you put it over to your clerk, whom I neither know nor 
had to do with; but as Mr. Williamson promised a correspondence 
from you, I beg you, if that courtesy is troublesome to you, to let 
me know, and I will then desist rather than offend you. My wife 
and family desire to be remembered to you and good cousin 
Aldridge. [S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 264, No. 54.] 


Rich. Watts to Williamson. The Return and Rainbow have

in the Dover Road. The Quakers increase, and most side with 
them, [Jbid. No. 55.] 


Hugh Salesbury to Williamson. The private meetings are less 
held than formerly ; the chief preachers at Southampton have been 
secured, and others have fled to escape imprisonment. [Zbid. No. 56.]

Jos. Lawrence to the Navy Commissioners. I viewed Mr. Fellows’ 
timber and set a mark upon 70 ends, about 110 loads, which will be 
useful for the new ship if you will treat with him about it; his 
dwelling is at Three Cranes Wharf, Thames Street. I have set 
sawyers to work in converting Mr. Mason’s trees, which are too big 
for carriage. With note that Mr. Fellows being at the Board. on the 
29th, insisted upon 3/. 10s. per load, which the Board refused, and 
the contract was broken off. [S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 264, No. 57.] 


Capt. Ant. Deane to the Navy Commissioners. I have been to 
the forest, where all endeavours will be used to get down the frame, 
which is already hewed. All the men will return at the end of the 
week, except four, who will go to Godshill Wood to mould the beams 
marked out I shall want 2007. for carriage, having had nothing 
more than the 150l. on the whole account. The purveyor has a 
great account to clear, and desires that it may be done; if money 
is wanted for carriage in his absence, we will let you know. We 
want a warrant to press some joiners. [14 pages. Ibid. No. 58.] 


Capt. George Liddell to the Navy Commissioners. I could not 
get any provision at Dover except bread, so shall victual at Ports- 
mouth; pray order the provisions to be ready. I shall make all 
despatch to Holyhead, having to take Lord Robartes in there, to 
carry him to Ireland. [Jbid. No. 59.] 


Fr. Crane to Rob. Francis. I have no news, and that from 
England about M. Beaufort and Candia is made sport of. I hope 
the house in St. Alban’s Street is furnished, and your wife all ready. 
Being so long concluding the match, I hope it will be so firmly 
ratified that there will always be a free content, and no trouble with 
State jealousies. I cannot desire a letter, as I am not yet settled at 
my journey’s end. Pray forward the letters enclosed. [/bid. No. 60.] 


Thos. Holden to Hickes. Four great merchantmen have come in 
from Ostend, bound for Cadiz, under convoy of the Castle Rodrigo ; 
they came out with 2 more bound for the Canaries, but left them at 
sea, one having broken her mast,and being supposed to have put in 
at Plymouth. They met a Dutch fleet of 5 sail and one convoy, also 
bound for Cadiz. The St. Peter of Aldborough has come in, laden 
with fish for Bristol. [Jbid. No. 61.] 


Fras. Bellott to Williamson. Particulars of the arrival of ships. 
[Zbid. No. 62.]

in my friend’s business at Stratford. May he wait upon you, as he

Rob. Bransby to Viscount Conway. I crave pardon for not 
answering your letter earlier, having been visited with the tertian 
ague; nevertheless I used all the industry possible to get such a 
chair as you described, which is effected. I had great trouble to get 
the iron frame made for it; I doubt not, as the chair is very com- 
modious, and runs on wheels, that it will please all who use it. 
I have seen your letter to Mr. Garret as to a piece of yellow drugget 
being wanting; I assure you that when the box was packed up, the 
whole quantity ordered was enclosed, and therefore beg I may not 
be a loser, as I got little by it. [Zbid. No. 74.]

Rich. Watts to Williamson. A ship from Virginia came aground 
on the Goodwin Sands, but was got off and piloted into Deal. The 
master, Jno. Southwell, brought her safe from Virginia to the 
Downs, without his instruments, or making any observations during 
the voyage. Those who know him say he has a familiar spirit. 
[Ibid. No. 76.]

Petition of Davis Morgan to the King. I was employed by the 
Earl of Oxford to recover some debts due to him from several 
persons of quality, and because I was very diligent in prosecuting 
them, they have maliciously procured me to be indicted at the 
sessions of barratry, at the suit of his Majesty, and are endeavour- 
ing by all ways and means to convict me, hoping thereby to get 
some protit to themselves, and make me incapable of any employ- 
ment. Your Majesty has, by letters patent, granted to one of the 
persons whom I sue all fines that shall be imposed on any person at 
the grand sessions of Carmarthen, so that if I am fined, my fine 
will turn to the profit of my prosecutor. I have also sued the high 
sheriff of the county, who must return the jury for the trial of the 
said indictment. I beg your letter to the judges of the grand sessions 
at Carmarthen, to stop all proceedings upon an indictment, and leave 
for the ease to be tried in the next adjacent English county.

justices of assize for co. Carmarthen, that in case the reasons

Jonas Shish to the Navy Commissioners. I have received three 
barges of Mr. Shorter’s oak timber into the stores. I know that 
you give ready money, and that you desire the works shall be 
carried on with it; but none of this timber is fit for the purpose, 
and there is no longer timber of his on the wharf. I hope I shall 
receive no more of this. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 264, No. 82.] 


Same to the Same. I viewed and bought 30 loads of knee and 
compass timber belonging to Capt. Gibbs, and find it good and fit 
for the works of the London. [Jbid. No. 83.] 


Capt. Edw. Moorcock and John Moore to the Navy Commissioners, 
Our success has not been so good as expected, by reason of some

want 2 months’ victuals for 70 men, if you think it convenient to 
go on with the work. [Zbid. No. 84.]

Anne Cole to Lord Arlington. Necessity, which is the misery of 
life, makes me a suitor to you. I beseech you—for God’s sake, and 
for the sake of Sir Anthony Desmarces, who lost his life in his 
Majesty’s service, and who was my dear friend—that you will move 
his Majesty to confer upon me some part of the reward that 
was intended for Sir Anthony, on his return; had he lived, I 
should have been partaker of all, but his death has been my utter 
ruin, as for his sake I am lost to all wy relations, and forced to 
quit the town, and sell the things I had, to pay some of his most 
pressing debts. [Jbid. No. 86.] 


John Clarke to Hickes. I enclose a letter, but have no news to 
communicate. [Zbid. No. 87.] 


Geo. Pley to Hickes. The London, laden with lemons from 
Genoa, met 3 Turkish men-of-war belonging to Algiers, who treated 
them very civilly, and only took from them wood and water, which 
they wanted. We hear of the safe arrival of all the Newfoundland 
ships, and that they are like to have good fishing, as on 24 May 
many had 3,000 fish to a boat. [Ibid. No. 88.] 


Sir Edw. Turner to Williamson. I have just finished the assizes 
at Ely, where I am chief justice. Amongst the offenders there were 
Wm. Nicolas, who was indicted for stealing a gelding ; Owen Bricke- 
wood for stealing a mare ; and Hannah Gowler for stealing 3l. They 
were all found guilty, and I pronounced judgment of death upon 
them; but as they are all young and unmarried, and able to do 
good service, and are desirous to be transported, and as most of the 
justices of the Isle have begged me to move the King for their 
pardon, and the bearer has agreed to send them to some foreign 
plantation, I desire you to acquaint Lord Arlington with it, and 
request him to move the King in the matter. [Jbid. No. 89.] 


Warrant for a grant of pardon to Edw. Maddox, condemned for 
highway robbery, on account of his former loyalty and services in 
discovering other malefactors. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 28, f. 286.] 


Warrant for payment of 200.. to John Baptista Dateil, towards 
his expenses to the dominions of the Grand Duke of Tuscany, and 
elsewhere. Minute. [S P. Dom., Entry Book 30, f. 166.] 


The King to the Sheriff of Wiltshire. We are informed by Sir 
John Coventry, Edw. Hyde, and Wm, Willoughby, justices of peace, 
that Matthew Best, keeper of Fisherton Anger gaol, has beaten and 
abused gentlemen debtors, suffered several convicted by statute of 
premunire and owing fines to go to their own dwellings, and one 
Humphreys, condemned to death for perjury, felony, and murder, 
to escape; Best is to be examined, and if found guilty, removed 
from his place. We recommend Hen. Sadler as a fit person to 
succeed him. [S.P. Dom., Entry Book 31, f. 32.]

Edw. Gregory to the Navy Commissioners. I send a list 
[missing] of ships under my muster in 1668. With note that it

John Brooke and Wm. Rand to the Navy Commissioners. We 
have launched the Dreadnought, and laid her near the dock, that 
the shipwrights may the sooner finish her works. We desire an 
order for entering 20 riggers to fit her rigging. [Ibid. No. 91.] 


Capt. George Liddell to the Navy Commissioners. Thanks for 
your informing me of the receipt of a petition, which neither I nor 
my officers knew anything about. I shall be very careful in not 
granting tickets to those named, and in having an eye over them. 
Two are servants who agreed to serve for 40s. a year, and have had 
more than their voyage comes to, and several of the others have 
but little wages due; another is a tailor, who begged his employ, 
being ready to starve, and I judye him to be as idle a rascal as any 
of them. I received 4 months’ provisions; and as the victualler 
deals unworthily with respect to my necessary money, having 
stopped 13s. 4d., I shall give Sir Denis Gauden an account, hoping 
he will see things otherways satisfied. [Zbid. No. 92.] 


Hugh Salesbury to Williamson. The Roebuck and Sweepstakes 
have come in from the Downs, as convoy to some merchant ships 
bound for the southern parts. [Zbid. No. 93.] 


[J. Williamson] to Rob. Francis. You have been much to blame 
in not sending the letters I left behind on leaving town. I have 
been disappointed in doing some business intended, as two of those 
letters were to have given advice thereof at Oxford. I take it 
very ill, and am sorry for your own sake, as you will find it to 
your loss another day. I resolve to be in town on Tuesday, and 
desire that all business matters may be left at Lady Anderson’s. 
I would have you find out Mr. Povey, and request him to proceed 
in the Thetford matter, according.to his own discretion and friend- 
ship for me. [Jbid. No. 94.] 


Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. Arrival of 4 East India ships; the 
Madaras from Bantam, supposed to be lost, has arrived ; welcome 
news to that company. [Jbid. No. 95.] 


Same to the Same. The fleet of merchant ships sailed with a 
fair wind; the Sweepstakes and a Virginia man only are in the 


Downs. [Zbid. No. 96.] 


Fras. Bellott to Williamson. The Spanish man-of-war, with

Report of the Royal African Company, drawn up by order, of 
the state of their trade, showing its good condition when founded, 
124,000/. being subscribed for stock; its losses by the seizure of 
6 vessels for the King’s service in 1664; by the taking of 8 more 
by the Dutch; by the damage received from the same in Africa, 
and the ill payment for negroes in Barbadoes. Being unable 
therefore to trade on their own account, they have granted private 
licences for trade, within the limits of their patent, so as to keep up 
their forts and factories. They entreat, by way of remedy, that the 
King would pay in the remainder of his own subscription to the 
stock, which would lead others to do the same; thus their debts 
could be paid, and then new subscriptions would come in; that he 
would assist them in recovering their debts at Barbadoes, and grant 
them a vessel or two to protect them on the African coast, on 
which they will try to raise a new stock. [5 pages. S.P. Dom., 
Car. IT, 264, No. 106.]

Petition of Brome Whorwood to the King. On my petition 
showing that during the usurpation, on a petition of my wife tothe . 
then Commissioners of the Great Seal, (I being obnoxious to them 
for my loyalty), she procured a decree in June 1659, in my absence, 
that I should pay her 300/. a year from Feb. 1656-7 to the date of 
the decree, being 750/., and continue the same yearly, from my lands 
in Staffordshire, whilst we live apart. After the Restoration, I was 
served with a Chancery process to perform this decree, and for not 
complying, my estate was sequestered. 


At length you settled the difference by an award of 18 Feb. 
[1663-4. See Calendar, p. 488], that I should settle part of my estate 
on trustees for payment of the 3007. a year ; but this I conceive was 
only meant to be for the time that I was content to live apart, but 
not to give her liberty to live away from me longer than I chose. 
Yet the decree was kept on foot, and I threatened with sequestra- 
tion, and my house and grounds would have been ruined, had I not 
taken what conveyances were obtruded on me. I was also forced to 
pay 500l. in part of the arrears of alimony, and you ordered pay- 
ment of 500/. on 20 Aug. 1668, in lieu of all remainders of alimony, 
which sum was also paid. 

My wife then complained of the sequestration expenses, and you 
ordered that she should bear what she had already paid, but that I 
should pay what was unpaid. On this she and her agents advanced 
their bills to 1,000/., and although this was paid, another sequestra- 
tion was ordered, because I had not performed your award. On 
16 July last, I applied to you, ard you referred me to the Lord 
Keeper and Attorney and Solicitor-General. They summoned my 
wife, but she would not appear, and is carrying on several trials 
these assizes to gain my estate. I beg you to appoint a time when 
you can hear me yourself, and order my relief. 

With order thereon that the Lord Keeper, before whom the matter 
betwixt Whorwood and his wife is depending in the Court of Chan- 
cery, is to be at liberty at the hearing to proceed to the determina- 
tion thereof, according to the equity of the whole matter, and as if 
his Majesty had not interposed therein, Mrs. Whorwood declining 
his Majesty’s extra judicial judgment; this is not to be in any 
way conclusive to his lordship in making a decree, but he is to 
proceed as if nothing had been done or ordered by his Majesty. 
[S.P. Dom., Entry Book 33, p. 65.] 


Copy of the said order. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 264, No. 136.]

Rich. Bower to Williamson. The person who tore down the 
proclamation against conventicles at the Market Cross is known, 
but it has been passed over as a foolish unadvised act. Woodroffe 
the bailiff sent for 3 chiefs of the independent faction, and advised 
them to forbear meeting, but Thos. Lucas refused, and said the 
bailiffs had nothing to do with it. Mr. Rowe and Gabriel Wood- 
roffe, brother to the present bailiff, were elected bailiffs for the 
ensuing year, after a long opposition between Clement Feltham, 
and Rich. Huntington, an alderman, Ald. Thaxter, Justice Michael 
Tills, and his son. They laid aside the Act ordering the Sacrament 
to be taken, as not half [the corporation] had taken it, and this had 
been done at Norwich and elsewhere. Two ships have arrived 
from Gallipoli, and another from Dantzic. [bid. No. 140.] 


Chris. Musgrave to [Williamson]. I owe the favour received 
from Lord Arlington to your friendship. Baron Turner gave in 
charge the law against conventicles, and the justices have issued 
out their warrants for presenting those who are absent from church, 


-and will proceed upon the statute for 12 pence a Sunday, which 


they conceive the best way to reclaim the rabble. The Baron was 
acquainted with the actings of some of the justices at the Christmas 
sessions of the gaol delivery, and was much dissatisfied therewith. 
I hope that business will be so prepared that they may be made 
sensible of their error. Mr. Curwen was prosecuted with great zeal, 
but it was only proved to be manslaughter. [Jbid. No. 141.]

Pet. of Thos. Moore, soldier, to the King. Standing sentinel near 
St. James’ Park, and ordered to let none pass, Thos. Cook came 
running down, and in spite of remonstrances, leaped over the ditch. 
I struck him with the muzzle end of a musket, of which blow he 
died. I was sent to Newgate thereon, but the trial being on a 
point of law, it is to be before the judges, when they return from 
their several circuits, and not till after next term, and meanwhile 
I must perish in prison. I beg his Majesty’s pardon for my offence.

John Snell to Rob. Francis. A weed or grain, growing among 
oats and barley in the West of Scotland, makes the ale or beer so 
intoxicating that a gill “will fuddle a man more than a gallon of 
other drink,” and the very bread makes people fall asleep. It is 
called roseger, or in Latin lolium. [S.P. Dom., Car. IJ. 264, 
No. 184.]

Thos. Turney and W. Fownes to the Navy Commissioners. We

Majesty. [Zbid. No. 187.] .

Alexander, as to fitting up lodgings at Hampton for Lord Arling- 
ton on his arrival, and keeping the tables, for all the tables are 
ordered to be kept there. 

Direct Secretary Trevor to repair to Hampton Court, and let orders 
be taken about his lodgings; forward the enclosure to Lord Arlington 
at Kimbolton or Althorpe. I will be at Hampton on Monday, and 
hope Mr. Marriott, the housekeeper, will find mea lodging. Tell 
Mr. Coling, at the Lord Chamberlain’s, of the King’s resolve. 

Let Mr. Perrott hear that the Queen died at 4 a.m. on Tuesday, 
at Colombiers near Paris, after a long indisposition, with great 
regret to that Court, and with infinite affliction to his Majesty and 
his Royal Highness, who received advice of it this morning by 
express. Mr. Perrot is also to take notice of the death of Sir Edw. 
Nicholas, one of his Majesty’s Privy Council, and Secretary of State, 
as well to his Majesty as to his late Royal father; he died at his 
house at Horsley, in Surrey, after a long and tedious sickness. 
Inform Sir Rob. Southwell, or the Clerk of the Council, that the 
King will expect to meet the Lords on Monday night at Hampton 
Court, and that I will be at their service if necessary; give 

{these two words to Dr. Jenkins, and let me have his reply. Send 
me my letters and the Book of Treaties, news-books, &c., to 
Hampton Court. [22 pages. SP. Dom., Car. II. 264, No. 219.]

Sept 5. Commissioner J. Tippetts to the Navy Commissioners. I desire 

Portsmouth. directions on Rich. Faulkner’s information. I demanded why he 

concealed the matter until this time; he answered that he was an 

apprentice, and bound to keep his master’s secrets. I know not 

what truth there is in the charge, but it is too evident that the 

practice is much in use; I should be glad to see the guilty found 

and punished, that others might be afraid to do the like. I sup- 

pose this matter had never been mentioned but that a difference 

happened between the master and servant; the master, going 

to correct the servant, was beaten by him, and the servant, being 

‘turned out of doors, expected his wages from the King. I have 
forborne payment until your advice be had. 

The hoy with spruce deals arrived; I desire that the brass and 

lignum vite shivers and blocks for the new ship may be sent, as

Information of Rich. Faulkner, ropemaker. About 2 years 
since, being apprenticed to Ralph Heather, I was com- 
manded by him to go aboard divers of his Majesty's ships 
in the harbour at Portsmouth to fetch goods. I brought 
2 hawsers and a cable from the Ostrich hulk, &c., and with 
the help of my fellow-servant Roye, lodged them in my 
master’s storeroom. Also information of Henry Roye. 
I went aboard the Ostrich hoy while serving Ralph Heather, 
and brought away old splices and clenches to my master’s 
house.—3 Sept. 1669. [Lbid. No. 91.] 


Sept. 5.: Certificate by Col. John Strode, that the Lenox was sent from 
Dover to Chatham, and was cleaned and tallowed for the service, 
and that he paid 301. for her fitting. [Zbid. No. 10.] 


Sept. 6. Commissioner J. Cox to the Navy Commissioners. I shall provide 

Chatham. brooms and buckets, for the service, and desire to know the prices 
of candles sent, which were much broken, that I may deal for them 
here. Isendan account from the master shipwright of things re- 
quired, and of what may be purchased here. I find no engine in 
store, and the old ones were sent up to be repaired; I leave it to 
your consideration if a fire should happen. 

I went to Mussle Bank, and stayed for the lifting of one of the 
ships ; I have spared them for one day more the same help they had 
the last three days, so as to get her further on to the bank. Three 
more are left, which will save charge if blownup. I will send the 
fellow charged with stealing the rope before a justice at Maidstone, 
but I believe he will only be imprisoned ; by the time of the Assizes, 
he will learn his lesson to plead not guilty, having no witness to 
bind over to prosecute. Capt. Pyne tendered a shipload of Norway 
hes and I have sent Mr. Lawrence to view it. [2 pages. Ibid.

Sept. 6. Levant Company to Sir Dan. Harvey, ambassador. We acknow- 
London. ledge receipt of letters; we notice your meeting with our ships 
going to Smyrna; the intimation you gave to your predecessor, 
the Earl of Winchelsea, of your arrival, and your pressing his 


1669. 
Sept. 6. 


CHARLES II. 477 


Lordship’s return, as it was expected by his Majesty and the Com- 
pany ; your delivery of our orders; your administering the oath 
for due payment of consulage ; and your reconciling the differences 
between the factors and others ; for all which we return thanks, 

We are sorry that no sufficient remedy can be found for the 
abuses in raw silk, but meantime you must have recourse to the 
method prescribed in our instructions, and enjoin the factors not 
to make advantage to themselves by the tare and weight of silk. 

We approve of what has been tendered by the Consul and Fac- 
tors at Smyrna, to be inserted in the capitulations, save the 
3rd Article——that transactions at Leghorn and other parts of Chris- 
tendom, between English and Armenians or Jews, shall not be called 
to account in Turkey ; and that writings at Leghorn, &c:, shall be 
evidence in Turkey ;—this clause you are to expunge, as it will 
be of no advantage to the trade of England with Turkey, but will 
tend to an increase of the trade between Turkey and Italy, and 
encourage the Armenians to enlarge their trade, and bring their own 
commodities into Christendom, which has already damaged our 
trade in Turkey. 

We do not understand the dragomen’s motion concerning ls. 5d. 
of brokage, pretended by them to be their ancient right, and to be 
now swallowed up by the Jews. The number of dragomen has 
always been limited, and we desire it may not be exceeded; and 
when an account of their number, and of the Giovanni di lingua 
has been received, we will consider their condition and requests, 
but shall not be willing to enlarge expense. 

We are satisfied with your opinion touching the proceedings of 
the Consul at Smyrna, about the Anne and Christopher, and the 
John and Abigail, as also the foreign vessel of Leghorn bearing 
English colours, whereby we might have been prejudiced; we 
desire that we may be eased of that fear, and that no ship may be 
permitted to carry English colours. 

We notice the information given to our Governor of apprentices 
being sent over with a few clothes, and being afterwards deserted 
by the master, which is an abuse; we will take time to consider 
redress. We are ashamed that any amongst us should so far forget 
the oath and engagements they are under, as to direct their factors 
contrary to our public orders. It is a practice we had cause to 
suspect was formerly in use, although not easy to be discovered ; 
could that be done, the business would be capable of a remedy, 
which would be of advantage to the Company and their trade. 

Your endeavours to suppress the false moneys have been very 
prosperous, and we hope to find the good effects in future trade. 
Be careful against admitting another sort of counterfeit coin in 
circulation in France and Germany, called lion dollars or “ abokelps.” 

Weare sorry if our treasurer at Smyrna, Rich. Langley, has given 
you distaste by forbidding Mr. Hedges to draw money upon him; but 
we observe that Mr. Hedges had then 2,600 dollars in hand ; and 
needed not to draw more. However, your entertainment will be 
punctually made good, and we hope there will be no occasion of urging 
our treasurers, or discouraging the thrift they are bound to observe.

Having formerly had disputes concerning the charge for shoot- 
ing guns in Turkey, we judged it necessary that some expense 
should be incurred upon some occasions, but have now resolved 
that the Company shall be at no charge, unless the Ambassador or 
Consul give express orders for the shooting, when they may allow 
one-third of a dollar for each gun round, and shall not exceed half- 
a-dollar for good guns, well Jaden; considering the cheapness 
of powder, this will be a competent rate, and be a means of pre- 
venting the masters from being too much the gainers, for what is 
as much for their own as the Company’s reputation, [4 pages. 
Levant Papers, Vol. 5, p. 211.] 


Levant Company to Wm. Hedges [Treasurer at Constantinop!e]. 
We are glad that affairs are carried on without disturbance, and 
presume you will use all endeavours to continue this, and,as promised, 
to lessen expenses. We observed in a letter from his lordship 
(Sir Dan. Harvey) that he had taken a dislike to Mr. Langley, for 
forbidding you to charge money upon him without order ; but as he 
probably had no cash, he did not amiss, and we observe that you 
had 2,579 dollars balance of account in hand. We have promised 
that his lordship shall be paid for his entertainment, and in case our 
ordinary duties there and at Smyrna fall short to defray that 
and other expenses, you are to draw bills for England upon our 
Treasurer. 

We received your two years’ accounts, which shall be perused, 
and an opinion given; but as we observe several extraordinary 
presents put to our account, without the occasion being shown, we 
desire further information. Resolution adopted as to firing guns, 
as mentioned in the letter to Sir D. Harvey. [Jbid. p. 215.] 


Levant Company to [Paul] Ricaut, Consul [at Smyrna]. We 
expect accounts of the interest made of the 2,000 dollars deposited 
by the owners of the Greyhound, and credit for half the capital, 
which is in our Treasurer’s hands. We approve your courses against 
the importation of false moneys, which have effected its abolition, 
but we caution you against a new sort of foreign coin, a great 
parcel of which was imported by the Genoa Merchant. 

We have your articles sealed, and the accounts of Mr. Mowse, 
which we shall settle with his executors. We expect you to satisfy 
us as to the exceptions to the former treasurers, and care to be 
taken for the brokes of interlopers’ cloth brought by our ‘general 
ships. Our letters of 9 Aug. 1667 will explain our meaning about 
the 159 dollars difference between treasurers Hedges and Langley. 

We are sorry you cannot redress the abuses in raw silks, as it 
much concerns the trade and poor of England. Meantime the 
factors must be enjoined not to take any silk without full allowance 
of tare, and what they receive from the silk merchants is to be 
made good by them to their principals. 

We are glad our affairs there stand so well, and the consulage is 
so considerable, and trust it will continue, by your care in prevent- 
ing fraud by concealment. Only disburse what is necessary, or we 
must except against your accounts; we except against 500 dollars

for furnishing your house, beside half the former Consul’s house 
rent; nor shall we allow hereafter 200 dollars usually paid the 
Consul beforehand for petty disbursements, but shall allow needful 
sums quarterly, so that they do not exceed 200 dollars a year. 

We find that a mitigation of strangers’ consulage, on goods consigned 
to our factors, though it might benefit particular men, would preju- 
dice the trade of England, and encourage that of Italy, and would 
endanger the privileges the English enjoy there, if our factors 
should colour their goods, and defraud the Grand Seignior of his due 
custom. But you are to use your discretion as to the favour to be 
allowed to those that trade in English ships, lest others undermine 
us by going cheaper. 

We observe your account about the Leghorn ship under English 
colours, and other ships; also about Mrs. Mason and her daughter. 
They had not our consent for going over, and it would be well to 
clear the place of both. 

From respect to you, we have ordered that your kinsman, 
James Ricaut, be Chancellor there during our pleasure, at 200 dollars a 
year; we have also ordered you a gratuity of 2,000 dollars, for your 
first two years’ employment, and 250 dollars for your expenses on 
the Countess of Winchelsea, and on your journey from Constanti- 
nople; but the exceptions already named will be deducted from this. 
Resolutions about discharge of powder in shooting guns. [Levant 
Papers, Vol. 5, p. 216.) 


Levant Company to Rich, Langley [Treasurer at Smyrna]. We 
have received several letters from you since ours of 8 Sept., and ac- 
knowledge your pains and care in our affairs, and commend your 
frugality, the want of which would have a bad influence; the dis- 
pleasure of the factors, and the complaints of your parsimony, will 
not act to your disparagement, since you do but your duty, and 
that tends to the advantage of a most considerable, though languish- 
ing trade, requiring all support. But we wonder that you kept so 
great a sum as 14,000 dollars, the balance of your account, and 
then charged 11,000 here without any apparent cause, and require 
an explanation thereon. 

We enclose a copy of a letter sent to the present Consul, 10 June, 
as to our concerns with the late Consul Cave, and beg you to assist in 
the business and only to retain 2,504 dollars, the interest due from 
the Greyhownd, and to deliver the rest of the estate, and the 
books and papers, to the administrators, and then render an 
account ; if the pawn was not in your hand, say where it is, when 
you need not doubt of receiving an indemnity from us. 

We have considered touching the consulage of strangers’ goods 
consigned to the Company’s factors, and the proposal for a mitiga- 
tion thereof to 1 per cent., in respect of the difficulty of its recovery, 
and the dependence of the factors upon employment by strangers; 
but as it would encourage the trade of Italy, and hinder that of 
England, and besides hazard the Company’s privileges in Turkey, 
we Shall still expect the full duty ; we desire that if any indulgence 
is shown, it may be upon our own ships, wherein the Consul has liberty 
to go so low that none may undermine us by going cheaper, so that

1669. 

the interest of English navigation may be improved. We notice 
your complaint of the irregularity of the Consul in sending away 
the Mary and Martha without notice, before your business was 
done ; but think the reason given by him that an embargo was 
feared is a sufficient excuse. Details of exceptions made to the 
Consul’s accounts. We shall continue to except against any charge 
for eating and drinking, or other novelties; where presents are 
made, the name and the occasion are to be stated, and your accounts 
are to be sent every 6 months. 

We have left tbe business of saluting to the Ambassador and 
Consul, and agreed that the Company shall be at no charge, unless 
they give express order in writing, when allowances are to be made, 
as mentioned in former letters. Sir D. Harvey complains of your 
forbidding Mr. Hedges to draw money; although we do not well 
understand the matter, we have excused it, supposing that he had 
good reason for it, and knowing that Hedges had money in hand at 
Constantinople. We have ordered Consul Ricaut 2,000 dollars as a 
gratuity for 2 years’ service, as also 250 more towards his expenses 
upon the Countess of Winchelsea, and his journey from Constanti- 
nople; but you are to deduct out of it the 500 dollars for furnishing 
the Consul’s house and half his house rent, in case it is already put 
to our account. [4 pages. Levant Papers, Vol. 5, p 219.]

We approve of your not complying with the desire of the Genoa

cloth brought up, and your agreement with the Emyn for customs, for

for customs. We notice your disputes and trouble with the masters 
concerning freight to be paid in Seville and Mexico coin, which 
is not to be had there under 20 per cent.; we will rectify that 
matter by a positive agreement with our ships. 

We are sensible of the damage done by the number of English 
ships expected at Scanderoon so soon after our general ships, but 
know not how to remedy it. We approve of your preserving 
English ships from the service of transporting the Turks to Candia. 

We have excepted against the accounts received from the Treasurer, 
they not being properly signed, and prescribed a mode to be adopted.

Dr. Jos. Bentham to Williamson. I would have waited on you had 
I known of your sudden coming to Billing, but I know you are active 
for me. What I wrote about has been granted by the Archbishop’s 
means to Dr. Outram, who is worthy of it. Our bishop has issued 
citations to the Nonconformist preachers, who still continue their 
conventicles, to appear before him at Peterborovgh next court day. 
Browning, who was sent to gaol on Whitsunday for 3 months, 
returned to Rowel [Rothwell ?] a fortnight since in great triumph, 
and seeks to redeem the time lost in prison, by doubling his pains 
since his return. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 265, No. 14.] 


James Baskerville to Williamson. The Little George has arrived 
from Jamaica, and gives a good account of its condition, and of 
their late successes against the Spaniards in the neighbouring parts, 
and particularly that of taking the town and castle of Malacaj and 
Giblatore, and destroying 2 of their great men-of-war and taking 
another of 12 or 14 guns, so that they returned with much prize. 
The King’s proclamation against conventicles takes little effect, 
though one of the speakers has been secured; but he preaches out 
of the grate to a numerous congregation. [Zbid. No. 15.] 


Rich. Bower to Williamson. Gabriel Woodruff, one of the newly 
elected bailiffs, has got off by means of his brother, the present 
bailiff, paying a fine of 40/.; Capt. Thos. Ravens, head Chamber- 
lain, who never goes to church, and goes regularly to the meetings, 
was elected, but he also got off by paying 10/.; thereupon they 
chose Peter Caulier, a merchant, who removed hither from London, 
is a discreet man, and attends the rites of the Church, so that he 
and John Rowe stand as the bailiffs for the ensuing year, com- 
mencing at Michaelmas. Public meetings, to the number of 1,200 
or 1,400 in one place, are held twice every Sabbath, besides once on 
every Thursday, notwithstanding the proclamation. 

About 200 vessels lie at the quay, ready for the herring fishing. 
The Forester, one of the Iceland convoy, has arrived, and the fleet 
is daily expected, a few having already come in. [bid. No. 16.]

H. M[uddiman] to the Earl of Exeter, Burleigh, Stamford. 
Letter of news. The Lord Lieutenant departed from his house 
in Chelsea on the 6th instant with a train suitable to the grandeur 
of so great an office. l 

Letters from Malaga report that the English frigates have taken a 
Sally man-of-war of 8 guns, and had hopes of destroying the 
remainder, there being 5 looking after them. The Providence of 
Lyme has arrived at Lyme from Morlaix. The Constant Warwick 
and 2 others have sailed from Genoa for Leghorn. The man-of-war 
never saluted, but sent to ask the Duke if he had ordered any 
officer to come aboard and command him to strike; the Duke 
denied sending any such order, but said the man-of-war could use 
his own discretion whether he went out of the Mould or not, on 
which the captain went out, and cast anchor, expecting the other 
ships that went along with him. 

The Spanish Ambassador has at last promised to pay the Swedes 
20,000 rix dollars, being the first payment of the subsidies. The 
ceremony of installation at Stockholm was far more magnificent 
than was ever known; one of the medals struck for the occasion 
is about the size of a crown, and bears the George on one side, with 
the inscription, “ Salus populorum,” and on the other 2 crowns and 
2 X, with a little George underneath, and the inscription, “ Honi soit 
qui mal y pense,” and overhead an inscription, “ Concordia Regum.” 

The accounts from Candia make the French valour to be much 
abated, the Turks to have gained on the garrison since their 
coming, and the city to be in a more desperate condition than when 
they landed. [3 pages. Ibid. No. 35.] 


James Banister to Lord Arlington. Have you received orders 
from Holland for my going to Surinam, or has Sir Wm. Temple 
given any assurance of obtaining the States General’s order for the 
removal of my family and estate from thence? I desire your 
advice how to obtain a speedy end of my troubles, being banished 
from my wife and property, for no other reason than my loyalty to 


my King and country; without your favour, I shall be utterly 
ruined. [|Zbid. No. 36.] 


Petition of Wm. Fergison, mariner, to the King. My father was 
your Majesty’s shoemaker, and received at Worcester, where he 
was taken prisoner, a wound of which he died. I served. in all the 
wars since the Restoration, under Rear-Admiral Utber, Capt. Reeve— 
with whom I was taken prisoner, and suffered 11 months’ imprison- 
ment in West Friezland—and Sir Thos. Allin, and was forced to 
leave the sea in April last, having broken the thumb of my right 
hand. I have been sentenced to death for picking the pocket of 
one Dowen of 46s., though I never wronged any man of one penny. 
I beg for a pardon. With report of Sir John Howell, Recorder, 
that Fergison was convicted upon the single testimony of Dowen, 
who might have been mistaken in the person that robbed him, and 
that divers credible persons appeared on his behalf. [Zbid. No. 37.]

Sept. 7. Commissioner J. Tippetts to the Navy Commissioners. I send 
Portsmouth. the names of 6 calkers who have not appeared, and hope they will 
be found out, and dealt with as they deserve. I think Cole’s plank 
tit for the yard, but he will make no proposals till he has been in 
Sussex. I shall see Peter Hasler’s, and oblige him not to dispose of 
it till I have seen it, though I know inquiries are made for such 
goods, and a greater price set than you give; but it must be paid 
for on delivery. 

I hope an allowance of 607. or 80/. will be granted to fence the 
King’s house with a wall, and fit it with other needful conveniences. 
I would gladly set it in hand before I take my journey to York- 
shire, that it might be done before winter, which would encourage 
me to get down my family for the time I am appointed to reside 
here, and would save my successor the trouble when his time comes. 
The examination of Hunt is in your solicitor Mr. Jones’ hands, and 
I have no copy. Pray send the bill for 2007. to be signed by 
Eastwood the purveyor, that the carting of the new ship’s frame 
may not be hindered, for want of money for bringing in the timber. 

[S.P. Dom., Car. TI. 265, No. 38.] 


Sept. 7. Jonas Shish to the Navy Commissioners. I want to lay the 
gun deck and calk it, to keep the frame of the ship dry, and 
employ the shipwrights and calkers in wet weather. I could do 
it in 3 weeks or a month, if I had 20 loads of knees, and 6 beams. 
A barge of Mr. Shorter’s timber has come to the quay, but there is 
none fit for the service ; there is a New England mast at Woolwich 
that will make a mainmast for the London, and save the King 301. 
in timber and work, if you will give order to the storekeeper to 
deliver it. [Zbid. No. 39.]

Petition of Hen. Coe to the King. Was condemned at the Old 
Bailey sessions for 2 felonies, in stealing a few books of small value. 
Is a young man, and sorry for past offences, and asks, in memory
