Ralph Hope to Williamson. The Lord Lieutenant of Ireland 
arrived last night, and lodged at the Bull. He was received at the 
entrance of the city by the Mayor and brethren, and the several 
companies in their robes, and was entertained with a most excellent 
speech from the Mayor, in the name of the rest, and also—which 
was a better present—with 2 dozen of wine, 2 sugar loaves, and 
a keg of sturgeon. The Earl of Denbigh, Countess of Southampton, 
and others, also waited upon him, and will accompany him to 
Sir Clement Fisher’s, who intends a treat ; thence he goes forward 
to Lichfield to-night. 

There was a fire at Northampton on Monday, which in less than 
3 hours, destroyed 17 dwelling-houses. The repairs of the cross 
at Coventry are almost finished, and it will be “more glorious and 
beautiful than ever.” A very contagious distemper is raging about, 
of which many die, but the city is perfectly free. There is no 
cessation of the conventicles as yet. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 265, No. 50.] 


Advertisement that Dr. Wm. Sermon, who lately cured Lord 
General Albemarle, is removed from Bristol, and may be seen daily, 
especially in the forenoon, at his house in West Harding Street, 
in Goldsmiths’ rents, near Three-legged Alley, between Fetter Lane 
and Shoe Lane, London. [See the London Gazette of the day. 
Ibid. No, 51.] 


The King to John, Bishop of Durham. Capt. Marmaduke Allen- 
son, of the bishopric of Durham, holds a lease of Quarrington 
Grange for a number of years. As he has suffered much for 
loyalty, we recommend that his lease be exchanged for one for lives, 
on his submitting to reasonable fines and conditions. [S.P. Dom., 
Entry Book 27, f. 12.]

Rob. Francis to [Williamson]. I send some letters, with an 
extract for the Lord Keeper. We expect the French mail to-morrow, 
and I will send the letters with all speed, that they may be with 
you before you begin your journey for this place. Your house 
goes on apace. I crave your pardon for all my miscarriages: Mr. 
Perrott desires to keep the Gazettes for further use, as there is 
nothing in them which is not in your letter. [Jbid. No. 60.] 


[Jos. Williamson] to Francis. I wonder I heard nothing of you 
yesterday. As I shall be at Lady Anderson’s to-morrow, you need 
not send the French packet, unless it arrives early enough to be 
used for the Gazette, and is sent here before 3 or 4, when we shall 
leave. Send to Arundel House and inquire for Mr. Marriott, Lord 
Hen. Howard’s steward ; if he is not there, send to Lord Brouncker’s 
house in Covent Garden, where he is sure to be heard of, being 
Clerk of the Council to the Queen; I must see him on Monday. 
Pray hasten the presses of the Paper Office, and have my little 
house in Scotland Yard ready. L want M. Merinville and my 
tailor to meet me on Monday, at Lady Anderson’s. [14 pages. 
Ibid. No. 61.] 


Earl of Castlemaine to Lord [Arlington]. I am much surprised 
to find that the English relation of the Dutch war, which you de- 
sired me to publish, has been stopped by you. I sent it to you 
first, knowing that things that appear good seem the contrary to 
those that stand at the helm, and then you could have done as you 
thought fit; but now, having printed it 14 months ago in French, 
and promised it in English, its suppression will seem very strange, 
and people will think there is treason or faction in it. It is a short 
account of a glorious victory, of which falsities and ignorance, both 
at home and abroad, would rob us. There was nothing more than 
you saw, except an epistle saying things of you which I knew you 
deserved, but this could have been laid aside. I suppose you 
have reason for this, and as I never merited an unkindness, I will 
not deem this one. Pray deliver my papers to my steward, with 
your further commands. [Jbid. No. 62.] 


Jonas Shish to the Navy Commissioners. Mr. Mayors, the pur- 
veyor, has marked 5 loads of Mr. Glyde’s knees, and has treated for 
the lowest price, which will be 4/. 18s. 6d. a load, ready money. 
They are worth the money, and will put the work of laying the 
middle gun-deck forward. [Zbid. No. 63.]

Sept. 13. Sir Geo. Reeve [Bart.] to [Williamson]. After the death of Sir 

Thwaite. Rob. Brooke, I understood that the Duke of York bad commanded 
Lord Howard to appoint Capt. Peaps to succeed him, so I could give 
you no encouragement in that enterprise; but if Lord Arlington 
will write to Lord Howard, now at Tangiers, he may secure his 
interest at Thetford before the election. The letter should be sent 
to the porter at Arundel House, to be forwarded to his lordship’s 
agent, Mr. Fox, at Stradbroke, Suffolk. 

I am confident that on his lordship’s return at Michaelmas, he 
will go to Thetford, and Burridge Martin, and Osmond Clarke, 
his tenants, will then so settle the business that you need not doubt 
the result, though I hear Sir John Knevett will stand for it. If 
my lord would write to Lord Townshend, to employ Capt. Kendall, 
another of Lord Howard’s tenants living at Thetford, to join the 
other two in your behalf, you might sit still and fear no opposition. 
I will wait upon you and Lord Arlington before the opening of 
Parliament. [Jbid. No. 76.]

Commissioner John Cox to the Navy Commissioners. I hear 
nothing of the 300/. promised, and if I have no money by the end 
of the week, I must keep the men employed upon the wrecks 
longer than needed; as soon as the deals come down, I shall set 
the carpenters to repair the hemp storehouse. I ordered the horse- 
boat to Deptford, there being moorings to be taken up the ensuing 
spring [tide], which will be put into her at less charge than the 
lading of her with the junk on the wharf. 

The work of the new ship is well followed, and in a month, her 
beams will be in, if we can have a ship’s lading of plank. I bought 
3,000 brick bavins at 11s. per 100, and the bricklayer needs 50,000 
tiles for the store and dwelling-houses. Justice Wood has sent 
down the spars bought of him, and the rest of the tar and pitch 
is also received from [John] Stacy. [Zbid. No. 81.] 


Edw. Gregory to the Navy Commissioners. Ant. Charleton

gave press and conduct money to Charleton ; but although in good 
health, he never made his appearance. [Jbid. No. 82.]

Thos. Holden to Williamson. Arrival and departure of ships.

There are several bottoms of wrecks in the river, and as it is

of the yard ought to have a warrant for their appraisement. I 
shall be able to give little account of the bottom of the Oak and 
Defiance, if they lie here this winter, for now people steal the iron 
and timber of both. I directed Mr. Moore and Capt. Moorcock to 
demand what powder, granadoes, and other materials they need for 
blowing up the wrecks. [Jbid. No. 97.]

Adventure for the dock. I am glad you are putting Hunt’s busi-

keep within bounds. Tell me whether the Act giving you power to

John Moore and Capt. Edw. Moorcock to the Navy Commis- 
sioners. We have overcome the difficulties in weighing the wreck, 
and laid her on shore, where she will ebb dry. We shall be ready in 
a few days to remove another; there will then be but one in the 
channel, which Capt. Cox advises to be blown up; if it proves 
effectual in wholly removing her, it will be the cheapest way of 
working. [S.P. Dom., Car. LI. 265, No. 108.] 


Wm. Williamson, master of the Black Dog hoy, to the Navy 
Commissioners. We sailed on 2 Aug. from Deptford, anchored in 
Hull on the 7th, and came to Stockwith the 13th, where we 
loaded, and returned to Deptford with timber and plank, by order 
of John Russell. Where shall we unload, we being now in the wet 
dock? [Jbid. No. 109.] 


Advices received, being extracts from letters calendared above, 

and from the following :— 

Friday, 17th.—Sir Wm. Coventry, who was put out of the Council 
and Treasury for challenging the Duke of Buckingham, has 
been received into favour again, and kissed the King’s hand. 
There was 5,000/. allowed for mourning [for the Queen 
Mother], but 500/. more has been already expended, although 
his Majesty allows it to such only as receive liveries out of the 
Wardrobe by virtue of their places. The Earl of St. Albans 
has gone to attend his Majesty at Hampton Court. 

Saturday, 18th.—His Majesty and the Court returned this day 
to Whitehall, and the Queen is expected in the evening. The 
King has some thoughts of going to Newmarket in a few days. 
Some persons going down to Hampton Court, and being the 
worse for drink, offered something unbecoming them near 
where his Majesty was in person, and they were ordered into 
custody. One of them is a captain in the trained bands. 

The judges on circuit have fined some Quakers; in default of 
payment, they are to remain in prison, and others that would 
not be bound over for good behaviour are remanded back to 
gaol till the next assizes. 

The Comte de Prado came ashore incognito at Leghorn, on his 
way to Rome, and intends remaining there 8 or 10 days, and 
thence to proceed by land. Sir Peter Wyche is leaving Moscow ; 
and that Emperor has some thoughts of sending an Envoy to 
England, to make a compliment of the privileges, &., enjoyed 
in those territories by the English, and to desire his Majesty to 
be umpire in the difference between him and the Swede. 
[22 pages. Ibid. No. 110.] 


James Hickes to [Williamson]. Nothing has come for you from 
Billing. I hope that my letter with the enclosure found you at 
Hinchingbroke, and that the present will find you at Mr. Summers’ in 
Northampton. I have not seen your writing since you left London, 
but hope for your safe return. Here are 14 packets, containing 
the maps of Candia, come from your clerks for several of your 
correspondents, which were forced to be taxed, they weighing 
3 ounces apiece. [Zbid. No. 111.]

Commissioner John Cox to the Navy Commissioners. Let 
Humphrey Bray receive the 500/. imprested to Mr. Gregory; but _ 
Gregory is “unwilling he should receive it by content,” having 
formerly suffered in a like case in the want of money. I have 
ordered Bray to receive your commands; I wish it were here, for 
the persons concerned appear with their bills, and want their money. 

I went to Maidstone to see what compass and knee timber 
Mr. Mason and others had, and found little upon the wharves but 
what belonged to Mason. I could not prevail upon him to send 
any down, until I promised that I would use my interest with you 
and the Treasurers, for payment of a small bill for 507. odd, for 
goods served in in 1668; the great want of the timber for the new 
ship made me undertake the promise. I was also at Milale [Mill 
Hall], but could find none except what has been bought by the 
Ordnance officers, at 40s. a load. I saw Mayor More, who is very 
free to let us have 24 pieces of compass timber at the price they 
cost, allowing a proportionable charge for their procuring it, or 
delivering timber in lieu of it. 

One of the wrecks that was upon the Mussle Bank is hove over, 
and lies dry at low water. I cannot say more concerning the dis- 
posal of wrecks lying in the river, but they would be better out of 
sight than lying as they do. I have ordered Mr. Moore and Capt. 
Moorecock to demand of the Ordnance officers such powder, &e., as 
they need. Is the Marmaduke to be sold for ready money, or on 
account of bills? Pray order timber and ironwork for the new ship 
and carrying on other works. I send an account by Mr. Bowtwell,

Ant. Thorold to Hickes. The Francis of Lyme has arrived from 
Morlaix, laden chiefly with oakum, and complains of the deadness 
of English manufactures there, owing to the quantity of wool 
received from Ireland and other parts; she reports the raising of 
forces and fitting of ships at Brest, for Candia. Another ship of 
Lyme, from Rotterdam, reports that they speak there of a war 
with France, and are fitting up several great ships, and that an 
eminent French Protestant was lately put to a torturing death by 
the King, for holding intelligence with the States. Several vessels 
are in port, outward bound for places named.

parts will soon cease. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 265, No. 167.]

Sir Thos. Allin to Wren. The part of owr general instructions 
which limits the price of clothes is very troublesome and 
impracticable, and our men are likely to suffer extreme 
wants thereby. The pursers plead that they have received 
clothes from the slopseller, to sell at certain rates, or else 
to return, and that they will not engage in suits by 
underselling them. Most of the clothes are too fine, as for 
instance, laced waistcoats from 14s. to 20s., and worsted 
stockings from 4s. to 6s. It had been well if the Navy Commis- 
sioners had agreed with the slopseller, before the commanders 
had been put to this necessity of breaking orders, or under- 
going suits as soon as they are out of commission, which 
they must do if they take the clothes by force; and you may 
consider whether it be fit that his Royal Highness order 
Major Beckford to give an accownt to the Commissioners 
why he has set exorbitant prices on his clothes, and sent 
none that he can suffer to be issued to the men at the rates 
appointed.—Cadiz, 11 Aug. 1669. [Ibid. No. 1711]

Petition of Sir Thos. Clutterbuck, Consul at Leghorn, to the 
King, for such consideration and assistance as may be thought fit. 
By warrants of the Duke of York, dated 28 Mar. 1661 and 
27 Feb. 1664, I was appointed agent at Leghorn, as well for 
supplying all your Majesty’s ships which should come in to any 
port belonging to the Grand Duke of Tuscany, with provisions and 
other necessaries, as also for assisting them and their commanders 
in all things needful. I performed the office of agent for the whole 
of your Majesty’s affairs there for 4 years, there being no other 
public minister at that place, and have been put to great expense 
and trouble, from"which I am not yet altogether freed, and which 
has been greatly aggravated by my being forced to come to England, 
for no other purpose than to adjust my accounts for victualling 
ships. I hope his Royal Highness has reported that I have dis- 
charged my duty. [Jbid. No. 175.]

CHARLES II. 507 


Sir Thos. Clutterbuck to Lord [Arlington]. I send two narra- 
tives of transactions between me and Ralph Hooker, a Barbadoes 
merchant, and others by whom I sent goods, of which my five- 
sixteenths is worth near 2,000/., and I think that Hooker or his 
heirs ought to make good my losses mentioned, besides the interest 
for 124 years. 

In Dec. 1658, I trusted John Allin, merchant, supercargo of the 
ship Hunter bound for Barbadoes, with a considerable cargo of 
sugar, wherein I had half an interest, and gave him full power, on 
arriving at Barbadoes, to call Hooker to account; but he effected 
nothing save aggravating the loss, by going away in my debt 8100. 
Allin confesses himself debtor for the product of my half interest in 
the cargo of sugar, which—had he sent it to Leghorn, instead of un- 
justly detaining it in his own hands, and using it for his own 
occasions,—would have yielded me nearly 2,0007. This I have lost, 
as well as the interest on it for 10 years. Allin likewise kept the 
ship for some time, promising to give her a full loading, and at last 
returned her to Leghorn with only a third part loading, upon the 
freight of which I lost 1,000/. As Hooker's heirs are residing at 
Barbadoes, and the two English merchants complained of in the 
enclosures are yet living, I beg your lordship will commiserate my 
fate, and procure his Majesty’s speedy and effectual commands to 
the Governor, and those in authority on the island, that justice may 
be done without delay, and that such estate and effects as shall be 
declared due to me may be consigned to the gentlemen upon the 
island holding the procuration, which has been sent to enable them 
to appear for me. [S.P. Dom., Car. TI. 265, No. 176.] Annexing, 

Narrative by Sir Thos. Clutterbuck, of the case between him and 
John Canham and Slaughter Lee, merchants. In 1657 I 
despatched from Leghorn a frigate to Barbadoes, in which my 
share,—being five-siateenths, value 2,0001.,—was consigned 
to Ralph Hooker of Barbadoes, from whom I did not receive 
3007. in return. In 1663, I attached goods sent by Hooker 
on the ship Companion to John Canham and Slaughter Lee, 
for the balance due, and called them before the magistrates, 
which caused an expensive suit im the Court of Chancery at 
Florence, in Nov. 1663, and I obtained a favourable sentence ; 
but I was persuaded to put the case on a reference to 4 English 
and 2 Italian merchants, and we swore to abide by their deci- 
sion. In April 1664, they awarded that Canham and Lee 
should pay me 2,167 pieces of 8, being Hookers part of the 
effects brought over, and 128 pieces of 8 as Hookers part of 
cards brought over by the said ship; the award was con- 
firmed by the magistracy of Pisa, and the said moneys were 
paid to me. Yet their oaths notwithstanding, last April 
Canham and Lee arrested me in an action of 1,5001., with- 
drew that, and, entered a writ against me for 600l., and 
after some imprisonment, I was forced to give in bail. 

My wife hearing that Canham and Lee had treacherously 
fallen upon me here, consulted some lawyers in Leghorn, 
who advised her to make application to the Grand Duke,

1669. 

citing as a precedent for such interference the case of 
Mr. Child and Rob. Foote, English merchants, against Veltz, 
a German. She—reflecting on her sufferings by my absence, 
and being in a strange country with 4 children without a 
provider—went to Florence, and made known her condition, 
when commands were sent to the Governor of Leghorn for 
the imprisonment of Lee ; but he, hearing of the proceedings 
against him, went to Florence also, and demanded the protec- 
tion of Sir John Finch, his Mayesty’s Resident there, who so 
effectually recommended Lees interest at Court, that what 
was before granted according to custom was suspended, 
although Mr. Longland offered himself as security on my 
behalf. [8 pages. S.P. Dom., Car. II. 265, No. 1761.]

Sept. ? Notes [by Williamson, probably on the death of the Queen 
Mother] of precedents relative to messages of condolence inter- 
changed between princes. Sir Nicholas Armorer was presented on 
being sent over to notify the death of the Princess Royal, and 
Duke of Gloucester; Mons. Soigne, who was sent in return to 
condole, was also presented. Upon the death of the Queen of 
Bohemia, none were sent, it being done by letters. Upon the death 
of the Queen Mother of Portugal, Mr. Roper was sent to condole , 
and was presented, as also upon the death of the Duchess of Savoy ; 
and if any are sent to England from Savoy on a like occasion, their 
presentation will be expected. M. de Bellefonds, sent from the 
King of France to condole on the death of the late King of Spain, 
was reported to have been presented, and so was Des Moulens, sent 
on the same occasion from the Queen of France. [S.P. Dom., 
Car. IT. 265, No. 179a.]

I desire my money may be ready within a fortnight, so

CHARLES II. 515 


Declaration by the trustees appointed for management of all 
lotteries for loyal necessitated commission ofticers, that though the 
list of those concerned in this grant is impatiently expected, they 
have met with great trouble and intricacy in preparing it, several 
making claims who, on inquiry, are found to have no right thereto ; 
and they have had to give time and liberty to claimants, to prove 
their rights. 


The trustees are very sensible of the wants of the truly meri- 
torious persons for whom they are entrusted, yet wonder at their 
clamours for a speedy supply, not considering that the affair is 
attended with much charge and care, and that if the stocks of 
plate were broken to satisfy present wants, it would prejudice 
future interests. They are sorry to find that, though for 14 months 
they have given the lotteries their constant care, and reduced them 
to lower odds than has been’ done before, for encouragement of 
adventurers, they do not turn out as well as was hoped for; though 
4,0007. has been paid to Lewis, the goldsmith, a remaining debt of 
2,0007. to him and others is still unpaid. [1 sheet, printed. S.P. 
Dom., Car. IT, 266, Nos. 24, 25. Two copies.] 


Commissioner John Cox to the Navy Commissioners. I send a 
demand from the shipwright and storekeeper for provisions wanting, 
and an appraisement of several wrecks. The sides of the Constant 
John giving way, I shall not be able to weigh her, and to save 
charge, I have ordered all provisions and vessels to be brought up, 
except the Hardereen, which will be convenient to lodge the men 
to be continued in pay, till they have completed blowing up the 
wrecks. The powder and granadoes, with other materials, have 
arrived from the Tower, but I cannot prevail with the storekeeper 
of the Ordnance to let Capt. Moorcock and Mr. Moore use any of 
their conveniences in filling the chests, he having an order to the 
contrary, as the Ordnance officer here thinks it dangerous. I desire 
you will speedily obtain leave, or his Royal Highness’s commands ; 
I cannot apprehend that the danger will be greater here than at 
Woolwich, where all things were received and fitted in their store- 
house, and on their wharf. 

The Macklier and Black Post Horse hoys will be ready to sail on 
Wednesday, and to victual for 2 months apiece; I have ordered 
Capt. Moorcock and Mr. Moore to supply them, and also the 
Black Dog, with the provisions in their custody, their men being 
now upon discharge. I sent to Maidstone to inquire whether there 
is any timber there fit for the new ship. I informed Mr. Gregory 
that you will not send down to pay till Monday. I find the water 
engine was all decayed, and only the brass work was sent up. 
[13 pages. Ibid. No. 26.] Enclosing,

T. Aslaby, collector of the customs at York, to Williamson, at 
his office, Scotland Yard. A conventicle is held at York every 
Sabbath day by Luck, a Nonconformist minister, and is frequented 
by a great many of the town. These unlawful assemblies look like 
the forerunner of the late sad rebellion; therefore I hope they 
may be suppressed, before they come to too great a head. To 
avoid all distaste or resentment, being a stranger here, I desire 
all communications to be sent to Wm. Warter, in the post office 
at York. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 266, No. 30.] 


Fras. Bellott to Williamson. Sixty sail of ships are in port, out- 
ward bound, some being for the Straits and other ports, but most 
for France, for wines. The African, and divers others, put to sea, 
but were forced back again. A small vessel from Ireland reports 
that 30 sail of French wåtered at Barbadoes some time since, and 
that it is reported in Ireland that they have since fallen on 
Hispaniola, and taken it. [Zbid. No. 31.]

News-letter. The elections for Parliament are taking place in 
Scotland. There is a sudden change amongst the people, and none 
are to be chosen that will not sign a declaration against the cove- 
nant and other seditious practices, and that the indulgence to the 
exiled ministers was only a trepan. The provost of Dumfries de- 
clared that he hoped within 6 months the whole Book of Common 
Prayer would be used in Scotland. The borough of Annan refused 
Brice Blair as their burgess, because he would only pass his word, 
but not subscribe the declaration, so [Wm.] Graham, a country 
gentleman, was chosen. [Jbid. No. 33.]

A. Ellis to [Williamson]. The mails beginning to languish every 
day, and the postmasters growing proof against rebukes, I think 
it my duty to inform his lordship of the faults of Dalton Clark, 
and pray that you will have him sent for with all speed. We must 
spur the postmasters up before winter begins, otherwise we shall 
lose the course of the mails. [Jbid. No. 37.] Enclosing, 


A. Ellis to Lord Arlington. Dalton Clark, being deputy 
postmaster of the stage of Witham, is thereby obliged to ride 
with the mails through his stage, at the rate of 5 miles an 
hour; but on 30 June 1669, he was 9 hours riding to the 
neat stage, a distance of 18 miles; on 21 July he was 
6 hours riding the same distance, and on 26 Sept. he was 
7 hours. These neglects are of infinite prejudice to general 
despatch, especially of the foreign mails, in relation to the 
state of that passage at Harwich. Clark having refused 
to appear upon summons, at the Letter Office in London, to 
show cause, I pray you to send a messenger for him, to 
answer such defaults and contempt.—Letter Office, 5 Oct. 
1669. [Lbid. No. 371.]

Col. Thos. Middleton to the Navy Commissioners. There is a 
quantity of good timber in the yard, but it is not of fit length for 
the works on the new ship; as she is likely to be a gallant one, it 
will be a great pity if she should want materials to make her com- 
plete. The timber demanded should be provided, if it is to be had. 

Mr. Wilson, the storekeeper, desires all the canvas measured, 
which will be a work of time; but it is not reasonable for me to 
desire that of another man that I would not accept of myself; that 
is, to take things by contents. There is more canvas here than I 
should have judged, considering the ships that have been sent out 
of this port since my last survey ; some of it has been in store 
several years. Shall it be measured by the sail-makers here, or 
will you send down Mr. Harris, the King’s sail-maker, to see it 
done? It requires care and skill, and will take a month to 
accomplish. ; 

Capt. Cox being gone for London, I opened his letter of instruc- 
tions to the masters of the galliots, and have ordered them both for 
this place; it is possible some beams may be brought, which are 
more wanting here than in any other yard. All diligence shall be 
used, when the time comes for selling the wrecks. Shall the Minion 
be sold with the rest, or broken up and burnt? The single dock is 
empty and much decayed, and will require much time before it can 
receive a ship into it. Mr. Mason has a quantity of timber to sell 
at Maidstone ; he has been too hard with you about converting his 
great timber in the woods; some of it I have seen, but it does not 
answer my expectation ; it is very good, but short, and not fit for 
the service intended. [24 pages. Ibid. No. 46.]

Remarks on Dr. [John] Price’s MS. as being too detailed, and

Thos. Holden to Williamson. A vessel has arrived from Ireland,

Anne of London, Capt. Reed commander, bound for the Barbadoes ; 
he reports that when off Kinsale, she suddenly sprang a leak, and 
went down, and that out of 26 men, only 11 saved themselves in 
the boats, the captain and the rest perishing with the ship. Three 
ships from Newfoundland speak of a great tempest there, and the 
loss of many men and boats; 50 or 60 sail of merchantmen are 
in harbour, outward bound. A passenger from Holland reports ' 
that great military preparations are made there, and that they 
talk of a speedy war with France. [Jbid. No. 51.]

Dr. Rich. Clayton [master of University College], to Williamson. 
I have received a letter from Lord Arlington, through Mr. Thomp- 
son, a scholar of this house, which is so tender of the welfare of 
the University in general, and so sensible of the unsettled condi- 
tion of this poor old college, that it is a great perplexity to us that 
we cannot at present comply with it. Our whole society have 
joined in a letter to him, wherein we have laboured to acquit our- 
selves, and yet have written very sparingly of the young man who 
has deprived himself of the good effects of his lordship’s letter, by 
his great indiscretion, as Dr. Lamplugh fully understands, to whose 
letter you will give credit. 

Though I am but a stranger, I am not a stranger to your care to 
preserve the freedom of our elections, which have so great an in- 
fluence on the public; it will not be forgotten how much we owe to 
you and his lordship therein, so long as those hopeful young men re- 
main whom we have had the freedom to elect. We have sent a 
messenger expressly to present these letters, containing a sober recital 
of our state, and a grateful acknowledgment to his lordship for 
withholding the mandate, as no greater obligation could have been laid 
upon us. We pray you to present our addresses to his lordship as 
fairly, and with as much advantage, as you can. [Jbid. No. 73.] 
Annexing, 


Statement by Rich. Thompson that, whereas the Master and 
Fellows of University College [Oxford] are obliged by their 
statutes to elect to a fellowship as soon as any falls void, 
they have not done it, although 3 have been declared void for 
4 years. Upon supplication to the visitors of their house, the 
Master and Fellows had a grant to suspend the profits of such 
vacant places, and to convert them to the payment of their 
debts, which grant expired on Trinity Sunday last; but 
they have not proceeded to an election according to the 
Statute. Lord Halifax urging them with a mandate on 
behalf of his friend [John] Savile, they are now commanded 
to receive him into the first of the three vacant places, and 
there is nothing more common now in the College than that he 
will be a Fellow before St. Simon and St. Jude’s instant. 
No excuse can be urged why they did not elect me on Lord 
Arlington's recommendation. [14 pages. Ibid. No. 731]

Rich. Watts to Williamson. The Nonsuch ketch has come in 
from the North West Passage. They were six months environed 
with ice. First hauling their ship ashore, and building a house, 
they carried provisions on shore, and brewed ale and beer, and 
provided against the cold, which was their work. They report the 
natives to be civil, and beaver plentiful; those who carried out 
no venture have brought home 10/. or 12l. worth of beaver. A 
pink has arrived from Barbadoes, and reports that colony to be in 
a good condition. [Ibid. No. 80.] 


James Hickes to Williamson. The northern and Norwich mails— 
which were taken from the Royston boy on Sunday night, half-a-mile 
from the town, by two horsemen with a dark lantern, and found 
open in a ditch by the constables —have been received ; horse and foot 
are out in pursuit of the fellows. We wait our packets from Not- 
tingham, Peterborough, and Bury; they are taken away, unless 
found at daylight, near the place where the mail was; acquaint 
Mr. Ellis if you see him. [Jbid. No. 81.] 


Levant Company to Wm. Hedges. We revoke our order of the 
6th, empowering you to draw bills on our treasurer in England, to 
defray the expenses of Sir D. Harvey’s entertainment, in case 
there should not be sufficient cash at Constantinople and Smyrna 
to meet that and other expenses, and you are to wait our further 
directions. [Levant Papers, Vol. 5, p. 226.]

Account that though the import of spicery from Holland was 
prohibited by proclamation, 26 Aug. 1663, a dispensation 
was granted under certain conditions, till the war with the 
Dutch, when all imports from them were forbidden, since 
which time none were brought over but by special licence ; 
in the present case, the owner, by connivance of the Customs’ 
officers, procured an entry for a small quantity, and, on 
pretence thereof, got a larger quantity admitted, which was 
seized. Proofs of the intention of fraud on the part of the 
owner, and of the falsehood of the pretences on which he 
petitions for entry of his goods. [Lbid. No. 911.] 


Report of Attorney-General Palmer on the above case, stating at 
full the grounds on which Benj. Waller of Yarmouth pleads for a dis- 
pensation to import certain nutmegs, but that, in strictness of law, 
it cannot be granted. [Jbid. No. 92.]

P. [B.?] Gordon to [Williamson]. I am intending to return to 
Russia, though the pay there is a bare subsistence ; but in Scotland 
soldiers of fortune can obtain no honourable employment for 
persons of quality. In England aliens are scarcely employed, so that 
foreign service becomes a necessity. I travelled to Scotland with 
the Lord Commissioner, who was received in many places with 
ringing of bells and music. At Doncaster some of the Scottish 
nobility met him, and at other points on the road, the Earls of 
Roxburgh and Hume, with numerous troops, and the militia in the 
several counties. At Musselburgh were the King’s horse, the Lothian 
regiments of foot, the Lord Chancellor, Duke of Hamilton, and others. 
As he approached Edinburgh, ordnance was fired; the city troops 
and 400 citizens, with the provost and magistrates, met him. He 
entered with the Lord Chancellor and Duke of Hamilton on each

Rich. Tolson to Williamson, at his office or chambers in Whitehall. 
I presumed on your courtesy to my child, and since my wife left 
her in London, I have written several letters to your cousin, for in- 
formation as to her welfare and your intentions, but have received 
no answer. I hear my daughter is very melancholy and discon- 
tented, by living so solitary, and at such a distance from her rela- 
tions and friends. Is she settled, or what hopes are there of it? I 
am resolved to provide her a portion, rather than be at vast charge 
in the south. If your intentions are not declared, I will send for 
her home next term. Thanks for all favours. [Jbid. No. 98.]

treason, the party is not bailable by any justices of the peace in the

to be made, and in whose power it will be to do as he sees cause,

John Man to Williamson. Several colliers are detained by the 
stormy weather. I hear from Llanelly, 7 miles distant, that 2 col- 
liers, the Providence of Foy, and the Nicholas of: Croisic, have 
been cast away, and not a man saved. The Desire of Swansea has 
arrived from Boston in New England, and reports a great hurricane 
and the probable loss of much shipping, there being several vessels 
for Bristol and other ports there at the time. A passenger by the 
Desire says that New York is likely to flourish, it being a pleasant 
country, having wholesome air, and a good trade. [Lbid. No. 106.] 


Dr. Rich. Clayton to Williamson. The society are sorry they 
could not comply with his lordship’s desires, but the young man 
must thank himself for failing in the business, as the society can 
make appear. His lordship desiring a speedy account of the 
Fellows’ resolution, I called them together, when they unani- 
mously resolved to go to an election, and thus we supplied all the 
vacant fellowships, so that there is now none left for our obedience 
to his Majesty’s commands. As there is a statute that no elections 
are firm till approved by the Vice-Chancellor, the doctors, and 
proctors, we obtained these nemine contradicente, but the getting 
of them took until Saturday, so we were delayed replying to his 
lordship’s letter, and beg this may be explained. Dr. Lamplugh is 
at Reading; Mr. Thomas and Mr. Farrar are thankful for being 
remembered by you. [Jbid. No. 107.]

Commissioner J. Tippetts to the Navy Commissioners. Mr. New- 
land looks for the pitch, tar, timber, &., by the first easterly wind. 
He said that the prices of all sawn work were much risen, by want 
of water for the sawing mills in the country, and that deals are 
sold 4s. or 5s. in the pound dearer in London than 6 weeks since: 
let me know if it is so, or to what proportion they have risen, as 
also the price of masts, as I have agreed for 60 at the London price. 
Mr, Ridge expects some direction from Mr. Littleton about drawing 
the money. The quarterly books of the yard will be ready by 
Tuesday. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 266, No. 125.] 


Commissioner John Cox to the Navy Commissioners. Laurence 
has been to Sir Roger Twysden, and finds Mason has been twice, and 
proffered money for the timber ; I shall meet Sir Roger at Maidstone 
on Thursday with the Surveyor, and bring him to as low terms as I 
can. The master of the Harwich hoy is dead; having no occasion 
for her, I have ordered her to Deptford with the horseboat, to 
take in deals for the new ship. Mr. Lewsley has proffered 10 loads 
of very good plank at 5l. 5s. a load. I desire your order thereon. 
[Lbid. No. 126.] 


Same to the Same. John’ Clerk of Gravesend has tendered

Thos. Corie to Williamson. On my return here, I stayed 3 hours 
at Thetford, and found Mr. Martin in bed with afever. Mr. Ken- 
dall wasnotin town. I delivered your letter to the Mayor, who is 
confident there will be no opposition to your election ; he expects 
you down on Thursday, and will provide for your and your friends’ 
entertainment. The Mayor and Martin had sent for Mr. Barber, 
the under-sheriff, and on my arrival at Norwich, I heard that he had 
been there, and given orders to Lambert, the deputy under-sheriff, 
not to appear at Thetford upon this business, as he would make a 
precept out himself. Martin says that Barber was at Thetford last 
week, endeavouring to make interest for Sir Geo. Vyner, but with- 
out success. I will bring Lambert with me on Thursday to prevent 
the worst ; it would be a good medium to set Barber right, who is 
over-greedy of the reward for executing his office. I have written 
to Martin to send to Denver, where Barber lives, to prevail for his 
attendance on Thursday. I hope Mr. Marriott has been with 
you, as he has gone for London, and promised to attend Lord 
Arlington. Martin is not inclined to his coming, in respect of 
the pique between him and Kendall. I have ordered the keeper 
of Croxton Park to have a brace of does ready for you. [Jbid. 
No. 130.]

M. De Breval to Williamson. I am ashamed to write you so 
often, but I hear that in this change of the bishopric of Chichester, 
there will be a revolution of other places, one of which might suit 
me. I have told the Bishop of Oxford and Mr. Trevor, so as to 
facilitate things. You are one of the principal reasons why I 
incline to the Savoy Church, but I shall not go there in my present 
uncertainty as to whether the bishops will do for me what I told 
you. But I should be very glad if the friends of that church would 
give me 50 pieces; this would not be difficult if you would interest 
yourself in it. I should only preach there one Sunday a fortnight, 
that there may be leisure to obtain a pension for me. [French. 
This letter is endorsed 20 Oct., but dated only Wednesday ; the true 
date is therefore probably 18 Oct., which is a Wednesday. Ibid. 
No. 134.] 


The King’s speech on the opening of Parliament. I am glad to 
see you, and hope it will be a happy meeting. I have had great ex- 
perience of your affection and loyalty, and am very confident of its 
continuance. It is almost a year and a half since the last sitting, 
and though my debts have pressed me very much, yet I was unwil- 
ling to call for your assistance till this time. What you last gave 
me was wholly applied to the Navy and extraordinary Fleet, for 
which it was intended. I desire you will consider my debts. I 
have something to propose of great importance, concerning the 
uniting of England and Scotland; but as it will require some time, 
I have left that and some other things to be opened by the Lord 
Keeper. [14 pages, in the King’s own hand. Printed in Lords’ 
Journals, Vol. XII., p. 251. Ibid. No. 135.] 


Copy of the above. [14 pages. Printed. Ibid. No. 136.] 


The Lord Keeper's speech to both Houses of Parliament. [4 pages. 
Printed. Ibid. No. 137 ; also in Lords’ Journals, XII., p. 251.) 


Precedents of the proceedings of the Houses of Lords and Com- 

mons, in reference to their transactions with the King :— 

18 Jan. 1666-7.—A message from the Lords, by Sir John 
Kyton, Usher of the Black Rod, that the King commanded 
the Commons to attend him in the House of Lords; the 
Speaker went up, and on his return, acquainted the House of 


1669. 


CHARLES II. 537 


the King’s reasons for hastening the supply, and for the 
members going into the country to put the Poll Bill in execu- 
tion, and that he would prorogue the House on Monday next. 

29 Jan. 1667.—A message from the Lords, by Sir Wm. Child and 
Sir John Coell, that his Majesty will receive the address from 
both Houses on behalf of the French merchants at 3 p.m. 

7 Feb. 1667.—Sec. Morice acquainted the House that the King 
intended to put an end to the sessions to-morrow morning, and 
to prorogue Parliament. 

8 Feb. and 20 July, 1667. — Messages whereby his Majesty 
prorogued Parliament. 

10 Oct. 1667—Message by Sir John Eyton, summoning the . 
Commons to attend him in the House of Peers. 

15 Oct. 1667.—A message from the Lords, by Sir Nath. Hobart 
and Mr. Proctor, that the Lords concur with the Commons in 
the address of thanks to his Majesty, and will go in a body 
with the Commons therewith to the King, and have sent to 
him to appoint a time and place. 

9 Dec. 1667.— Sec. Morice delivered a message in writing from 
his Majesty, stating that as Christmas is near, the members 
should return to their houses, and therefore there is to be an 
adjournment on 17 December, until the beginning of February. 

17 Dec. 1667.—Sec. Morice acquainted the House that his Majesty, 
taking notice that some Bills requiring a speedy despatch were 
not yet finished, desired the House to continue its sittings till 
Tuesday next. 

19 Dec. 1667.—Sec. Morice delivered a written message from the 
King, that 6 February will be a convenient day to which 
their adjournment may be made. 

10 Feb. 1668.—A message from the King by Sir John Eyton, Usher 
of the Black Rod, commanding the House to attend him in the 
Lords; the Speaker went up, and on his return, acquainted 
the House that to prevent mistakes, his Majesty had delivered 
his speech in writing, which he read. 

5 March 1668.—Lord Fitzharding acquainted the House that his 
Majesty had appointed for the Commons to attend him at 3 p.m. 
in the Banqueting House, Whitehall. 

6 March 1668.—Sec. Morice delivered a message from the King 
for hastening a supply for building more ships, &e. 

30 March 1668.—A message from the Lords, by Sir Justinian, 
Lewin and Sir John Coell, that they have sent down the Act 
„for the better securing of a portion of 5,0007. to Lady Frances 
Savile, infant daughter of Thomas, late Earl of Sussex, out 
of the estate of James Earl of Sussex. also an infant, in pur- 
suance of the will of the said Thomas Earl of Sussex, to which 
they desire the concurrence of the Commons. 

30 March 1668.—Sec. Morice delivered a message from the King,

Mr. Speaker and the members went in a body, when his Majesty 
said that the season was far spent, and it was high time for 
setting out a fleet, and therefore conjured the House to finish

The King to the Parliament of Scotland. We acknowledge the 
loyalty and ready compliance of our subjects; we much desire 
to settle union between our kingdoms, and request you, on these 
and other matters, to give full credence to our Commissioner. 
[Printed. Ibid. No. 139. Printed in Acts of Parliament of 
Scotland, as dated 15 Sept. 1669, Vol. VII., f. 551.] 


Speech of the Earl of Lauderdale, Lord Commissioner. Declares 
the King’s resolution to uphold the Episcopal Church, repress con- 
venticles, and bring their ringleaders to punishment; also to prose- 
cute a closer union between the kingdoms than that brought about 
by King James, as alone able to settle the contested points about 
trade, &c.; this union his Majesty will also urge forward in the 
English Parliament. [4 pages. Printed. Ibid. No. 140.] 


Copy of the above. [24 pages. Ibid: No. 141.] 


Rob. Mein to Williamson. The members of Parliament rode in 
state from Holyrood House to the Parliament House, where the Lord 
Commissioner presented the King’s letter, and made a speech thereon, 
expressing great favour to his Majesty’s ancient kingdom ; declaring 
his dislike to private conventicles and unlawful meetings, to prevent 
which some of the silenced ministers are restored ; and his determi- 
nation to uphold the Episcopal Church. The Chancellor then made 
an excellent speech, and all the members, with lifted hands, took the 
oath of allegiance, and then subscribed the declaration against the 
covenant. The members of Articles were then chosen, and a committee 
appointed, and Parliament was adjourned. The Lord Commissioner 
entertained the whole members and other persons of quality, with 
all the ladies in town, at a magnificent supper at Holyrood, “ where 
nothing was wanting that Brittane could affourd.” [Jbid. No. 142.]

Demand by Mr. Burroughs of plank for the King’s two engines

Commissioner John Cox to the Navy Commissioners. I fear 
there must be some mistake as to Clerk’s timber served, in; 
particulars of what has been received; he is free that you shall 
have choice out of 300 trees, and if any prove bad, it must be the 
fault of the choosers. When Mr. Brunsden comes down, I shall give 
him the best instructions, and order him to bore at the butt end, to 
see that there be none rotten or red. There was no mistake in the 
price of Lewsley’s plank; I knew it was extravagant, but being 
tendered, I thought good to acquaint you; I will tell him it is 
not to be bought unless he will sell at a lower rate. 

I caused the wrecks to be appraised at 20l. more than what they 
were first appraised at; if there were not the forts in hand, which is 
their hopes of selling plank and timber to the Ordnance officers, 
hardly any would have taken them for breaking up; there would 
not have been so much given for them, if we had not ordered some 
of the officers to be bidders. I will let the pressed men know that 
they must not expect allowance to go to market any longer. 

The Black Dog hoy is not yet returned with Mr. Moorecock’s 
timber. I send the appraisement of the Minion wreck, which 
will be put to sale on Tuesday next. There is a small empty 
house standing on the King’s ground near the teamer’s house, 
formerly built by Commissioner Pett in the time of the sickness, 
for a pest house; if you approve of its being glazed and fitted, it 
may make two small tenements, and let for 6l. or 8l. a year. 
[2 pages. Ibid. No. 149.] Encloses, 

Certificate by Wm. Rand and 3 others, that they have viewed

her, she may be worth 16l.—19 Oct, Chatham. [Ibid.

Anonymous paper headed “The Alarum,” directed to Mr. Gara- 
way. Like the dumb man who found his tongue when he saw an 
arm lifted to kill his father, so I, who never meddled with anything 
beyond my private concernments, being an enemy to knowing, 
much more to writing, state matters, yet I cannot forbear— 
when I see my country in danger by the united villainy of 
so many that conspire against it; when I see that it is be- 
come the office of men in power to lay snares for Englishmen’s 
liberties, and the practice of men in trust to betray them, and when 
all the industry which should be used to maintain the Government 
is applied to alter it; when I see that the end is resolved, and that 
they only differ in the means, the only question remaining being 
whether they are to be enslaved by deceit or, violence—from im- 
parting my fears, and the grounds of them, to some of those few 
English gentlemen whom the corruption of this age has left, who 
love freedom and hate slavery. 

The present counsels go upon these foundations; first, to gain 
Parliament so that they shall be liberal of their money, and sparing in 
their grievances, and supply the King, without looking back upon 
ill conduct, or falling heavy upon the authors of it. If this Parlia- 
ment fail, it must be dissolved, and a new one chosen; and if that 
should not answer what is expected from it, force is to be set up, 
as the last and surest expedient. Money that is wanting to pay 
wages is found to corrupt members of Parliament. The great instru- 
ment of this is Lord Arlington who, besides promises of this or 
that place, tells out ready money to hirelings, who engage to betray 
their country for it. He desires the King may be put into a con- 
dition not to want Parliaments, knowing they are saucy things, 
and make bold to inquire both into the faults and the abilities of 
men in power, and he has just wit enough to be sensible that he can- 
not bear scrutiny. This poor man is but the sign of a secretary, 
and can do nothing that belongs to his place but receive the profits 
of it. To do him right, he loves business no better than business 
loves him; but he has not yet got 10,000/. a year, and till then, he 
will not leave the box, though he cannot drive, and were he freed 
from the fear of Parliament, would be as insolent as he is ignorant. 

The next in the negotiation is his man Clifford, who has a great 
mind to be a minister, probably because his father was one. He 
plays no small game, nor catches at small profits, by which he 
would seem to neglect his fortune, but it is that he may make it all 
at once. He sets up to be generous, by being free of the King’s 
wine at his table, and of his money in the Treasury; but don’t 
mistake the man, he has too much ambition and too little money to 
be content. If things succeed as he has laid them, he will throw 
off Lord Arlington’s livery, and set up for himself; but in order to 
do this, the great work of cheating the Parliament must be carried 
on, in which he neither spares his own pains, nor the King’s money ; 
it is worth observing how he behaves when anything concern-

with reputation and honour, but were recalled a year since, and have

A. Ellis to Williamson, I knew nothing of your journey to 
Thetford until yesterday ; if you kept it private through fear that 
I should cross your election, you are an unkind man. I have not 
been able to obtain an answer to any of my letters to the Thetford 
postmaster, as to settling the post office, and I hope you will have 
him before you, and see the post house settled. This you can 
hardly deny, seeing it is Lord Arlington’s affair. I wonder which 
way you could get to Thetford without passing our quarters, where 
you have so many servants; I hope you will have no cause to 
repent your journey. 

To-day the House [of Commons] has been on the subject of the 
Lords’ jurisdiction, and one of the members advised an adjournment 
from day to day, till the Lords had erased all their proceedings 
against the East India Company ; this reminds me of the Romans, 
when they disputed with the Fathers for magistracy, and gained 
ground on every argument. The reputation of Lord Ormond in- 
creases so much amongst the Commons that the torrent begins to 
turn, or at least, to lose much of its violence. M. Richard has 
returned to Paris, finding the sea too tempestuous; Thos. Lloyd 
and several others were starved at sea between Holland and Eng- 
land, from not taking sufficient provisions with them. [2 pages. 
Ibid. No. 158.]

Col. Thos. Middleton and Commissioner John Cox to the Navy

discourse with the teamer about the pest house, but fear there may

there may be in any others having it; we will take the best course. 

We could not agree with Sir Roger Twysden about his timber, he 
now asking 45s. aton ; and we could not bring him lower than 42s., 
he affirming that Mason had proffered 41s.; he has given us a week

Barnstaple, and a trow of Swansea were forced on the banks at the

men got on to the other, with the aid of a rope, and so saved them- 
selves and their stock. I expect the trow will come off the next 
spring tide, as she has endured the brunt, and is a strong vessel. 
We heard of more disasters westward, but not the particulars.

Answer of the Scottish Parliament to the King. We cheerfully 
concur in all your wishes, and especially in that of bringing about 
a closer union between the kingdoms. We are willing to appoint 
commissioners to treat thereon, reserving the final approbation to 
Parliament, and offer to your Majesty the nomination of the com- 
missioners. We will give cheerful obedience to Lord Commissioner 
Lauderdale. [14 pages. Ibid. No. 171. Printed in Acts of 
Parliament of Scotland, Vol. VIL, p. 552.] 


Copy of the above. [4 pages. Printed. Ibid. No. 172.] 


News-letter. On the 19th, the Lord High Constable, the Earl of 
Errol, sat in the Parliament House, to welcome the members as they 
alighted. About 11 am., the Lord Chancellor and [George Keith] 
Earl Marshal, with the purse and mace, and 6 trumpeters, came as 
usual to see all in readiness, and receive the Lord Commissioner. 
Description of his procession, the Earl of Mar carrying the sword, 
the Earl of Argyle the sceptre, and the Marquis of Douglas the 
crown before him. The road was lined with citizens in arms. As 
he entered the Parliament House, the castle guns fired. He took the 
chair of state, and the regalia being laid on the table before him, the 
Bishop of Dumblane [Rob. Leighton] prayed. The King’s letter was 
then read, and the Lord Commissioner and Lord Chancellor spoke to 
second it. The commissions of shires and boroughs were received, and 
doubtful ones referred for examination. The nobility then chose 
8 bishops, the bishops 8 nobles, and those 16 chose 8 knights and 
8 burgesses who, with the officers of State, make up the Lords of 
Articles, to prepare business for Parliament. The answer to the 
King’s speech has been twice read and debated, andis passed and 
printed. [14 pages. Ibid. No. 173.] 


Rob. Mein to Williamson. Parliament met again, and after 
much dispute, concluded that there should be an Union between 
England and Scotland, and that the King should nominate com- 
missioners to treat thereon, and the place of treaty; it was then 
adjourned till Tuesday. [Ibid. No. 174.] 


Sir Thos. Allin to Williamson. Until 14 October, we so curbed the 
Algerines that few or none of them durst venture to sea; but I was 
forced off that coast, and separated from my fleet, by a hard gale, 
and have now only 4 men-of-war and a ketch with me. Standing 
in close to the Mole of Algiers, I found that 4 sail had got out, and 
thereupon sent 3 men-of-war, with the ketch, to watch their 
motions, and secure our trade along the coast of Spain; I am 
going to Port Mahon in Minorea—being the place designed for 
cleaning and repairing our ships—to put our affairs in order. I fear 
we shall find the Governors there “severe in point of pratique,” as 
they have already refused it to Sir Edw. Spragg’s ketch. I have 
written very often to Sir Wm, Godolphin about it, and he gives 
hopes that all will be well,

CHARLES. II. 547 


I met a prize on the 19th, going to Algiers, which we cut off 
from the town, and forced the men to leave her; but they first fired 
the ship; after her masts were burnt down, our men went on 
board, quenched the fire, and saved “a parcel of poor jack,” which 
I distributed amongst our ships, and appointed shares for those 
absent. The prize was one of our Newfoundland men, who venture 
all to get the first market. Send me a little news, as after 2 months 
on this coast, and being in expectation of many months more on 
the seas, it will be refreshing. [14 pages. S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 266, 
NOIE] 


Sir Thos. Allin to the Navy Commissioners. I must complain of 
the victualler’s agents in the Thames and at Portsmouth ; 28 butts 
are certified by Sir John Harman to have quite leaked out, the 
casks being old, new wrought, and my purser is 23 tuns of beer 
short for his 3 months’ beverage; Sir Edw. Spragg has lost near 
the same quantity. I was forced to send all the fireships and 
2 men-of-war to the coast of Spain, for water and beverage wine, or 
we must have gone off the coast of Algiers, and suffered the Turks’ 
fleet to go clean out, to the great prejudice of our nation. I had to 
supply pursers with wine out of contingent money in hand. 

Gascoigne, the victualler’s agent at Tangier, would only pay half 
the sum for the 3 months’ beverage wine, but that would not satisfy 
me, knowing how basely he used me the last time I had credit 
upon him; so I informed him he must either pay me so much money 
or go with me to sea; rather than do that, he paid my agent the 
money in light pistoles at 4 dollars apiece, which is a loss in every 
pistole of 2s. 6d. l : 

The seamen complain for want of clothes, and fall daily by 
agueish distempers, many being pressed men, who brought no more 
than is on their backs. Some of the ships are out of victuals, and 
others nearly so; but you will have their complaints by Sir Edw. 
Spragg, who with 4 ships left us 10 days ago. The Nonsuch in a 
hard gale carried her foremast by the board elose to the deck, and 
cut all away. I have sent her to Port Mahon, but I fear there is no 
mast fit for her there. I hope, if you send victuals, you will also 
send 2 or 8 masts, [2 pages. Ibid. No. 176.] 


Commissioner J. Tippetts to the Navy Commissioners. I freely 
subscribe to your opinion that such as have spent most time in his 
Majesty’s service should be preferred before others of like abilities, 
and for your better satisfaction, I have sent the enclosed. John Rogers 
served Mr. Leadman, carver for Deptford and Woolwich, and has

Edw. Byland to the Navy Commissioners. What I did as to 
Sir John Austin’s timber was clearly for his Majesty’s service; I 
confess we have no urgent occasion for it, but another such bargain 
will scarcely be found. It is a very unseasonable time of the year

Ant. Thorold to Hickes. The Windsor and Elizabeth of Lyme 
have arrived from St. Malo, with canvas and other goods, and 
report that there was a proclamation out there, calling home all the 
subjects of the French King within 6 months, on pain of death ; 
also an order for pressing carpenters, and for prohibiting the import 
of drapery from Holland, and that they spoke of doing the same as 
to England. They also heard of Sir Thos. Allin taking 2 Algiers 
men-of-war of 30 and 40 guns. They touched at Guernsey on their 
way home, and found the place in good equipage, and such a great 
quantity of cider made this year, that they have refused any wines 
being brought to them from France. I expect my [news]-letter, 
having received but one. [Zbid. No. 179.]

Charles Whittington to Williamson. Three Hull vessels have 
arrived from Holland, and report a great storm of wind on Sunday 
last, which brought the sea with such rage into the Texel, that a 
vessel laden with stuffs and cloth from Holland was cast away on 
Fugell Sand, as were also several other vessels riding in the Texel, 
one being bound for the East Indies. A Newcastle vessel lost 
all its masts, and for greater security, heaved much of the lead 
and cloth overboard. 

Four vessels of London were driven back into the Texel from 
Yarmouth Sands, and still remain there. I hear from Bridlington 
that 4 laden colliers were cast away on this coast. The fury 
of the storm has driven the water into Amsterdam, and done 
much damage to the warehouses and cellars of the merchants. The 
Relief of Hull, laden with flax from the East, has put in to stop a 
leak. I have provided you a barrel of excellent ale; how shall it 
be sent? [Jbid. No. 182.]

Petition of Martha, relict of John Warner, lute postmaster of 
Thetford, to Williamson, M.P. for Thetford. My husband 
was postmaster for a long time, and met his death by falling 
into the river on a dark night, when returning home with 
Lord Arlington’s letters, which were found next day in his 
pocket. I have carried on the office since his death, to the 
good liking of Lord Townshend, the Lord Lieutenant of Nor- 
folk, “ for whose letters especially that pipe was erected” ; as 
at is the sole subsistence of myself and 4 children, I desire I 
may continue to do so, according to my contract and agree- 
ment, having, with consent of the Lord Lieutenant, made a 
contract with the present postmaster to hold it till Michael- 
mas; it is the general desire of the Mayor, burgesses, and. 
commonalty, as is testified by their affixing the corporate 
seal to my petition. [Ibid: No. 1841.] 


Representation of Rob. Tyrrell, Mayor, and the burgesses and com- 
monalty of Thetford, to Sir Allen Apsley and Jos. Williamson, their 
two burgesses in Parliament. Notwithstanding the Act of Oblivion, 
our charter is not yet renewed, and we conceive that neither our- 
selves nor our proceedings are safe without it ; we request the speedy 
effecting thereof, and power for the corporation to add or alter such 
clauses as may be deemed necessary. 

Our corporation comprehends part of Norfolk and part of 
Suffolk for its boundary, and that part of Thetford which 
lies in Suffolk, during the rebellion and for 7 or 8 years be- 
fore the Restoration, paid all duties, &c., to that part of Thetford 
which lies in Norfolk. We beg to be restored to our former 
rights and immunities, either by some clause in an Act of Parlia- 
ment, or in our charter, so that there may be no dispute for 
the future, and that all subsequent payments and duties which shall 
be imposed upon the Suffolk side in Thetford, as well as on 
Thetford in Norfolk, may be paid to Thetford in Norfolk, as if that 
part lay in Norfolk. 

By reason of such payment of taxes to Suffolk, by that part of 
Thetford lying in Suffolk, and not to Norfolk, an arrear of 2001. has 
been laid upon the latter, and a suit is depending in the Exchequer, 
between Thetford in Suffoik and Thetford in Norfolk, as to payment 
of the arrears; this is of many years’ standing, and the persons 
liable having removed or died, Thetford in Norfolk. is condemned 
to pay, if they show no cause to the contrary during this term. 
This condemnation has crept in upon us through the ill management 
of those we trusted, and not having the money, we ask a hearing 
de novo of the whole matter, at the Exchequer or in Parliament, 
proceedings to be stayed in the Exchequer meantime. 

From time out of mind, Thetford has been the place for loading 
and unloading commodities from the upper countries to our 
borough, and from thence to divers counties down the stream,

Sir Denis Gauden to the Navy Commissioners. Not having 
obtained the final determination of the Treasury Commissioners, on 
the accounts referred to them by his Majesty in Council, I have not 
been able to represent properly what I have disbursed; but I send 
the state of my disbursements, lest I may suffer for want of laying 
that and other things before you. I have been, and still am, under 
great difficulty to preserve myself from ruin, by these disbursements, 
and the provisions sent to the Barbadoes in the time of the war, 
which amount to 23,000/.; I shall not be able to contend much 
longer, unless I receive some satisfaction. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 267, 


No. 14.] 


Col. Thos. Middleton to the Navy Commissioners. I will send a 
man to mark out what timber of Mr. Mason’s is fit for present use, 
and he will bring the least price. Iam of your opinion concerning 
the teamer and the house; it is far better to have one knave that 
he knows live near a man, than 2 or 8 that he knows not; besides, 
the teamer has more reason to have it than any other man. 

I wish you had given me a positive order about Sir Roger Twysden’s 
timber, because I would do in it as if for myself, and the bargain 
would be much to the King’s advantage. Brunsden cannot meet 
with any knees except what Mason has. Ruffhead is gone to 
London; if you do not make an agreement with him before he 
returns, I and Commissioner Cox will do what we can. You will 
not do amiss to treat with some other, to see how the market stands, 
albeit I would give him 5s. per cwt. more than any other, unless 
it be the King’s smith at Deptford; I believe that such anchors as 
we require are not to be made by any other man in England, and 
there are 30 anchors wanted for the new ship and others. [24 pages. 
Ibid. No. 15.]

Hugh Salesbury to Williamson. The Queen’s ship is to be 
launched to-day ; Sir Philip [Honeywood] still continues very bad. 
[S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 267, No. 25.] 


Rich. Watts to ‘Williamson. Letters from France report that 
Dieppe is very much visited with the pestilence, and that the King 
has sent two companies of foot, and a troop of horse, to lie near the 
town, and keep the inhabitants in. Calais is also reported to be 
visited. I hear of only one house in Dover, but the north-east 
winds keep all news and trade from our town. [Jbid. No. 26.] 


Thos. Butler to Williamson. I trouble you this time on my own 
account. The Bishop of Chichester resigning not long since, I hear 
of several designed as his successor, but think the Dean of Winton 
is as likely as any. The Dean, besides Stepney, holds the living of 
North Crawley in Buckinghamshire, worth 160/. or 2002. a year. 
I earnestly beg any living vacated by Bishop King’s successor. 
The death of the Bishop of Worcester, and the removal of Dr. Clerk 
from Winton, give his Majesty the patronage of many livings, and 
if you will advise me, I will be at Whitehall with my petition for 
one of them; but the living of North Crawley is the object of my 
present application. [14 pages. Ibid. No. 27.] 


Council to the Earl of Winchelsea, Lord Lieutenant of Kent. His 
Majesty has received frequent informations of the fraudulent prac- 
tices of persons in and about Canterbury and other parts of Kent, in 
sending large quantities of wool on board French shallops and other 
vessels, for transportation into France, to the prejudice of the trade 
and manufactures of this kingdom; and notwithstanding the laws 
made to inhibit the same, yet the persons have so many devices to 
evade seizure, and have become so bold and confident, as openly and 
frequently to transport great quantities, and to resist the officers 
authorised to seize. His Majesty has thereupon directed the Lord 
High Admiral of England to send 2 double shallops to ply upon the 
coast, and to search all suspected vessels, and when any wool is 
found, to seize the same, and also the transporters. His Majesty 
likewise ordered the Duke of Albemarle to send a troop of horse 
guards to be quartered in and about Canterbury, with directions to 
obey the orders of your lordship, or the deputy-lieutenants, to 
prevent the transportation of wool. You are therefore to use your 
utmost endeavours to inform yourself of the persons who practise 
such unlawful transportation, and give order to search for and seize 
all wool found combed, and designed for transportation, apprehend 
the owners, and do all other needful acts to put a stop to its export, 
rendering from time to time an account to the Council Board of 
your proceedings therein. [Zbid. No. 28.] 


Copy of the above. [11 pages. Ibid. No. 29.]

Thos. Covell to Williamson. I received 50/. from Mr. Povey’s

might know the total of your charges; but the Mayor pretended 
that, as bills were outstanding, he could not settle the reckoning 
without wrong to himself or you. I hope to settle it soon, and 
present you the bills. Endorsed by Williamson, “Thetford Elec- 
tion.” [ibid. No. 35.]

East Friesland, and laden with masts, deals, and other Norway 
goods, was put ashore at Wells on Saturday last, and has not a mast 
standing, or a man on board. I request this news to be inserted in 
the Gazette. These parts have been very sickly for the last two 
months, with agues, distempers, and fevers. [S.P. Dom., Car. IJ. 
267, No. 36.] 


Ja. Baskerville to Williamson. A great part of the winter fleet 
has put to sea. There are some ships bound for the Straits, but 
on account of the rumours of a war with Algiers, the merchants 
cannot get seamen to sail them. I have no report of the hurricane 
at Barbadoes, but much reason to believe it, as vessels expected 
3 weeks since have not yet arrived, and wrecks have been discovered 
in the Channel. [Jbid. No. 37.]

hope we shall close the survey. [Jbzd. No. 41.]

Report of the Committee for trade, on the dispute between the 
Bristol merchants and the Merchant Adventurers, Hamburg 
Company and Turkey Company. The former company offers to 
admit the Bristol merchants on their taking the freedom of the 
company, and on payment of 20 marks each; the latter on 
payment of 25/. a man. The Bristol merchants will observe the 
rules, and contribute to the charges of the Turkey Company, in 
trading at Constantinople, Smyrna, and Aleppo; but both companies 
urge that if the Bristol merchants have a distinct charter to trade in 
their regions, it will be destructive to their trade, which will be a 
loss to the whole nation. [S.P. Dom., Car. IT. 267, No. 44.] 


Earl of Castlemaine to Lord [Arlington]. Iam ashamed my little 
intended present has not come to hand, but I doubt not it will come 
safe, as the captain of the ship is a very honest and careful man; 
this made me choose him, though when he left Leghorn, he was 
to call at Naples, and load oil at Gallipoli for England. The per- 
fumes I sent you are the best, and most useful of Italy, being all 
sorts of Florence essences, pomatum and oils of Genoa for the hair, 
Roman powder and perfumed paste, and 2 dozen pairs of the best 
Roman gloves, being 12 pair for your lady, and as many for your- 
self. Pardon the meanness of the present, since it comes from one 
that bears you all the respect imaginable. I shall begin my voyage 
to Spain in 3 weeks, and I expect about midsummer to reach Paris. 
[2 pages. Ibid. No. 45.] 


Mary Carleton to Lord [Arlington]. I was left in debt by an ill 
husband, and not being able to overcome it, I resolved to go with 
the little I had left for Holland, and employ it and myself as I saw 
fit. I took my way for Harwich, but an adversary informed 
Jacom Layfitt, the King’s chief searcher, who would not let me go 
on board the packet unless I gave him 5l, which not having, 
I gave him two of my best rings, till I redeemed them with 
so much money, which I have witnesses to prove. Particulars of 
going aboard. Layfitt, in conversation with Sam. Newton over 
some wine, said that Arlington must be removed, or the King 
would not be safe. Judge if such rebels are good either for King 
or subject, or fit to be employed in his Majesty’s service; I hope 
you will not let this varlet go unpunished, which will oblige the 
oppressed at Harwich. If such serpents are hugged, you will be 
stung to death. With Latin postscript, urging on bended knees 
the granting of her requests. [4 pages. Ibid. No. 46.] 


Henry Ford to Williamson. I received your letter, with an en- 
closure from Council, which I presented to his Excellency. We are 
full of expectation to hear of the meeting and proceedings of 
Parliament. His Excellency and family are in good health, and if 
much exercise and very great industry will contribute to it, I hope 
he will continue so. [Zbid. No. 47.]

Ant. Thorold to Hickes. Col. Stowell died at his house at Ham

Henry Rumbold to Lord Arlington. Mr. Leigh told me that a 
certificate was required from the merchants, before the Consulship 
of Sevile and St. Lucar could be effected. I desired him to peruse 
the one you have in the office; it was under the hands of all the 
able Spanish merchants, dated when Malaga and St. Lucar were 
granted to me, and no complaint has since been made against me ; 
yet if needful, delivering me that, I could get it renewed ; but Leigh 
said Mr. Williamson would not part with it, being your security. 
I know of nothing to justify the taking away of Malaga from me, 
and hope I am not prejudiced by the certificate not being renewed. 
Sevile and St. Lucar being one port, it will be more satisfactory to 
the merchants, who will think the disposing of Malaga an act of 
mine, as being unable to assist in both places; so I shall remain 
better in my reputation, and Colston more quiet in possession of 
Malaga. [Jbid. No. 51.] 


Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. Some vessels arrived from -Bor- 
deaux report that most of the Dutch ships which went there to load 
have gone home empty, fearing an embargo, as the French King 
is expected to break with the Dutch; that the Bishop of Munster 
is beating drums in France and his own country, to enlist soldiers, 
and that it is thought he wil! join with the French. The wind is 
S.S.W., with very violent storms. [Ibid. No. 52.]

Ant. Thorold to Hickes: Arrival of ships named, with wine and 
salt. The great ship of 100 guns building at Brest is ready to be 
launched. Many of the French soldiers and sailors have returned 
home. A vessel of Tynemouth foundered at sea, about 2 or 3 leagues 
from Lyme Harbour, and two of her men were drowned. I thank 
you for the [news] letters, and as Parliament is sitting, I hope they 
will be continued. [S.P. Dom., Car. II. 267, No. 81.] 


Fras. Bellott to Williamson. Arrival and departure of ships to 
and from France, Bilbao, Algiers, &e. [Zbid. No. 82.] 


John Maurice to Williamson. Three vessels named have been 
cast away by the violence of the storm, 5 men drowned, and very 
little of the goods, consisting chiefly of wool, saved; we hear of 
several other wrecks off the coast of Ireland. [Jbid. No. 83.] 


Thos. Holden to Hickes. The Prince William, a Dutch man-of- 
war, arrived with 3 merchantmen under convoy, bound for Bilbao. 
The fleet of merchantmen bound for France put to sea, but were 
forced back, and are now in harbour. The St. George of Dieppe, 
laden with salt for Ireland, which left us 14 days since, has been 
cast away on the coast of Ireland, but her men were saved, and 
some of them have returned to Falmouth for a passage home.

Ralph Hope to Williamson. To-day the new Mayor and officers 
were sworn according to custom, viz.: Thos. Lindzey, tallow- 
chandler, Mayor ; Hugh Capell and Fras. Cater, mercers, Sheriffs ; 
and Wm. Snell, mercer, and Rob. Whittell, dyer, Chamberlains. 
The latter, being an Anabaptist, would not take the oath, and paid 
the fine, when John Winterton, butcher, was chosen in his stead, and 
Jos. Nicholls and Rob. Chandler, Wardens. The two sheriffs were 
very refractory at first, refusing either to swear or pay the fine; 
they offered to take the oath of sheriff, but not of abjuration, 
designing by that trick to evade both office and fine. They were, 
however, frightened out of their plea, by apprehensions of some 
severity from above, which the city were resolved, if possible, to 
procure, rather than be baffled. After all were sworn, they had 
the annual feast, but it was very inferior, the new Mayor not being 
so bountiful as many, though few believe him so wise as wealthy. 

We need not fear the suppression of conventicles, which never so 
abounded, since the principal governors have been favourers of 
them. The Mayor's religion and parts may go together, he being 
judged not over burdened with either; but every man here must 
have his turn, and every dog has his day. [Jbid. No. 89.]

Sir Alex. Frazer to Lord Arlington. Parliament is busy in 
settling grievances. We are impatient to know how your Parlia- 
ment likes the Union; a disaffected party is glad it is so little 
considered as yet. The Lord Commissioner waits with patience, 
but our people are not so wise or patient; business with us is best 
done when least deliberated. The longer your Parliament suspends 
their answer to the Union Treaty, the more scruples will be created 
in the minds of many of us. Yet it is not reasonable that your 
Parliament should be pressed to an answer that would spoil all 
that so many wise persons have been doing in order to this treaty.

but this being a business of concernment, I am not willing to leave 
a stone unturned ; if we agree he will expect 600/. in hand. Mason 
has 400 loads of excellent timber at Maidstone, and I have pre- 
vailed with him to let you have 100 loads for the new ship at 
31. 6s. a load, or you may have the parcel at 55s. or 56s. a load, 
which will be a good pennyworth, and with Sir Roger Twisden’s, 
will furnish the yard here for this year’s expense. 

The instances of amendment of the King’s affairs are many; as 
much work is done for 8d. as was formerly done for 1s., and if any- 
thing be amiss, here is one to set it to rights; whereas before no 
man had power to find fault, and every man did as he liked. I 
wish there was such a man as Commissioner Cox in all the yards. 
We shall consult together and put in writing, before I come to 
London, such things as we judge for the King’s advantage, and 
leave them to your consideration. I have ordered the masters of

[Nov. 6.] Case of the navigation of the River Wey, co. Surrey, showing 
that the Corporation of Guildford obtained an Act to make it navi- 
gable in 1651; that Sir Rich, Weston undertook the navigation, and 
then sold his interest to Mr. Pitson, who finished it in 1653; but 
much dispute arising among the land-owners, it was determined to 
have recourse to Parliament; giving the heads of the Bill tendered 
to the House. [Printed, with MS. additions. Ibid. No. 114.] 
[Nov. 6.] Answer to the above case, controverting some of the allegations, 
showing that Sir Rich. Weston was the first propounder of the 
navigation, but being a royalist, transferred it to Pitson in 1651, to 
pass an Act for it; tracing the progress of the disputes since, and 
proposing that Parliament should give power to some gentlemen 
residing near, to give satisfaction to those that have adventured 
money. With note that Mr. Sandys and Mr. Pitson have had 
one Bill thrown out in the Lords and one in the Commons, and 
Mr. Radcliffe one thrown out in both Houses. [JZbzd. No. 115.] 


[Nov. 6.] Statement of the case relating to the navigation of the river Wey, 
from Guildford to the Thames, made navigable by James Pitson ; 
his interest therein, after the Restoration, was transferred to John 
Ratcliffe, who repaired the river, locks, &., and in Jan. 1665, sold 
his interest to Thos. Cressey. They were impleaded about the 
possession in the Exchequer, but many delays ensued, during which 
Ratcliffe died, leaving four small children, without other provision 
that what he had expended upon the river. With MS. note that a 
speedy end is requested, the Lord Chief Baron having had the cause 
before him 3 years. [Printed. Ibid. No. 116.] 


[Nov. 6.] Heads of a Bill for settling the river Wey in Surrey, and com- 
posing the difference between the contractors and the landowners, 
touching its navigation. [Printed. Ibid. No.117. See Commons’ 
Journals, Vol. IX., p. 103.]

Rich. Watts to [Williamson]. Another Jamaica man has arrived,

Same to the Same. The 2 Spanish ships taken by our priva-

power through having so many men, so they fired them; then the

made themselves very rich. Some of the plate was sold in Deal 


esterday. This was not the May exploit, but was done in August.
